Key references: OSHA 1910 Subpart O (machine guarding, 1910.212), Subpart P (hand and portable powered tools, 1910.242-.244), 1910.23 and 1926 Subpart X (ladders), ANSI B11 series, ANSI/RIA R15.06 and ISO 10218 (robots).
topics.easy: Tools and machines hurt people through the moving parts, flying pieces, electricity and stored pressure. Guard the moving parts, inspect tools before use, use the right tool for the job, and lock out energy before maintenance.
points: Machine hazards: point of operation, power transmission (belts, gears, shafts) and other moving parts; motions (rotating, reciprocating, transverse) and actions (cutting, punching, shearing, bending). Guard types: fixed (preferred - simple and permanent), interlocked, adjustable, self-adjusting. Devices: presence-sensing (light curtains), pullback, restraint, two-hand controls/trips, gates.
Guard requirements: prevent contact, secure (not easily removed), protect from falling objects, create no new hazards, allow safe lubrication.
Hand tools: most injuries come from misuse and poor maintenance (mushroomed chisel heads, cracked handles, wrong tool). Employer is responsible for tool condition, including employee-owned tools.

Power tools: double-insulated or grounded; GFCI on construction sites; never carry by the cord; disconnect before changing blades; guards in place on circular saws; powder-actuated tools require training and licensed operators; compressed air for cleaning limited to < 30 psi with chip guarding (never on the body).

Grinders (1910.215): work rest ≤ 1/8 in. from the wheel; tongue guard ≤ 1/4 in.; ring test wheels before mounting; never exceed rated RPM; stand aside during first minute of startup; face shield plus safety glasses.

Ladders: 4:1 rule (base 1 ft out for every 4 ft of height, about 75.5°); side rails extend 3 ft above the landing; Type IA = 300 lb, Type I = 250 lb, Type II = 225 lb, Type IAA = 375 lb; top step/cap of stepladder not used; inspect before use; three points of contact. New fixed ladders over 24 ft need a ladder safety system or PFAS (1910.28).
Hydraulics: high-pressure fluid injection injuries are surgical emergencies; never check for leaks with hands; relieve pressure and block raised parts (gravity energy) before work.

Robotics: perimeter guarding with interlocked gates, teach mode at reduced speed (≤ 250 mm/s) with enabling device, LOTO for maintenance; collaborative robots use power and force limiting, speed and separation monitoring, hand guiding or safety-rated monitored stop - all based on a risk assessment (ISO/TS 15066).
topics.example: Operators on a packaging line keep opening a guard to clear jams, and one suffers a finger injury. The safety professional finds that the jams happen at a fixed spot. Engineering adds an interlocked access door with a jam-clearing tool slot and adjusts the infeed guide so that jams drop by 80%. Training alone had not stopped the behavior because the guard was blocking the job.
tips: When workers bypass guards, the BEST answer fixes the reason (design the task so the guard is not in the way) rather than only disciplining.
Fixed guards are generally the preferred guard type; light curtains are devices, not guards.
Grinder numbers: 1/8 in. work rest, 1/4 in. tongue guard - learn them together.
Ladder angle calculations use the 4:1 rule and the Pythagorean theorem (ladder length = √(height² + base²) + 3 ft extension).
topics.yates: Ch. 25 Construction Safety (tools, ladders), p. 567; Ch. 29 Walking and Working Surfaces, p. 657
subs: Hand tools
Most hand-tool injuries come from misuse and poor maintenance.
Employer is responsible for safe condition of all tools, including employee-owned.
Hazards: mushroomed chisel heads, cracked handles, wrong tool, dull blades; inspect, dress or remove from service.
Use spark-resistant tools near flammables; tether tools at height.
Power tools
Electric, pneumatic, hydraulic, powder-actuated and fuel-powered tools.
Electrical: double-insulated or grounded; GFCI on construction sites; never carry by the cord or yank to disconnect; disconnect before changing blades/bits.
Guards stay on (circular saw lower guard); anti-kickback pawls and riving knives on saws.
Pneumatic: secure hoses, safety clips on tools; compressed air for cleaning < 30 psi with chip guarding, never on the body.
Powder-actuated tools: trained operators, never point at anyone, wait 30 s after misfire.
Locking triggers/continuous-run features need dead-man or automatic shutoff; sequential-trip nailers reduce injuries.
Ladders
Portable and fixed ladders (1910.23, 1926 Subpart X).
4:1 rule (~75°); side rails extend 3 ft above the landing; secure top and bottom; three points of contact.
Duty ratings: IAA 375 lb, IA 300 lb, I 250 lb, II 225 lb, III 200 lb.
Do not use the top step/cap of a stepladder; non-conductive side rails near electricity; inspect by a competent person; remove defective ladders.
Rungs 10-14 in. apart; a ladder or stairway is required at a break in elevation of 19 in. or more (construction).
Grinders (abrasive wheels)
Bench, pedestal and portable grinders can burst and throw fragments.
Work rest ≤ 1/8 in. from wheel; tongue guard ≤ 1/4 in.
Ring-test wheels before mounting; never exceed the rated RPM; stand aside during start-up.
Safety glasses plus face shield; side guards in place.
Grinder clearances 1/8 in. and 1/4 in. appear often.
Hydraulics
Hydraulic presses, jacks, lifts and lines store high pressure and gravity energy.
Relieve pressure (bleed lines, accumulators) and block raised parts before maintenance - part of LOTO.
Never search for leaks with hands; use cardboard. Fluid injection injuries are surgical emergencies.
Inspect hoses and fittings; rated components only.
Robotics and emerging technology
Industrial robots, cobots and other new technologies (AI, AR, digital twins, data mining).

Robots: perimeter guarding with interlocked gates, light curtains/pressure mats, accessible e-stops; ANSI/RIA R15.06 and ISO 10218 require risk assessment; LOTO for maintenance; teach mode at reduced speed.
Cobots share workspace with humans (ISO/TS 15066): power and force limiting, speed and separation monitoring, hand guiding, safety-rated monitored stop.
AI: computer vision for PPE compliance, NLP of safety reports, wearables for fatigue; concerns - privacy, bias, over-reliance; AI supports, does not replace compliance.
Digital twin = virtual replica to simulate hazards; AR = real-time hazard overlays; predictive analytics/data mining find leading indicators (ANSI/ASSP Z16.1).
Shared workspace with humans = cobot; virtual replica = digital twin; real-time visual overlay = AR.
Machine guarding requirements
OSHA 1910.212 general requirements and Subpart O.
Guards must prevent contact, be secured, protect from falling objects, create no new hazard, allow safe lubrication and not obstruct visibility (e.g., polycarbonate).
Point-of-operation guarding on presses, shears, saws; power-transmission parts < 7 ft enclosed.
Guard types: fixed (preferred), interlocked (stops machine when opened), adjustable, self-adjusting; devices: light curtains, mats, pullback, restraint, two-hand controls.
Woodworking: circular saw guard covers blade above table; radial arm saw returns automatically.
CSP prefers engineering controls (guards, interlocks) over PPE.
mcq: James must change a hydraulic hose on a press used earlier that day. The press is powered off, but he does not bleed residual pressure before loosening the fitting, and a burst of fluid causes an injection injury to his forearm. What should he have done before loosening any fittings?
Removed the drip pan from under the couplings, then powered off the press
Opened the reservoir vent cap and loosened the fittings immediately
Raised the hose 6 in. so gravity could drain the fluid
Shut off and locked out the press, then relieved and verified dissipation of stored hydraulic pressure
LOTO covers stored energy: residual hydraulic pressure must be relieved and verified as zero. High-pressure fluid injection injuries are surgical emergencies.
On a bench grinder, what is the maximum distance allowed between the wheel periphery and the adjustable tongue guard (upper peripheral guard)?
OSHA 1910.215 sets the tongue guard at 1/4 in. or less and the work rest at 1/8 in. or less. Mixing up the two is a classic trap; remember 'rest 1/8, tongue 1/4'.

A worker mounts a new grinding wheel that fits the arbor correctly but has not been ring tested. When the grinder is started, the wheel shatters. Which action would have MOST effectively prevented this?
Inspecting and ring testing the wheel before mounting
Wearing a face shield and gloves during startup
Running the grinder at full speed for 10 minutes before use
Reducing the tool rest clearance

1910.215(d)(1) requires wheels to be inspected and sound (ring) tested before mounting to detect cracks. PPE only reduces the injury after failure. Standing aside during the 1-minute run-up is also good practice.

A robotic welding cell is running in automatic mode. The operator powers off the teach pendant, assumes the robot cannot move, and reaches between the arm and fixture to clear a jam. The robot cycles and pinches his hand. Which procedure would MOST effectively have prevented the injury?
Keep the pendant off and wear cut-resistant gloves when reaching in
Lock out the robot's main power (and other energy sources) and verify zero energy before entering
Use single-block mode to jog the arm away without powering off the controller
Press the pendant E-stop and rely on it to de-energize the robot
Entering the robot envelope for jam clearing requires hazardous energy control. E-stops and pendants are control-circuit devices, not energy-isolating devices.
A robotic cell has interlocked gates, but workers prop a gate open with a tool so they can make minor adjustments without stopping the robot. What is the BEST corrective measure?
Install cameras to monitor worker behavior
Install tamper-resistant interlocks and investigate why workers feel the need to bypass, retraining as needed
Post signs telling workers not to enter
Reduce the robot's operating speed
Defeat-resistant interlocks restore the engineering control. Addressing the production pressure behind the bypass prevents it from recurring.

A roofer shoots his thumb with a pneumatic nailer set to contact (bump) actuation. He was holding the trigger down and tapping the nose on the shingles to drive multiple nails. The tool was in good working order. What is the BEST recommendation?
Issue verbal discipline for the injury
Require puncture-resistant gloves
Tell the worker to go slower
Switch to nailers with a full sequential trigger
NIOSH found full sequential triggers cut nail gun injury risk roughly in half compared with contact triggers. This is an engineering fix; gloves, pace and discipline are weaker.
A technician leans a straight ladder against a wall to reach a platform 15 ft high. The base is only 2 ft from the wall, and the ladder shifts during use. What is the proper correction?
Reposition the ladder using the 4-to-1 rule (base about 3.75 ft out), on firm footing, and secure it
Have a coworker hold the base
Use a shorter ladder
Tie off the top but leave the base unsecured
The 4:1 rule (1 ft out for every 4 ft of working length, about 75 degrees) gives stability. For 15 ft that is about 3.75 ft; the side rails should also extend 3 ft above the landing.
A ladder is used to access a roof 20 ft high. It will be set at a 75-degree angle and must extend 3 ft above the roof edge. What ladder length is needed?
20 ft
22 ft
24 ft
26 ft
Length to the eave = 20 / sin 75 = 20 / 0.966 = 20.7 ft; adding 3 ft gives 23.7 ft, so a 24-ft ladder is needed. Forgetting the 3-ft extension gives about 21 ft.
Operators on a conveyor repeatedly remove an interlocked guard to clear jams. What is the BEST long-term solution?
Train operators and enforce discipline for violations
Install a camera to monitor compliance
Post warning signs about removing guards
Modify the design to provide a jam-clearing tool or access point that does not require removing the guard (or eliminate the jam cause)
Fixing the design removes the reason to bypass the guard. Discipline, cameras and signs treat the symptom and are weaker controls.
During a tool crib inspection, several cold chisels and drift pins are found with mushroomed heads. What is the BEST action?
Issue them only to experienced workers
Require safety glasses whenever they are used
Remove them from service until the heads are dressed or the tools replaced
Tape the heads to contain fragments
OSHA 1926.301 and 1910.242 require unsafe hand tools to be removed from service. Mushroomed heads can shatter and throw fragments when struck.

topics.title: Benchmarking and Gap Analysis
topics.bp: Compare performance against established benchmarks (e.g., gap analysis)
topics.definition: Benchmarking is the systematic comparison of an organization's safety performance, processes and practices with a reference point - industry averages, best-in-class peers, internal sites or a standard. Gap analysis identifies the difference between the current state and the desired state and the reasons for that difference.
topics.easy: Benchmarking tells you where you stand compared with others. Gap analysis tells you how far you are from where you want to be and why. Together they show what to fix first.
points: Types: internal (site vs site), competitive (same industry peers, e.g., BLS rates by NAICS code), functional/generic (best practice from any industry), performance (metrics such as TRIR, DART) and process (how work is done).
Common benchmarks: BLS injury and illness rates by NAICS code, EMR (1.0 = industry average), industry association data, ISO 45001/ANSI Z10 requirements, OSHA VPP criteria.

Gap analysis steps: define the desired state (standard, benchmark, objective) → assess the current state (audit, data, interviews) → identify and quantify the gaps → analyze causes → prioritize → action plan with owners, resources and dates → monitor.
Compare like with like: same NAICS code, same rate formula (200,000 hours), same time period, similar size.
A gap is a starting point for root-cause thinking, not the conclusion. Do not 'fix' a gap by changing how cases are recorded.
topics.example: A plant's DART rate is 2.1 and the BLS rate for its NAICS code is 1.4. The gap analysis shows that 70% of DART cases are hand injuries at two press lines, where guarding is older than the rest of the plant. The action plan targets guarding upgrades at those lines first.
tips: The next step after finding a gap is almost always 'analyze the cause and create an action plan', not setting a slogan goal.
Recognize that benchmarking against BLS data must use the correct NAICS code and the 200,000-hour base.
An EMR above 1.0 means worse than the industry average and higher premiums.
topics.yates: Ch. 36 Measuring Safety and Health Performance, p. 797; Ch. 37 Safety Program Auditing Techniques, p. 818
subs: Benchmarking

Benchmarking compares your safety performance against a reference point so you know where you stand. The reference can be regulatory, industry, internal or best-in-class, and it must fit your risks, size, processes and safety maturity.
Regulatory/national: BLS injury and illness rates by NAICS code; OSHA recordkeeping formulas (TRIR, DART).
Industry: NSC annual averages and best-in-class statistics, trade association data.
Internal: your best site, best year or an aspirational company target.
Best-in-class/world-class: leading organizations in or outside your sector.
Process (functional) benchmarking compares how a task is done (e.g., how a peer runs MOC), not just the outcome number.
The guide states regulatory benchmarks are 'legally required' (e.g., keep TRIR at or below the BLS average) - in fact OSHA sets no required TRIR; BLS averages are comparison data only.
Pick the benchmark that is relevant (same NAICS, size, hazards). A small specialty shop compared to a national all-industry average is a weak benchmark.
Gap analysis
Gap analysis is a systematic comparison of current performance (or current program) against a benchmark or standard, followed by finding why the gap exists and closing it with an action plan.
Steps: select benchmark -> collect and validate data -> compare and quantify gap -> analyze root causes -> action plan -> engage management and workers -> communicate -> monitor and adjust.
Quantify clearly: 'Our TRIR is 2.5, industry average 1.6, best-in-class 1.0' -> gap to average = 0.9 (56% above).
Program gap analysis: compare your SMS element by element against ISO 45001 or ANSI Z10 clauses before certification.
Use both lagging (DART, lost-time rate) and leading (near-miss reports, observations) data.
Raise the benchmark as performance improves (continuous improvement).
A gap analysis is done BEFORE implementing a new management system - it tells you what is missing. The first step is choosing an appropriate benchmark/criteria.
Data collection and validation
Benchmarking is only as good as the data. Records must be accurate, complete and comparable (same definitions, same time period, same hours basis).
Sources: OSHA 300/300A logs, audit results, training records, workers' comp claims, observation data.
Under-reporting makes lagging data look better than reality - validate against first-aid logs, clinic visits and comp claims.
Normalize to exposure: rates per 200,000 hours, not raw counts.
Compare like with like: same NAICS code, similar size and work type.
A low injury rate with very few near-miss reports suggests under-reporting, not excellent performance.
Root cause of performance gaps
Numbers show a gap exists; analysis shows why. Look for system causes such as training, leadership, equipment, procedures or reporting culture.
Tools: interviews, 5 Whys, fishbone diagrams, audit findings.
ANSI/ASSP Z16.1 and Z10 support analyzing causes, not just measuring outcomes.
Segment the data (by site, shift, department, task) to find hot spots - Pareto helps here.
Communicating and sustaining benchmark results
Share results and the improvement plan widely and track progress over time with dashboards; technology makes benchmarking visible at all levels.
Communicate through dashboards, reports, toolbox talks and digital platforms - transparency builds buy-in.
Review gaps in management meetings and safety committees.
Document results; they are evidence of improvement during audits.
EHS software automates data collection and visualization (NSC best practice).
mcq: Your plant's DART rate is 2.1. The industry benchmark (same NAICS) is 1.4. Management asks what to do next. What is the BEST next step?
Set a goal of matching the benchmark next year and announce it
Analyze the causes of the 0.7 gap (injury types, tasks, controls) and build an action plan with owners and dates
Change the recordkeeping method to reduce DART cases
Start an incentive program for zero injuries

Benchmarking shows where you stand; gap analysis must then find why the gap exists and drive an action plan with owners, dates and measures. Goals without causes, recordkeeping changes and incentives do not close the gap.

You manage safety operations at a construction company aiming to reduce workplace incidents by comparing your safety performance WITH industry leaders. What benchmarking procedure would you initially follow?
Internal Benchmarking - Analyze safety performance within your own teams first.
Functional Benchmarking - Examine safety practices in different industries.
Competitive Benchmarking - Directly compare safety incident rates against similar companies.
Generic Benchmarking - Benchmark against unrelated industries to find innovative safety practices.
Comparing incident rates directly against similar companies/industry leaders is competitive benchmarking. Internal compares your own units; functional/generic look at other industries.
As a safety coordinator in a logistics company, you're tasked with improving vehicle incident rates. Which benchmarking approach would provide the MOST practical insights?
Performance Benchmarking - Measuring specific safety processes against industry best practices.
Strategic Benchmarking - Evaluating long-term safety strategies of competitors.
Product Benchmarking - Comparing safety equipment with competitors' offerings.
Financial Benchmarking - Focusing strictly on financial investment in safety.
Performance benchmarking compares specific measurable processes (e.g., vehicle incident rates, driver programs) against best practice, giving the most practical, actionable insight.
The main purpose of benchmarking in safety program management is to:
Compare safety budgets with competitors
Eliminate need for management review
Replace internal audits
Identify best practices and performance gaps for improvement
The purpose of benchmarking is to identify best practices and performance gaps that drive improvement; it does not replace audits or management review.
Benchmarking is a/an
Form of injury/illness measurement used by large corporations
Process to develop an annual safety and health budget
Process to compare company safety program to industry peers
Systematic approach to organizational change
Benchmarking is the process of comparing your safety program and performance to industry peers or recognized leaders.

Plant A recorded 6 recordable cases in 300,000 hours worked. Plant B recorded 4 recordable cases in 160,000 hours. The industry (BLS) TRIR benchmark for the same NAICS code is 3.0. Which statement is correct?
Plant A performs worse because it had more recordable cases
Plant B has the highest rate (5.0); both plants exceed the 3.0 benchmark
Both plants are below the industry benchmark
Rates cannot be compared between plants of different sizes
TRIR = cases x 200,000 / hours: A = 6 x 200,000 / 300,000 = 4.0; B = 4 x 200,000 / 160,000 = 5.0. Both exceed 3.0. Trap: comparing raw counts instead of normalized rates.
In an EHS management system context, a gap analysis compares:
The organization's current practices and performance with a desired state such as a standard, regulation or benchmark
The safety budget with the operations budget
Last year's injury count with this year's injury count
Worker perception survey results with supervisor survey results only
Gap analysis = current state vs. desired/required state (e.g., ISO 45001 clauses, OSHA requirements, best-in-class benchmark); the gaps become the basis of the action plan.
Senior management decides to pursue ISO 45001 certification for a site that already has an OSHA-compliant safety program. What should the safety professional do FIRST?
Train all employees on ISO 45001 clauses
Schedule the certification audit with a registrar
Rewrite all safety procedures in ISO format
Perform a gap analysis of the existing program against ISO 45001 requirements
A gap analysis first shows which requirements are already met and which are missing, so effort and resources go to real gaps. Scheduling, rewriting or training before knowing the gaps is premature.
A safety manager wants to compare her plant's DART rate with national data. Which approach gives the MOST valid benchmark comparison?
Compare the plant's total number of DART cases with the national number of DART cases
Compare the plant's DART rate with BLS data for the same NAICS industry code, establishment size and year
Compare the plant's DART rate with the all-industry national average
Compare the plant's DART rate with a competitor's TRIR

Valid benchmarking compares like with like: the same metric, normalized to hours (rate), for the same industry, size class and period. Raw counts, all-industry averages or different metrics distort the comparison.
A company with 12 plants compares lockout/tagout audit scores and practices among its own sites to identify the best-performing site's methods and spread them. This is an example of:
Competitive benchmarking
Generic benchmarking
Internal benchmarking
Strategic benchmarking
Comparing performance and practices among units within the same organization is internal benchmarking; data are easy to obtain and comparable, but the view is limited to company practice.

topics.title: Performance Standards and Action Planning
topics.bp: Analyze performance standards to determine plan of action
topics.definition: Performance standards are the defined expectations for safety performance - regulatory requirements, consensus standards, company policies and objectives. Action planning turns gaps against those standards into specific, resourced, time-bound actions with accountable owners.
topics.easy: First decide what 'good' looks like and how you will measure it. Then write a plan that says who will do what, by when, with what money and how you will know it worked.
points: SMART objectives: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
Action plan contents: problem/gap statement, objective, actions, owner (one accountable person), resources/budget, due dates, success measures, status tracking and verification of effectiveness.
Prioritize by risk (severity × likelihood), legal requirements, cost and feasibility; quick wins plus long-term fixes.
Performance standards hierarchy: law/regulation (minimum) → consensus standards (ANSI, NFPA, ISO) → company standards (often stricter) → site procedures.
PDCA ties it together: Plan (objectives, plans), Do (implement), Check (measure, audit), Act (correct and improve).
topics.example: After an audit shows that 30% of forklift operators have expired evaluations, the safety manager writes an objective: 'All 120 operators will have a current evaluation by March 31; monthly status report to the plant manager.' Supervisors are named as owners for their crews, and trainer time is budgeted.
tips: Choose the answer that contains measurable criteria and a deadline.
'Improve safety' or 'zero injuries' without measures are weak objectives on the exam.
Action plans need verification of effectiveness - closing an action is not the same as solving the problem.
topics.yates: Ch. 31 Safety Management System, p. 717; Ch. 36 Measuring Safety and Health Performance
subs: Performance standards

A performance standard defines the expected level of performance (an outcome, rate or activity level) that people and programs are measured against. Analyzing performance against the standard tells you what action plan is needed.
Examples: 100% of corrective actions closed within 30 days; 95% training completion; TRIR below 1.5; 4 safety observations per supervisor per month.

Regulatory 'performance' standards state the required outcome but let the employer choose the method (e.g., PSM, General Duty); 'specification' standards prescribe exact means (e.g., 42-in. guardrail).
Standards should be measurable, achievable and tied to accountability (performance reviews).
ANSI/ASSP Z16.1 provides consistent metric definitions for comparing performance.
If a question asks why a facility met all OSHA specification standards but still had a fatality, the answer usually involves missing performance/management system elements.
Action planning
An action plan converts a gap or objective into specific tasks with owners, resources, deadlines and measures, and is managed through PDCA.
Each action: what, who (single named owner), by when, resources, how success is verified.
Objectives must be SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
Prioritize actions by risk (severity x likelihood) and regulatory urgency.
Track in an action register; review status in management meetings; escalate overdue items.
'Reduce injuries' is not SMART; 'Reduce forklift-pedestrian near misses at Plant 2 by 50% by Dec 31 through separated walkways' is.
SMART objectives
SMART is the standard test for whether an objective is usable for planning and accountability.
Specific - clear scope; Measurable - a metric; Achievable - realistic with resources; Relevant - tied to key risks; Time-bound - a deadline.
ISO 45001 clause 6.2 requires OH&S objectives that are measurable (if practicable), monitored, communicated and updated.
Mix leading and lagging objectives.
Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) cycle
PDCA (Deming/Shewhart cycle) is the engine of continual improvement in every modern management system standard.
Plan: policy, objectives, hazard identification, risk assessment, actions.
Do: implement, train, communicate, provide resources.
Check: monitor, measure, audit, investigate incidents.
Act: management review, corrective action, improve - then repeat.
ISO 45001, ISO 14001 and ANSI Z10 are all structured on PDCA.
Audits and incident investigations are 'Check'; management review and corrective action are 'Act'.
Accountability and performance review
Performance standards only work if people are held accountable and results are reviewed regularly.
Tie supervisor and manager appraisals to safety activities (leading) not only injury counts.
Avoid incentive programs that reward 'zero injuries' - they suppress reporting (OSHA 1904.35 prohibits retaliation for reporting).
Management review at least annually or after serious incidents.
mcq: Which safety objective is written in the BEST SMART format?
Improve safety culture this year
Reduce hand injuries
Complete machine-guarding risk assessments on all 24 presses by June 30 and close 90% of high-risk actions by September 30
Everyone will work safely
SMART = Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Only C states a scope (24 presses), measures (assessments, 90% closure) and deadlines; the others are vague slogans.

A cross-functional team (engineering, operations, maintenance and safety) meets before a new press is installed to systematically identify its hazards, assess the severity and likelihood of each, and select risk controls (guarding, interlocks, PPE). Which phase of the Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) cycle does this activity represent?
Plan
Do
Check
Act
Identifying hazards, assessing risk and selecting controls before implementation is planning (ISO 45001 clause 6). Do = implementing the controls; Check = monitoring; Act = improving.
Safety data are reviewed but the checklist and training are never changed. Which PDCA phase is failing?
Plan
Do
Check
Act
Reviewing data is Check; changing the system (checklists, training) based on findings is Act. If nothing ever changes, the Act phase is failing.
A program evaluation determines that training, audit, and inspection goals were met but incident rates remain unchanged. What should be the next step?
Reassess whether indicators measure true system effectiveness
Close the program review
Reduce training frequency
Discontinue leading indicators

When activity targets are met but outcomes do not improve, the indicators may not measure what actually drives risk. Reassess and realign indicators rather than closing the review or cutting activity.
A program effectiveness review finds that objectives were achieved, but employee engagement scores remain low. What should management prioritize?
Develop new technical controls only
Enhance leadership visibility and communication initiatives
Reduce reporting transparency
Focus solely on lagging indicators
Meeting numeric objectives with low engagement signals a culture gap; visible leadership and two-way communication address engagement. Technical controls alone or lagging-only focus do not.
How does a Safety Manager's input in the development of a corporate business plan influence safety management and performance goals?
It ensures the allocation of resources to achieve a zero-injury target.
It identifies areas for improvement and sets specific, measurable safety objectives.
It integrates safety goals into the overall business strategy and resource allocation.
It determines the company's financial projections and resource allocation, with no direct impact on safety goals.
Safety input to the business plan integrates safety goals into the overall strategy and resource allocation, so safety is resourced like any other business objective.
Safety goals for any organization should possess the following characteristics:
They should be sufficiently broad to ensure their attainment.
They should be established by the executive management of the organization.
They should be based on injury rates.
Achievable and measurable.
Effective safety goals must be achievable and measurable (SMART). Broad goals cannot be tracked, and injury rates alone are lagging measures.
In PDCA, which step focuses on implementing processes and operational controls?
Plan
Do
Check
Act
Do = implementing the plan: operational controls, training, communication and procedures.
Following an audit, a safety manager writes an action plan to close 15 identified gaps. Which set of elements MUST the action plan contain to be effective?
A list of the gaps and the auditor's name
A description of each gap and a general statement that it will be fixed
Specific actions, a responsible person for each, target completion dates, required resources and a method to verify completion
The audit score and a comparison with last year's score

An action plan turns findings into accountable work: what will be done, by whom, by when, with what resources, and how completion/effectiveness will be verified. Lists without owners and dates rarely get closed.
A gap analysis identifies these deficiencies, but the budget will fund only one this quarter. Which should be addressed FIRST?
Outdated safety bulletin board postings
Missing fall protection at an unguarded 4.5 m (15 ft) mezzanine edge used daily
Training records stored in two different databases
Safety committee minutes not posted on time
Action plans are prioritized by risk (severity x likelihood). A daily exposure to a potentially fatal fall outranks administrative and documentation gaps.

topics.title: EHS Culture: Measure, Analyze and Improve
topics.bp: Determine how to measure, analyze, and improve EHS culture
topics.definition: Safety culture is the shared values, beliefs, attitudes and behaviors that determine how safety is actually managed in an organization - 'how we do things here when no one is watching'. Safety climate is a snapshot of employee perceptions of that culture at a point in time.
topics.easy: Culture is what people really do and believe, not what the policy says. You measure it by asking and watching, look for gaps between what managers think and what workers experience, and improve it through visible leadership, involvement and trust.
points: Measurement tools: perception surveys (anonymous, repeated over time), focus groups, interviews, observation, behavior-based safety data, near-miss reporting rates, participation in safety activities, corrective action closure.
Look for perception gaps between management and front-line responses; follow up surveys with focus groups to understand why.
Maturity models: Hudson ladder (pathological → reactive → calculative → proactive → generative); DuPont Bradley curve (reactive → dependent → independent → interdependent).

Characteristics of a strong culture: visible management commitment, employee involvement, just culture (fair accountability, no blame for honest errors), open reporting without retaliation, learning from incidents, stop-work authority.

Behavior-based safety (BBS): identify critical behaviors, observe and measure, give feedback (positive reinforcement), improve barriers. ABC model: Antecedent → Behavior → Consequence; consequences that are soon, certain and positive drive behavior most.
Culture killers: incentives tied to 'zero injuries' (suppress reporting), punishing reporting, production pressure, inconsistent discipline.
topics.example: A survey shows 92% of managers agree that 'production never comes before safety', but only 41% of operators agree. Focus groups reveal that supervisors praise crews for meeting quotas but rarely mention safety. Leadership starts daily safety conversations, adds safety metrics to supervisors' reviews, and repeats the survey a year later; the operator score rises to 68%.
tips: Culture questions usually reward involvement, communication and leadership by example over discipline or posters.
A rise in near-miss reports after a campaign is usually a positive sign of reporting culture.
BBS feedback should be immediate, specific and positive; public correction or write-ups are distractors.
topics.yates: Ch. 21 Management Theories, p. 505; Ch. 36 Measuring Safety and Health Performance
subs: Measuring EHS culture
Culture is the shared values, beliefs, attitudes and behaviors about safety. It is measured with several methods together, because no single tool captures it.
Safety climate/perception surveys (validated, anonymous) - climate is a snapshot of culture.

NSC 8 safety climate factors: management commitment, leadership communication, employee involvement, peer support, hazard recognition and reporting, safety training, supervisor support, accountability.
Behavioral observations (PPE use, procedure compliance).
Leading indicator review: near-miss reports, meeting participation, corrective-action closure.
Focus groups and interviews; system review of committees, communications and leadership visibility.
Best answer for 'how to assess culture' combines surveys + observations + leading indicators + interviews, not one tool.
Analyzing EHS culture
Analysis turns survey and indicator results into understanding of where and why culture is weak.
Gap analysis against ANSI/ASSP best practice and NSC benchmarks.
Segment data by department, shift, role - management often rates culture higher than front-line workers (perception gap).
Root cause tools (5 Whys, fishbone) for under-reporting or low engagement.
Benchmark against NSC national/sector data.
A large gap between management and worker survey scores signals a leadership communication/credibility problem.
Improving EHS culture
Culture improves through visible leadership, real worker engagement, open blame-free communication, empowerment and accountability, repeated through PDCA.
Leaders set expectations, lead by example, are visible on the floor.
Involve workers in committees, hazard ID, investigations and solutions; recognize positive behavior.
Share survey results and action plans; remove barriers to near-miss reporting.
Empower stop-work authority; train on the 'why'.
Tie manager performance reviews to culture goals; re-measure to track progress.
Model answer: measure (surveys, observations, indicators) -> analyze (gap/root cause) -> leadership-driven participative improvement plan.
Safety culture vs. safety climate
Culture is deep and slow to change (values, assumptions); climate is the measurable surface perception at a point in time.
Climate surveys measure perceptions now; culture change takes years.
Schein: artifacts, espoused values, basic assumptions.
Repeat surveys (e.g., every 1-2 years) to trend climate.
Safety culture maturity models
Maturity models describe stages organizations move through toward a generative culture.
Hudson ladder: pathological -> reactive -> calculative -> proactive -> generative.
DuPont Bradley Curve: reactive -> dependent -> independent -> interdependent.
Higher maturity = workers own safety, reporting is valued, leading indicators drive decisions.
'We do safety because we were caught' = reactive; 'safety is how we do business' = generative.
Just culture and reporting
A just culture separates honest error from reckless behavior so people report errors and near misses without fear, while accountability for reckless acts remains.
Human error -> console/fix system; at-risk behavior -> coach; reckless behavior -> discipline.
Blame-and-retrain cycles suppress reporting and hide system causes.
OSHA 1904.35: employees must have a reasonable reporting procedure and be protected from retaliation.
Behavior-based safety (BBS)
BBS uses peer observation and feedback on critical safe behaviors to reinforce safe practices and generate leading data.
Elements: identify critical behaviors, observe, give feedback, analyze data, remove barriers.
ABC model: Antecedent -> Behavior -> Consequence; consequences that are soon, certain and positive drive behavior most.
BBS must not replace hazard control - fix conditions first (hierarchy of controls).
BBS that blames workers while ignoring system hazards is a weak answer.
mcq: Organizational culture greatly affects implementation of a safety program, and each organization has its own culture. What is one way to measure safety culture improvement?
Regular safety perception surveys of all workers
Implementation of OSHA safety and health guidelines
Number of OSHA violations
Implement a formal Pareto Perception Analysis For All

Perception surveys of all workers, repeated over time, directly measure shared beliefs and attitudes, i.e., culture. Citation counts and guideline adoption are compliance measures, not culture measures.
A perception survey shows 92% of managers agree that 'safety is never compromised for production,' but only 41% of front-line workers agree. What is the BEST interpretation?
The workers misunderstood the question
A perception gap exists; investigate through focus groups and look at how production pressure is handled in practice
The culture is strong because management is committed
Repeat the survey until results match

A large manager-worker perception gap is a key culture finding. Follow up with focus groups/interviews to learn how production pressure is handled in practice; dismissing or repeating the survey ignores the signal.
Which of the following is NOT one of the five maturity levels in Hudson's safety culture maturity ladder (based on Reason and Westrum)?
Pathological
Reactive
Predictive
Generative
Hudson's ladder levels are Pathological, Reactive, Calculative, Proactive and Generative. 'Predictive' is not a level.
A "Just Culture" differs from a "Blame Culture" by:
Ignoring unsafe acts
Making safety optional
Allowing repeat violations without consequence
Focusing on learning and system improvements rather than punishment
A just culture separates honest error from reckless behavior, emphasizing learning and system fixes with fair accountability; it neither ignores unsafe acts nor blames by default.
Which of the following is the best indicator of a strong safety culture?
Compliance with documentation
High rate of near-miss reporting and visible management response
Low number of hazard reports
Strict enforcement without feedback
High near-miss reporting combined with visible management response shows trust and engagement. Low hazard reports usually mean underreporting, not safety.
A safety team notices that workers consistently bypass a machine guard to clear jams, even after reminders. Which BBS-based strategy should be prioritized to improve safe behavior?
Increase the number of disciplinary actions for non-compliance
Replace supervisors who fail to enforce the rule
Investigate workflow and equipment design to remove barriers to safe behavior
Post more signs and distribute reminder emails weekly
Repeated guard bypassing despite reminders points to a system barrier (jam frequency, design, workflow). Remove the reason for the at-risk behavior; discipline and signs do not address the cause.
A construction site has gone 60 days without a recordable injury, but unsafe shortcuts continue. Which BBS strategy best shifts focus to positive behaviors?
Track and reward safe behaviors like pre-task planning, safety suggestions or PPE compliance
Give gift cards only when there are no OSHA recordables
Focus future training on incident response
Publicly warn workers about disciplinary actions for violations
Rewarding injury-free outcomes encourages underreporting. Recognizing measurable safe behaviors (pre-task planning, suggestions, PPE use) reinforces the behaviors that prevent incidents.
As an organization's culture transitions towards a safety-centric approach, which indicators should stakeholders expect to observe?
Increased safety audits, revised disciplinary program, and mandatory performance goals.
Reduction in injury reports, fewer regulatory citations, and higher profits.
Additional safety professionals, more formal training, and monetary incentives
Management support, open communication, and company-wide participation.
A culture shift shows up as management support, open communication and company-wide participation. Fewer injuries and citations are lagging results, and more audits or incentives are inputs.

During a routine observation, you notice a worker using a grinder without safety glasses. When asked, he says, "I've done this for 10 years and never had a problem." What is the best BBS-based response?
Write him up to show accountability
Engage in a one-on-one conversation about risk perception and eye injury potential
Ignore the behavior since he's experienced
Add signage near the grinder as a reminder
BBS uses respectful one-on-one feedback that addresses risk perception ('never had a problem' is optimism bias). Write-ups or ignoring the behavior do not change beliefs; signs are weak controls.
An organization that openly shares lessons learned from incidents across departments is demonstrating:
Generative culture focused on learning and prevention
Reactive safety culture
Calculative culture based on data alone
Pathological culture that hides problems
Openly sharing lessons learned across the organization is a hallmark of a generative (learning) culture; pathological cultures hide problems and reactive cultures act only after events.

topics.title: Incident Investigation and Root Cause Analysis
topics.bp: Determine appropriate incident investigation techniques (root causes) and apply corrective actions
topics.definition: Incident investigation is the systematic process of collecting facts about an incident, determining direct, contributing and root causes, and implementing corrective actions that prevent recurrence. Root causes are the underlying management-system failures that allowed the immediate causes to exist.
topics.easy: Ask what happened, how it happened and why - then keep asking why until you reach something the organization can fix in its systems. Blame finds a person; investigation finds the fix.
points: Steps: secure the scene and care for the injured → preserve evidence → gather information (people, positions, parts, paper - the 4 Ps) → interview witnesses individually and promptly → build a timeline → analyze causes → develop corrective actions → report → track to closure → verify effectiveness → share lessons.
Interview tips: private setting, explain the purpose is prevention not blame, open-ended questions ('Tell me what you saw'), let the witness talk, review notes with the witness.
Causes: direct/immediate (unsafe act or condition, energy release), contributing, root (system: training, procedures, design, supervision, management commitment).

Techniques: 5 Whys, fishbone/Ishikawa (people, methods, machines, materials, environment, management), fault tree analysis, events and causal factors charting, change analysis, barrier analysis, MORT, multilinear events sequencing (MES), TapRooT, SCAT (systematic cause analysis technique), Swiss cheese model, bow-tie.

Accident theories: Heinrich domino (unsafe acts), Bird/Loss Causation (lack of control → basic causes → immediate causes → incident → loss), Reason's Swiss cheese (aligned holes in defenses), energy transfer (Haddon).
Corrective actions should follow the hierarchy of controls; 'retrain' and 'discipline' alone are weak. Assign owners and dates and verify that the actions work.
topics.example: An operator's hand is caught in a conveyor while clearing a jam. A 5-Whys analysis shows the guard was removed because jams were frequent, jams were frequent because a new box size was introduced without changing the guides, and the box change was never reviewed under MOC. Corrective actions: adjust the guides, install an interlocked access door and add packaging changes to the MOC procedure.
tips: 'The worker didn't follow the procedure' is a symptom - the BEST answer keeps asking why.
First action at an incident scene: care for the injured and make the scene safe.
Interview witnesses separately and as soon as possible.
Fishbone = categorize causes; FTA = top-down logic; FMEA = bottom-up component failures.
topics.yates: Ch. 22 Accident Causation and Investigation Techniques, p. 515
subs: Incident investigation process
A systematic, standards-based process (OSHA Incident Investigation guide, ANSI Z10, NSC) to learn why an incident happened and prevent recurrence - learning, not blaming.
Step 1: secure the scene and provide aid - protect people first, stop hazardous operations, LOTO, control spills; then preserve the scene.
Step 2: report and notify - internally at once; OSHA: fatality within 8 h, in-patient hospitalization/amputation/eye loss within 24 h.
Step 3: assemble a trained multidisciplinary team led by a neutral leader not involved in the incident.
Step 4: collect evidence - private witness interviews ASAP with open-ended questions, photos/sketches, physical evidence with chain of custody, records (SOPs, training, maintenance), video/logs.
Step 5: reconstruct the timeline (sequence diagrams, flow charts), then root cause analysis, corrective actions, report, follow-up.
Investigate near misses too - they are free lessons.
FIRST action at an incident scene is always care for the injured and make the scene safe - not interviewing or photographing.
Root cause analysis

Root causes are the underlying, systemic reasons (management, design, procedures, culture) that allowed the immediate causes. Fixing them prevents recurrence; fixing only immediate causes leads to 'blame and retrain'.
Immediate causes = unsafe acts (bypassed guard) and unsafe conditions (wet unmarked floor).
Root causes = why the system allowed them (no procurement policy requiring operator input, production pressure, poor design).
Tools: 5 Whys, fishbone, change analysis, barrier analysis, FTA, MORT.
ANSI Z10: RCA expected for significant incidents and near misses.
Never accept 'human error' or 'worker carelessness' as the final cause.
If an answer choice stops at 'employee failed to follow procedure', look for the one that asks why (training, design, supervision, pressure).
Corrective actions
Corrective and preventive actions must target root causes, follow the hierarchy of controls, be owned, tracked, verified and embedded into the system.
Prioritize by risk (risk matrix, bow-tie); life-threatening and regulatory items first.
Single named owner and due date for every action; track in an action register (NSC).
Verify completion AND effectiveness (re-assess risk) before closing; escalate overdue actions to management.
Update SOPs, training, permits, drawings; share lessons learned organization-wide.
Include preventive actions: 'how do we stop it happening anywhere else?'
'Retrain the employee' or 'discipline the worker' is rarely the best corrective action; engineering/system fixes are preferred.
5 Whys
Ask 'why?' repeatedly, using each answer as the basis for the next question, until you reach a system, policy or management cause (often about five whys).
Best for routine incidents, near misses and simple recurring problems; first step before more detailed tools.
Example chain: bypassed guard -> slowed production -> guard hard to access -> chosen on cost -> purchasing need not consult operators -> no policy for operator input (root cause).
Document each why; avoid blaming questions; go beyond five if needed.
If you reach a policy, culture or design issue, you are near the true root cause.
Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram
A cause-and-effect diagram with the problem at the head and main cause categories as bones; a team brainstorms causes in each category.
Common categories: People, Equipment (Machines), Process (Methods), Materials, Environment, Management (6 Ms variant: Man, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement, Mother nature).
Best for complex incidents with many possible contributors and group brainstorming.
Combine with 5 Whys on each branch; attach to the investigation record.
Change analysis
Compare the incident situation with the normal, incident-free situation and list every difference; then test how each change contributed.
Use when 'this has never happened before' or a system that normally works failed.
Typical changes: substitute operator, new material or pallet type, wet surface, time pressure, temporary workaround.
Ask: who approved the change, was risk assessed, were controls adjusted? Link findings to the MOC process.
Key question for change analysis: 'What was different today?'
Barrier analysis
List every barrier (engineering, administrative, PPE, alarms, physical) that should have stopped the incident and determine whether each was missing, failed, bypassed, ineffective or not updated.
Best in high-hazard settings with layers of defense (chemical, oil and gas, confined spaces).
Example: double-wall piping missing; permit bypassed; relief valve stuck; alarm ignored (alarm fatigue); face shield not worn; SOP not updated.
Leads to system-level fixes rather than behavior fixes; supports defense-in-depth.
Accident causation theories
Theories explain why incidents occur and shape where investigators look.
Heinrich domino theory: ancestry/social environment -> fault of person -> unsafe act/condition -> accident -> injury; remove the middle domino.
Heinrich ratio 1 major : 29 minor : 300 no-injury; Bird ratio 1 serious : 10 minor : 30 property damage : 600 near misses.
Reason's Swiss cheese model: latent conditions (organizational) line up with active failures to let a hazard through barriers.
Multiple causation: incidents have many contributing factors - system, management, culture.
Energy release theory (Haddon): incidents are unwanted energy transfer; control the energy or the barrier.
Swiss cheese = latent organizational failures + active errors; questions about 'layers of defense' point to Reason.
Interviews and evidence handling
Credible investigations depend on timely, unbiased, well-documented evidence.
Interview witnesses separately and privately, soon after the event, with open-ended non-judgmental questions.
Photograph before moving anything; tag and log physical evidence (chain of custody).
Compare what should have happened (procedures) with what did happen.
Gather environmental data (air, noise, lighting), control-system logs and video.
Group interviews create groupthink - interview individually.
mcq: Which of the following should be the first step in an incident investigation?
Interview witnesses
Secure and preserve the scene
Collect physical evidence
Develop recommendations
First secure the scene to prevent further harm and preserve evidence; interviews and evidence collection follow.
Which investigation tool focuses on "Why" questions to trace a causal chain until a systemic cause is found?
Fault Tree Analysis
Fishbone Diagram
5 Whys
MORT
The 5 Whys repeatedly asks 'why' to move from the immediate cause to the underlying system cause.

Following a chemical spill, the safety manager assembles a multidisciplinary team to
analyze deviations in valve operation, human error, and procedural gaps. The team uses a
structured worksheet to identify causes and corrective actions for People, Procedures,
Equipment, Environment, and Management Systems.
Which investigation technique is being applied?
Cause-and-effect (fishbone/Ishikawa) analysis
Barrier analysis
Event and causal factor charting
Energy trace and barrier analysis
Categorizing causes into branches such as People, Procedures, Equipment, Environment and Management Systems is the cause-and-effect (fishbone/Ishikawa) method.
After a worker falls from a ladder, the investigation reveals the ladder had worn, uneven steps. What type of cause does this represent?
Root cause
Personal failure
Contributing cause
Direct cause
Worn, uneven ladder steps are the unsafe condition that directly produced the fall (direct/immediate cause). The root cause would be why the ladder was not inspected or removed from service.
Verification of corrective actions should occur:
Before the root cause is identified
Immediately after implementation
After a reasonable period to confirm effectiveness
Only during management review

Corrective actions should be verified after a reasonable period to confirm they are effective and sustained and did not create new hazards; checking on the day of installation only confirms completion.
The most critical output of an incident investigation report is:
Recommendations and verified corrective actions
Assignment of blame
A record of injuries
Witness statements
An investigation's value is in actionable, verified corrective actions that prevent recurrence, not in blame or data collection alone.
When should the investigation be conducted following an injury?
Based on the evidence only because witness statements are usually biased or hearsay.
Immediately, with all witnesses simultaneously to get the most accurate statements.
The next working day after emotions have settled down.
Individually, with all direct and indirect witnesses as soon as possible.
Interview witnesses individually and as soon as possible, while memories are fresh and before accounts are influenced by others. Group interviews contaminate testimony.

A supervisor is being interviewed about a forklift near-miss. The investigator asks, "Did you see the forklift operator speeding?" The supervisor answers "No."

What would have been a better question to encourage useful information?
"Why didn't you stop the operator if they were speeding?"
"Tell me what you observed when the forklift entered the aisle."
"Did the forklift almost hit the pedestrian?"
"Do you think the operator is reckless?"
Open-ended, non-leading questions ('Tell me what you observed...') produce more complete, unbiased information than yes/no or accusatory questions.
The Bowtie method in incident investigation is best described as:
A brainstorming technique to list every possible hazard
A timeline that shows human errors in sequence
A method to calculate injury severity after incidents
A model that links threats, preventive barriers, the top event, and consequences
A bowtie links threats, preventive barriers, the top event, mitigative barriers and consequences in one diagram.

An investigation finds that an operator's hand was caught while clearing jams on a conveyor because the task requires reaching into the nip point while the belt runs, and jams occur about 20 times per shift. Which corrective action is MOST effective?
Retrain all operators on the hazards of nip points
Discipline the operator for reaching into the conveyor
Redesign the infeed to reduce jams and install an interlocked guard that stops the belt when opened
Post a warning sign at the jam location

Corrective actions should follow the hierarchy of controls and address the root cause: reducing jams (elimination of the task) plus interlocked guarding (engineering) beats training, signs and discipline.

topics.title: Management of Change (MOC)
topics.bp: Describe the Management of Change process (prior, during, after)
topics.definition: Management of Change is a formal process to identify, evaluate and control the hazards and risks introduced by changes to processes, equipment, chemicals, procedures, facilities, organizations or personnel before the change is implemented. It is required by OSHA PSM (1910.119(l)) and is a key element of ISO 45001 (8.1.3) and ANSI Z10.
topics.easy: Every change can bring new hazards. Before you change something, stop and check what could go wrong, fix it, tell and train people, and check afterwards that it worked.
points: Before (prior): request and describe the change, technical basis, hazard identification and risk assessment, impact on procedures, training, PSI and permits, approvals by authorized people.
During: implement controls, update drawings (P&IDs) and procedures, train and inform affected employees and contractors, pre-startup safety review (PSSR) for PSM changes.
After: verify effectiveness, monitor for unintended consequences, close out and document, retain records.

Types of change: permanent, temporary (with an expiry date), emergency (expedited but still reviewed); organizational changes (staffing, reorganizations, mergers) and personnel changes are often missed.
Replacement in kind (identical specification) does not need MOC; anything that changes specifications, materials, settings or conditions does.
Change management (people side): communicate the reason, involve those affected, address resistance, provide resources (e.g., Kotter's 8 steps, Lewin's unfreeze-change-refreeze).
topics.example: Maintenance wants to replace a pump with a higher-pressure model. The MOC review finds that the downstream piping, flange gaskets and relief valve are rated below the new pump's shutoff pressure. The relief valve is resized, gaskets are upgraded, procedures are updated and operators are trained before the pump is started.
tips: The FIRST step of MOC is to evaluate the hazards and risks of the proposed change before implementation.
Temporary changes (bypassing an interlock) and organizational changes are MOC triggers.
Watch for 'it's the same thing' traps - different material, rating or supplier formulation is not replacement in kind.
topics.yates: Ch. 38 Management of Change, p. 859
subs: MOC process

MOC ensures any change to equipment, processes, materials, personnel or organization is identified, assessed and controlled before, during and after implementation so it does not create new hazards or weaken controls.
Required for PSM-covered processes by 29 CFR 1910.119(l) and expected by ANSI Z10 and ISO 45001 (clause 8.1.3).
PSM MOC must address: technical basis, impact on safety and health, modifications to operating procedures, time period (temporary changes), authorization requirements.
Affected employees and contractors must be informed and trained BEFORE startup of the changed process.
Update PSI (P&IDs, procedures) after the change; PSSR for new or significantly modified facilities.
'Replacement in kind' (same specification) is not an MOC change.
Most-missed step: the risk assessment of a 'small' or 'temporary' change. Every change - even temporary - goes through MOC.
Before the change (pre-implementation)
Identify and log the change, define scope and impact, assess risk, check regulations, involve stakeholders and obtain documented authorization.
Triggers: new equipment, revised procedures, raw materials or supplier, software/controls, layout, staffing levels, organizational changes, temporary modifications.
Consider direct and indirect impacts (new chemical -> waste handling hazards).
Risk tools: JHA, What-If, HAZOP, FMEA.
Check permits, notifications, fire codes, EPA requirements.
Formal change request + risk assessment record + management/EHS approval before work starts.
If the scenario says the change was implemented and then reviewed, the MOC failed at the 'before' stage.
During the change (implementation)
Communicate, train, install and verify controls, supervise closely and document everything.
Tell affected personnel what, why and when; give clear new instructions.
No change is 'safe' until everyone affected is competent.
Engineering, administrative and PPE controls in place and verified before the system is activated.
Have contingency plans to pause or reverse the change.
Use an MOC checklist (ANSI Z10).
After the change (post-implementation)
Verify and validate that controls work, track deviations, update documents, review outcomes and share lessons.
Inspect/audit the changed system; get feedback from front-line users.
Track incidents and near misses linked to the change; update the risk assessment.
Revise SOPs, training, P&IDs, permits, emergency plans.
Review MOC outcomes in management review; close the MOC only when documentation is complete.
Organizational and personnel change
Changes in people and structure (downsizing, reassignment, new contractors, loss of experienced staff, shift changes) can degrade safety as much as hardware changes.
Assess loss of knowledge, reduced staffing at critical tasks, changed responsibilities.
ISO 45001 8.1.3 explicitly includes changes in work organization, staffing and knowledge.
Temporary changes need an end date and must be reversed or re-approved.
A reorganization that removes an experienced operator from a critical task should trigger MOC.
Common MOC pitfalls
Most change-related incidents come from skipped steps rather than missing procedures.
Skipping risk assessment for 'minor' changes.
Failing to update procedures, drawings and training afterward.
Not involving the people who will work with the change daily.
Allowing 'temporary' changes to become permanent without review.
mcq: Which step must occur first in an effective Management of Change (MoC) process?
Approve implementation
Identify the proposed change and screen risk
Train employees on new procedures
Close the change file
MOC begins by identifying the proposed change and screening it for hazards/risk; authorization, training and closure come later.

A facility plans to replace a key piece of production equipment with a newer model that operates at higher temperatures. What should a safety professional do FIRST as part of the Management of Change process?
Approve the purchase order to avoid project delays.
Update the safety signage to reflect the higher operating temperature.
Conduct a risk assessment to evaluate potential safety and health impacts.
Notify employees of the upcoming change via email.

Before approval, the change must be risk assessed for safety and health impacts (higher temperature, burns, materials, procedures). Purchasing, signs or emails before assessment skip the 'prior' stage of MOC.
Which of the following would NOT normally require a formal Management of Change review?
Replacing a pump seal with an identical part number from the same manufacturer
Increasing a reactor's operating temperature by 15 deg C
Changing a solvent supplier to a different chemical formulation
Reducing the number of operators on night shift
Replacement-in-kind (identical specifications) is excluded from MOC. Changes to chemicals, process conditions and staffing are all changes that need review.

A company merges two production departments to reduce costs. After the merger, safety
performance declines, and employees report confusion about responsibilities and
supervision. The MOC review focused only on equipment relocation, not personnel or
procedural impacts.
Which aspect of MOC was overlooked?
Engineering control verification
Shift handoff documentation
Vendor qualification for new suppliers
Organizational change impact on roles and communication
MOC covers organizational changes too (staffing, roles, supervision, communication), not just equipment. The review missed the people/organizational impacts.
Which step in the Management of Change (MoC) process verifies that modified equipment operates safely before returning to service?
Identification
Authorization
Pre-startup safety review
Documentation closure
The pre-startup safety review (PSSR) verifies that construction, procedures, training and controls are in place before the changed equipment is returned to service.
The final step in an MoC process is to:
Verify implementation effectiveness and close documentation
Train affected employees
Conduct a risk assessment
Approve engineering design
MOC closes by verifying the change was implemented as approved and is effective, then updating and closing documentation (P&IDs, SOPs, training records).
A written Management of Change Program is required by OSHA for:
Confined Space
Process Safety Management
Lockout
Emergency Response Program
OSHA's PSM standard (29 CFR 1910.119(l)) explicitly requires written MOC procedures. The other standards do not contain a formal MOC element.
Which of the following is the best verification method for determining MoC effectiveness?
Using only documentation reviews without observation
Management's verbal assurance
Delay of verification until next year's audit
Employee feedback and audit of implemented controls
Effectiveness after a change is best verified by observing/auditing the implemented controls and getting feedback from affected users, not by verbal assurance or paperwork alone.
During MoC, a new control room software is installed. Which hazard is most likely if communication training is skipped?
Physical hazard
Ergonomic hazard
Human factors / operational error
Environmental hazard
Changing an operator interface without training increases the likelihood of human error (human factors). MOC must address training and communication during the change.

The management of change process covers four primary concepts, regardless of the type of change. Three of these are:
Identification of hazards associated with the change
Assessment of the risks associated with the change
Consideration of the hazards and risks prior to the change
Which is the fourth primary concept?
Implementation of controls needed to address hazards and risks associated with the change
Performance of a "what if" analysis to identify expected risks
Hiring of additional management personnel to oversee and direct organizational change
Compliance with all applicable regulatory guidelines regarding changes in an occupational health and safety management program
The fourth element is implementing controls to address the hazards and risks identified for the change; identification and assessment are useless without control.

topics.title: System Safety Analysis
topics.bp: Describe system safety analysis techniques (e.g., fault tree analysis, failure modes and effects analysis [FMEA], Safety Case approach, risk summation)
topics.definition: System safety applies engineering and management principles to identify hazards and control risk across the entire life cycle of a system. Analysis techniques can be inductive (bottom-up: what happens if this part fails?) or deductive (top-down: what could cause this undesired event?).
topics.easy: Some tools start from a single part and ask what happens if it fails (FMEA). Others start from the disaster and work backwards to find every way it could happen (fault tree). A safety case puts all the evidence together to prove the system is safe enough.
points: Preliminary Hazard Analysis (PHA): early, concept stage, broad hazard list and rough risk ranking.

FMEA: inductive, bottom-up; for each component list failure modes, effects and causes; rate Severity, Occurrence and Detection (1-10); RPN = S × O × D. FMECA adds criticality. Limitation: single failures, does not handle combinations or human error well.

Fault Tree Analysis (FTA): deductive, top-down from a top (undesired) event using Boolean logic. AND gate: all inputs must occur (multiply probabilities). OR gate: any input (P = 1 − Π(1 − Pi), or approximately add for rare events). Minimal cut sets identify the smallest combinations causing the top event.
Event Tree Analysis (ETA): inductive, forward from an initiating event through success/failure of safeguards to outcomes.
HAZOP: team-based, guide words (no, more, less, as well as, part of, reverse, other than) applied to process parameters at nodes.
Safety Case: a structured, evidence-based argument that a system is acceptably safe (often to ALARP) for a defined use; required in UK offshore, nuclear, rail; goal-based rather than prescriptive.
Risk summation: total risk = Σ (frequency × consequence) for all scenarios, used to understand overall risk exposure and compare with tolerability criteria.

Other: Energy Trace and Barrier Analysis (ETBA), MORT (management oversight and risk tree), Job Safety Analysis, What-If, Checklist. Design terms: fail-safe, fail-passive (shuts down safely), fail-active (alarms/defaults to safe state), fail-operational (keeps working safely).
topics.example: A chemical company models a reactor overpressure (top event) with a fault tree. Overpressure occurs if cooling fails (OR gate of pump failure 0.01 and power loss 0.02) AND the relief valve fails (0.001). Cooling failure ≈ 0.0298; top event ≈ 0.0298 × 0.001 = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ per year, which the safety case compares with the company's tolerability criterion.
tips: Top-down/deductive = FTA. Bottom-up/inductive = FMEA (and ETA).
AND gate multiplies; OR gate adds (approximately). Series systems fail if any part fails; parallel/redundant systems fail only if all fail.
A high RPN ranks first, but many companies act on any severity 9-10 regardless of RPN.
Safety Case = an argument plus evidence that risk is acceptable.
topics.yates: Ch. 22 Accident Causation and Investigation Techniques (FTA), p. 515; Ch. 26 Risk Assessment and Management, p. 604; Ch. 15 Statistics (probability)
subs: Fault Tree Analysis (FTA)

FTA is a deductive, top-down (backward) technique that starts with an undesired Top Event and uses Boolean logic gates to map all combinations of equipment failures, human errors and external events that could cause it. It can be qualitative or quantitative.
AND gate: output occurs only if ALL inputs occur - P = P1 x P2 (independent events).
OR gate: output occurs if ANY input occurs - P = 1 - (1-P1)(1-P2); approx. P1 + P2 for small probabilities.
Minimal cut set = smallest combination of basic events that causes the top event; a single-event cut set = single point of failure.
Best for complex, high-risk technical systems (process, aviation, nuclear, utilities); output = fault tree diagram and cut sets.
FTA = deductive, top event, logic gates. Adding redundancy changes an OR into an AND and sharply lowers top-event probability.
FMEA / FMECA

FMEA is an inductive, bottom-up, proactive technique that lists each component, every way it can fail (failure mode) and the effect on the system. FMECA adds a criticality ranking of severity and likelihood.
RPN = Severity x Occurrence (probability) x Detection, each usually rated 1-10 (RPN 1-1000).
Example: S = 8, O = 5, D = 4 -> RPN = 160; act on highest RPN and on any high-severity mode.
Detection is rated inversely: 10 = almost impossible to detect.
Good for design, manufacturing and equipment reliability; poor at human error and combined failures.
Not a root cause/investigation tool - it anticipates what could fail, not why something did fail. PEM chart summarizes ratings.
FMEA = component failure modes, bottom-up, single failures; FTA = top event, top-down, combinations.
Safety Case
A structured, evidence-based argument showing that a system or facility achieves and maintains an acceptable level of safety, prepared for regulators and stakeholders.
Three elements: Claim (the system is safe under stated conditions), Argument (reasoning), Evidence (tests, analyses, records, audits).
Living document - updated after changes, incidents, audits or new regulations.
Must be documented, traceable, auditable and defensible.
Used in high-hazard regulated sectors: offshore oil and gas (UK), nuclear, rail, aviation, defense; often required for licensing.
If the question says 'demonstrate to a regulator that risks are reduced to ALARP with supporting evidence', the answer is a Safety Case.
Risk summation (risk aggregation)
Risk summation combines many individual risk values into a total risk profile so cumulative risk is not underestimated.
Risk = Probability x Consequence for each hazard; total = sum of individual risks.
Compare total to risk tolerance/ALARP; the largest contributor ($10,000) gets resources first.
Use consistent scales (all 1-5 or all real probabilities and dollars).
Several 'low' risks can sum to an unacceptable total - that is the point of risk summation.
Event Tree Analysis (ETA)
ETA is inductive and forward-looking: from one initiating event, it branches at each safety function (success/failure) to show all possible outcomes. No logic gates.
Outcome frequency = initiating frequency x product of branch probabilities along the path.
Example: fire starts 0.1/yr; alarm fails 0.05; sprinkler fails 0.02 -> worst outcome = 0.1 x 0.05 x 0.02 = 0.0001/yr.
Used to evaluate barrier effectiveness and redundancy and model consequences.
ETA = initiating event -> consequences (forward); FTA = top event -> causes (backward).
Cause-consequence analysis and bow-tie

CCA combines FTA (causes) and ETA (consequences). The bow-tie diagram shows threats and preventive barriers on the left, the hazardous top event (knot) in the middle, and consequences with mitigating barriers on the right.
Left side = prevention barriers; right side = mitigation/recovery barriers.
Fishbone often used first to brainstorm causes.
Excellent for communicating risk to non-technical audiences.
HAZOP
Team-based, node-by-node study of deviations from design intent using guide words combined with process parameters.
Guide words: No/None, More, Less, As well as, Part of, Reverse, Other than (plus High/Low).
Parameters: flow, pressure, temperature, level, time, composition.
Deviation = guide word + parameter (e.g., 'No flow', 'High pressure').
Led by a trained facilitator with a multidisciplinary team; output = report with recommendations; aims for ALARP. A PSM-accepted PHA method.
Guide words + nodes = HAZOP.
THERP (human reliability)
Technique for Human Error Rate Prediction breaks a task into steps and assigns human error probabilities to each to estimate overall task failure probability.
Uses task analysis and standard error probability tables, adjusted by performance shaping factors (stress, training, design).
Overall success = product of step success probabilities; e.g., 3 steps each 0.99 -> 0.97 success, 0.03 failure.
Feeds FTA/PRA; used in nuclear and process industries for routine procedural tasks.
MORT (Management Oversight and Risk Tree)
MORT is a pre-drawn logic tree used to find management and organizational causes of incidents ('oversights and omissions' and 'assumed risks').
Developed for the U.S. Department of Energy; very detailed checklist-style tree.
Focus is on management system failures, not just technical causes.
Used reactively (investigations) and proactively (program evaluation).
Management/organizational root causes + tree = MORT.
MIL-STD-882E and other hazard analyses
MIL-STD-882E is the DoD system safety standard defining risk assessment matrices and hazard analysis tasks across the system life cycle.
Severity: 1 Catastrophic, 2 Critical, 3 Marginal, 4 Negligible.
Probability: A Frequent, B Probable, C Occasional, D Remote, E Improbable, F Eliminated.
Preliminary Hazard List/Analysis (PHL/PHA) is done early in design; What-If and checklist analyses are simpler qualitative methods.
mcq: Two failure modes are analyzed in an FMEA. Mode X: Severity 10, Occurrence 2, Detection 3. Mode Y: Severity 5, Occurrence 6, Detection 5. Using RPN alone, which mode ranks higher and what is its RPN?
Mode X, RPN 60
Mode Y, RPN 150
Mode X, RPN 150
They are equal
RPN = S x O x D. X = 10 x 2 x 3 = 60; Y = 5 x 6 x 5 = 150, so Y ranks higher. Trap: many organizations also act on any severity 10 regardless of RPN.
In a fault tree, the top event occurs through an OR gate with two inputs: Event A (an AND gate of B = 0.1 and C = 0.2) and Event D = 0.01. What is the approximate probability of the top event?
AND gate multiplies: 0.1 x 0.2 = 0.02. OR gate: 1 - (1 - 0.02)(1 - 0.01) = 0.0298, about 0.03 (rare-event approximation: 0.02 + 0.01).
A facility has three loss scenarios: (1) 0.01/yr x $500,000; (2) 0.1/yr x $20,000; (3) 0.5/yr x $2,000. Using risk summation, what is the total annualized risk?
Risk summation adds each scenario's frequency x consequence: 5,000 + 2,000 + 1,000 = $8,000 per year. $522,000 adds consequences without frequency.
Which statement BEST describes a Safety Case?
A structured argument, supported by evidence, that a system is acceptably safe for a given application and environment
