Alarms audible/visible, tested; automatic fire department notification where required.
Evacuation wardens assist and account for staff and visitors; roll call at assembly point.
Extinguisher use: PASS (Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep); monthly inspection, annual maintenance.
Drills at least annually (best practice), more often in high-risk sites.
Severe weather
Severe weather plans cover tornadoes, hurricanes, floods, blizzards and extreme heat/cold with monitoring, shelter and shutdown procedures for hazards relevant to the location.
Tornado: interior rooms away from windows, lowest floor; tornado drills; supplies (water, radios, first aid).
Hurricane/flood: pre-arranged shutdown and evacuation, secure loose items, protect openings.
Extreme heat/cold: monitor advisories, hydration/cooling or warming stations.
Alerts: NOAA weather radios, text alerts; tornado watch = conditions favorable, warning = tornado sighted or on radar - take shelter.
Nuclear incidents
Plans for releases of radioactive material from nuclear plants, medical/industrial sources or weapons; required for facilities near nuclear plants and coordinated with NRC, FEMA and local agencies.
Shelter-in-place: designated rooms, seal openings, shut down HVAC if needed.
Evacuation routes and transport coordination; follow official advisories.
Radiation monitoring (dosimeters); potassium iodide (KI) protects only the thyroid from radioactive iodine and is taken only on official instruction.
Protective principles: time, distance, shielding.
Planning zones around nuclear plants: about 10-mile plume exposure and 50-mile ingestion pathway zones (FEMA/NRC).
Natural disasters
Earthquakes, floods, wildfires and similar events need location-specific procedures, supplies and post-event hazard checks.
Earthquake: drop, cover and hold on; secure heavy items; afterward check for injuries, gas leaks and fires before re-entry.
Flood: move critical equipment to higher ground, shut down utilities, use flood maps.
Wildfire: defensible space, clear combustibles, monitor air quality, respirators for smoke, rapid evacuation.
Kits: water, food, radios, flashlights, batteries, PPE.
Terrorist attacks and active shooter
Deliberate attacks and active shooter events require lockdown, mass notification and Run-Hide-Fight training, coordinated with law enforcement.
References: OSHA General Duty Clause, DHS guidance, NFPA 3000 (Active Shooter/Hostile Event Response).
Run, Hide, Fight (DHS) - escape if possible, hide if not, fight only as a last resort.
Lockdown procedures, silent alarms, mass notification.
Bomb threats: keep caller talking, use a bomb threat checklist, do not use radios/cell phones near a suspected device.
Post-incident medical, psychological and legal support; tabletop and live drills with law enforcement.
Chemical spills
Chemical spill plans cover immediate evacuation and isolation, containment by trained personnel only, decontamination, medical support and regulatory notification.
Evacuate, activate alarms, shut down sources only if safe.
Only trained responders with proper PPE clean up (HAZWOPER 1910.120(q) for emergency response; incidental spills handled by trained area employees).
Spill kits, neutralizers, booms; decontamination of people and areas; eyewash/showers.
Notify authorities when a reportable quantity is released (CERCLA RQ -> National Response Center; EPCRA 304 -> state/local).
Document: incident report, root cause, regulatory notifications.
Untrained employees evacuate and report; they do not attempt cleanup of a non-incidental release.
Utility systems failures
Loss of power, water or gas can create safety hazards and stop critical systems, so plans address safe shutdown, backup power and safe restoration.
Procedures to safely shut down and restart equipment; inspect before re-energizing.
Emergency lighting and backup power (NFPA 110 generators; NFPA 101 requires 90 min emergency lighting).
Alternative communications (radios, cell phones with backup power); alternative water for drinking and sanitation.
Gas leak: evacuate immediately, eliminate ignition sources, call utility provider.
Cybersecurity
Cyber incidents can disable safety controls, alarms and communications. There is no OSHA cyber standard, but NFPA 1600 and DHS recommend cyber response planning for safety and operational systems.
Train employees to recognize phishing, unusual activity and outages; report quickly.
Activate IT/cyber incident response team and plan.
Secure offsite backups and restoration protocols.
Maintain safety monitoring and alarms via manual backups; alternate notification methods if digital systems fail.
Industrial control systems guidance: ISA/IEC 62443, NIST Cybersecurity Framework.
Pandemic and bioterrorism
Biological emergencies need prevention, detection, communication, medical response, coordination with public health and law enforcement, and business continuity for high absenteeism.
Pandemic = global outbreak; epidemic = cases above expected in a community or region.
Pandemic controls: hygiene, ventilation/barriers (engineering), staggered shifts/remote work (administrative), PPE; symptom reporting and return-to-work criteria; cross-training.
Bioterrorism: recognize suspicious packages/illness clusters, isolate area, notify public health, law enforcement and FBI; decontamination; rumor control point.
References: OSHA General Duty Clause, 1910.1030 (BBP), 1910.120, CDC/NIOSH guidance, NFPA 1600.
mcq: A radiological release is expected from a nearby nuclear power plant and officials advise sheltering in place. Which action is MOST appropriate?
Open windows to dilute any contamination entering the building
Have all employees take potassium iodide to protect against all radiation
Shelter indoors, shut down HVAC and close openings, and take potassium iodide only if officials instruct it
Drive employees through the plume to reach a shelter farther away
Buildings provide shielding and closing HVAC limits infiltration. KI only blocks thyroid uptake of radioiodine and is taken only on official instruction.

During a night shift, a fire breaks out in a section of a warehouse. Several employees evacuate safely, but one forklift operator is unaccounted for. The plan identifies assembly points and alarm systems but has no accountability procedure. What element is missing from the emergency plan?
Communication procedures with insurance carriers
Coordination procedures with environmental agencies
Post-incident counseling for employees
A system for accounting for all employees after evacuation
OSHA 1910.38(c) requires procedures to account for all employees after evacuation; without it, missing workers may not be identified for rescue.
The National Weather Service issues a TORNADO WARNING for your county. What should the facility do?
Move personnel immediately to designated storm shelters or interior refuge areas
Continue normal work but monitor the weather radio
Evacuate everyone to their vehicles
Wait until the tornado is visible before acting
A warning means a tornado is occurring or imminent: shelter now in interior, lowest-level, windowless areas. Trap: treating a warning like a watch (prepare only).
A 1-liter bottle of a known solvent breaks in a lab. Trained lab staff in the immediate area can safely absorb it with a spill kit. Under HAZWOPER 1910.120(q), this is:
An emergency response requiring a HAZMAT team
An incidental release that may be cleaned up by trained employees in the immediate area
A release that automatically requires EPA notification
An uncontrolled release requiring evacuation of the building
Releases that employees in the immediate area can absorb or control without significant safety or health risk are incidental, not emergency responses under 1910.120(q).

A toxic gas plume is drifting toward a residential area at a steady 10 mph. It takes 15 minutes to mobilize and complete evacuation of the at-risk population. What is the MINIMUM distance the plume must be from the area when the evacuation order is given to ensure safe clearance?
1.5 miles
2.5 miles
3 miles
4 miles
Distance = speed x time = 10 mi/h x (15/60) h = 2.5 miles. Trap: forgetting to convert minutes to hours.
What is the MOST important step after conducting an emergency drill?
Repeat the same drill immediately until all employees pass
Send the drill results to OSHA for recordkeeping
Conduct an after-action review and document improvement areas
Dismiss employees early as a reward for participation
Drills exist to test and improve the plan; the after-action review captures weaknesses and assigns corrective actions. OSHA does not collect drill results.
During a drill evaluation, observers note confusion about who should contact external emergency responders. Which plan element MOST likely needs improvement?
Command hierarchy and communication chain
Evacuation route signage
Number and placement of fire extinguishers
Sprinkler system activation pressure
The plan must assign clear roles, including who notifies outside responders; confusion here is a chain-of-command and communication gap, not a hardware issue.
A ransomware attack encrypts the building automation and process control servers at a chemical plant during operations. According to the facility's emergency response plan, what should be done FIRST?
Pay the ransom quickly to restore operations
Restore the servers from backup while they remain connected to the network
Wait for the IT vendor to diagnose the problem before taking any action
Isolate affected systems from the network and activate the cyber incident response plan, placing processes in a safe state
Containment comes first: isolate infected systems to stop spread and move the process to a safe state. Restoring while still connected risks reinfection.
Employees report a strong odor of natural gas in an office building after nearby utility work. What is the BEST immediate action?
Turn on exhaust fans to ventilate the building
Locate the leak by checking appliances and connections
Evacuate the building without operating electrical switches, then call the gas utility and 911 from a safe location
Have employees stay at their desks while maintenance investigates
Utility gas leaks present an explosion hazard: evacuate, avoid ignition sources such as switches and phones, and report from a safe distance.
A receptionist receives a telephone bomb threat. According to a typical emergency response plan, what should the receptionist do?
Hang up immediately and continue working
Keep the caller talking, record details using a bomb threat checklist, and notify security and police per the plan
Personally search the building for suspicious packages
Announce over the public address system that there is a bomb in the building
Bomb threat procedures emphasize capturing caller details (checklist) and notifying authorities, who decide on search or evacuation; panic announcements and self-searches are inappropriate.

topics.title: Disaster Response and Recovery
topics.bp: Describe the elements in disaster response and recovery (e.g., incident command, business continuity, contingency plans)
topics.definition: Disaster response and recovery covers how an organization organizes the emergency response (Incident Command System), keeps critical functions running or restores them (business continuity), and prepares alternatives for foreseeable disruptions (contingency plans).
topics.easy: During a disaster one person is in charge and everyone knows their role (ICS). Afterwards, the business needs a plan to get the most important work running again fast (business continuity).
points: Incident Command System (ICS/NIMS): Incident Commander; Command Staff - Safety Officer, Public Information Officer, Liaison Officer; General Staff sections - Operations, Planning, Logistics, Finance/Administration.

ICS principles: common terminology, modular organization, management by objectives, Incident Action Plan (prepared by Planning), manageable span of control (3-7, ideally 5), unity of command, unified command for multi-agency incidents, formal transfer of command with briefing, accountability, integrated communications.

Business continuity: business impact analysis (BIA) identifies critical functions and impacts; Recovery Time Objective (RTO) = maximum acceptable downtime; Recovery Point Objective (RPO) = maximum acceptable data loss; strategies include alternate sites, backup suppliers, cloud backups, mutual aid.
Standards: NFPA 1600/1660, ISO 22301 (business continuity management systems), FEMA guidance.
Contingency planning: 'what-if' alternatives for supply disruption, utility loss, staffing shortages, pandemic; pre-arranged contracts; succession plans.
Recovery: damage assessment, restoration, employee assistance (EAP/counseling), insurance claims, lessons learned and plan updates. Disaster recovery (IT) focuses on systems and data.
topics.example: A regional power outage hits during peak production. The facility's generators run life-safety systems, but IT and supply links are down. The business continuity plan activates: critical orders move to a sister plant, data are restored from cloud backups within the 4-hour RTO, and the logistics section of the ICS arranges fuel deliveries for the generators.
tips: Planning Section prepares the IAP; Logistics provides resources; Operations does the tactical work; Finance tracks costs and claims.
Safety Officer, PIO and Liaison are Command Staff, not sections.
RTO = time; RPO = data loss.
Unified Command keeps each agency's authority while sharing objectives.
topics.yates: Ch. 39 Emergency Management and Preparedness, p. 870
subs: Incident Command System (ICS)

ICS is the standardized, scalable on-scene management system within the National Incident Management System (NIMS). OSHA HAZWOPER 1910.120(q) requires an ICS for emergency response to hazardous substance releases, led by the senior emergency response official.
Five major functions: Command, Operations, Planning, Logistics, Finance/Administration (Intelligence/Investigations may be added).
Command staff: Public Information Officer, Safety Officer (authority to stop unsafe acts), Liaison Officer.
Span of control: 3 to 7 subordinates, optimum 5.
Principles: common terminology, modular organization, unity of command, unified command for multi-agency incidents, Incident Action Plan, integrated communications.
The Incident Commander is responsible for everything until delegated; the IC position always exists.
Safety Officer is command staff (reports to IC), not general staff; unified command = several agencies sharing command, not several ICs giving separate orders.
Business continuity

Business continuity keeps critical functions running or restores them quickly after a disruption. It is driven by a Business Impact Analysis (BIA) and covered by NFPA 1600 (now NFPA 1660) and ISO 22301.
BIA identifies critical processes, dependencies and the impact of disruption over time.

RTO (recovery time objective) = target time to restore a function; RPO (recovery point objective) = maximum tolerable data loss (how far back backups must go); MTPD = maximum tolerable period of disruption (RTO must be shorter).
Strategies: alternate sites (hot, warm, cold), backup suppliers, data backups, cross-training, remote work.
Benefits: less downtime and financial loss, preserved reputation, insurance and regulatory compliance.
ISO 22301 = business continuity management systems (requirements).
A BIA comes before choosing continuity strategies.
Contingency planning
Contingency plans are pre-arranged 'what if' alternatives for specific disruptions - backup resources, alternate procedures and triggers for using them.
Examples: mutual aid agreements with neighboring plants or fire departments, pre-qualified restoration contractors, backup generators, alternate communications.
Define activation triggers, decision authority and resources in advance.
Test through tabletop exercises and update after use.
Phases of emergency management
Emergency management is a cycle of mitigation (and prevention), preparedness, response and recovery.
Mitigation: reduce the impact before an event (elevating equipment above flood level, seismic bracing).
Preparedness: plans, training, drills, equipment, agreements.
Response: protect life, stabilize the incident, protect property and environment (life safety -> incident stabilization -> property conservation).
Recovery: restore operations, repair, return to normal, lessons learned.
'Before the event, reducing impact' = mitigation; 'plans and drills' = preparedness.
HAZWOPER emergency response (1910.120(q))
Employers whose employees respond to hazardous substance releases need a written emergency response plan, ICS, training by role and medical surveillance for HAZMAT team members.

Training levels: First Responder Awareness (recognize, notify), Operations (8 hr, defensive containment), Hazmat Technician (24 hr, offensive stopping of release), Specialist (24 hr), On-Scene Incident Commander (24 hr plus competencies).
Annual refresher training or demonstrated competency.
Employers who evacuate all employees and do not respond may use a 1910.38 EAP instead of a (q) ERP.
Buddy system and backup personnel required in danger areas; positive-pressure SCBA in unknown atmospheres.
Defensive (contain from a distance) = Operations level; plugging/patching the leak = Technician.
Exercises and drills
Exercises test plans, train people and reveal gaps; results feed corrective actions.
Types (FEMA HSEEP): discussion-based - seminar, workshop, tabletop, game; operations-based - drill, functional exercise, full-scale exercise.
Tabletop: discussion of a scenario in a conference room, low cost.
Functional: tests coordination and command/communications without moving people and equipment to the field.
Full-scale: real-time deployment with multiple agencies; most realistic and costly.
Follow every exercise or real event with an after-action review and improvement plan.
Recovery and after-action review
Recovery restores safe operations and captures lessons learned so the plan improves.
Re-entry only after hazards are assessed (structural, electrical, gas, atmosphere) and authorities clear the site.
Restoration contractors, damage assessment, insurance claims and documentation.
Psychological support (EAP, critical incident stress management) for affected workers.
After-action review: what was planned, what happened, why, what to change; update ERP, training and resources.
Crisis and emergency communications
Clear, redundant communication protects people during response and protects the organization's reputation afterward.
Mass notification and redundant channels (PA, text, email, radios).
Single designated spokesperson / Public Information Officer; consistent, accurate, timely messages.
Pre-scripted messages and contact lists; rumor control.
Notify regulators as required (e.g., OSHA fatality within 8 hours, inpatient hospitalization, amputation or eye loss within 24 hours).
mcq: Which positions make up the command staff under the Incident Command System (ICS)?
Public Information Officer, Chief Executive Officer, and Safety Officer
Logistics Section Chief, Safety Officer, and Contracting Officer
Liaison Officer, Operations Section Chief, and Finance Section Chief
Safety Officer, Public Information Officer, and Liaison Officer
Command staff report directly to the IC: Safety, Public Information and Liaison Officers. Section chiefs (Operations, Planning, Logistics, Finance/Admin) form the general staff.
Which ICS component is responsible for developing the Incident Action Plan (IAP) and tracking resources?
Planning Section
Operations Section
Logistics Section
Finance/Administration Section
Planning collects and evaluates information, tracks resource status, and prepares the IAP. Operations executes it; Logistics obtains resources.
In business continuity planning, the Recovery POINT Objective (RPO) is:
The maximum acceptable time to restore a process
The location of the alternate recovery site
The maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured back in time from the disruption
The point at which the incident commander declares recovery complete
RPO is how much data you can afford to lose (drives backup frequency); RTO is how long a process can be down. Swapping the two is the classic trap.
What is the purpose of a Business Impact Analysis (BIA) in business continuity planning?
To evaluate the effectiveness of marketing strategies
To identify the most critical processes and the potential impact of a disruption on them
To determine the organization's key performance indicators
To analyze the overall financial health of the organization
The BIA identifies time-critical functions, their downtime tolerance and dependencies, which sets recovery priorities, RTOs and RPOs.
A plant's emergency coordinator is acting as Incident Commander when the fire department battalion chief arrives. What is the correct ICS practice?
Transfer command through a formal face-to-face briefing; the plant coordinator may remain in a supporting or unified command role
Both act as independent incident commanders
The plant coordinator leaves the scene immediately
Command stays with the plant regardless of the incident
ICS requires a formal transfer of command with a briefing on situation, resources and objectives; the facility representative often joins unified command or advises on plant issues.
A post-incident review finds that slow decision-making resulted from responders receiving orders from several supervisors. Which ICS principle was violated?
Common terminology
Modular organization
Span of control
Unity of command
Unity of command means each responder reports to only one supervisor. Span of control (3-7, ideally 5) limits how many people one supervisor manages.
During an emergency, which ICS function is responsible for obtaining and managing supplies, facilities, and equipment?
Operations Section
Planning Section
Logistics Section
Finance/Administration Section
Logistics provides facilities, services and materials (food, fuel, communications, equipment). Finance/Admin tracks costs, Planning tracks resource status.
A hurricane destroys a regional data center that stores critical safety inspection records and training files. As part of the disaster recovery team, what is the BEST immediate course of action?
Rebuild the data center at the same location as quickly as possible
Implement the disaster recovery plan by restoring records from off-site or cloud backups to an alternate site
Manually recreate records from employee memory and paper notes
Wait until insurance claims are processed before attempting recovery
Contingency planning pre-arranges backups and alternate sites so critical records can be restored quickly; rebuilding or waiting delays recovery.
Following a severe storm, a company activates its Business Continuity Plan (BCP). Which action should occur FIRST?
Conduct a financial impact review
File insurance claims
Schedule post-incident interviews
Restore the critical operations identified as essential in the Business Impact Analysis
BCP activation prioritizes restoring the time-critical functions ranked in the BIA; financial, insurance and review activities follow.
Which activity represents a continuity (recovery) objective rather than an immediate response activity?
Restoring IT systems and production operations
Evacuating employees from a fire
Coordinating with arriving fire services
Activating the alarm system
Response protects life and stabilizes the incident; recovery and continuity restore critical systems and business functions after stabilization.

topics.title: Fire Prevention, Protection and Suppression
topics.bp: Identify key components of fire prevention, protection, and suppression systems
topics.definition: Fire prevention removes or controls fuel, oxygen and ignition sources so fires do not start; fire protection detects fires and protects occupants and property (alarms, compartmentation, egress); suppression systems control or extinguish fires (sprinklers, standpipes, special agents, extinguishers).
topics.easy: Stop fires starting (housekeeping, hot-work permits, safe storage), find them fast (detectors and alarms), and put them out or keep them small (sprinklers and extinguishers) while people get out.
points: Fire triangle/tetrahedron: fuel, heat, oxygen + chemical chain reaction. Dust explosion pentagon adds dispersion and confinement.

Fire classes: A (ordinary combustibles), B (flammable liquids/gases), C (energized electrical), D (combustible metals), K (cooking oils/fats). Lithium-ion battery fires: large amounts of water for cooling; thermal runaway.

Flammable liquids (OSHA/GHS): Category 1 FP < 73.4 °F and BP ≤ 95 °F; Category 2 FP < 73.4 °F and BP > 95 °F; Category 3 FP 73.4-140 °F; Category 4 FP 140-199.4 °F. Cabinet limit 60 gal Cat 1-3 (120 gal Cat 4), max 3 cabinets per fire area; storage rooms 6 air changes/hour; bonding and grounding during transfer.
LFL/UFL: flammable range; work limit typically < 10% LFL. Flash point, autoignition temperature, vapor density (> 1 heavier than air).
Hot work (NFPA 51B, OSHA 1910.252): permit, PAI (permit authorizing individual), fire watch during and at least 30 min after, combustibles 35 ft away or covered.
Detection: heat (fixed temperature, rate-of-rise), smoke (ionization - fast flaming; photoelectric - smoldering), flame (UV/IR - fast, open areas).

Sprinklers (NFPA 13; ITM per NFPA 25): wet pipe (most common), dry pipe (freezing areas), pre-action (sensitive areas), deluge (high-hazard, all heads open). Q = K√P. Keep 18 in. clearance below deflectors.

Portable extinguishers (1910.157): monthly visual inspection, annual maintenance, hydrostatic testing per type; training annually if employees are expected to use them; PASS (pull, aim, squeeze, sweep).
Special agents: CO₂ (no residue, asphyxiation hazard), clean agents (FM-200, Novec 1230), dry chemical, foam (Class B), wet chemical (Class K).

Combustible dust: NFPA 652/660 dust hazard analysis (DHA), housekeeping (avoid compressed air), explosion venting/isolation/suppression, Class II electrical classification; secondary explosions cause most damage.
topics.example: A food plant's corn-starch dust collector is indoors with no explosion protection, and dust layers have built up on rafters. The safety professional orders a dust hazard analysis, moves the collector outdoors with explosion venting and isolation valves, starts a housekeeping schedule using vacuum systems approved for combustible dust, and bans compressed-air cleaning.
tips: Know which extinguisher class matches the fire: kitchen grease = K; energized panel = C (no water).
Fire watch: 30 minutes after hot work (NFPA 51B).
Prevention vs protection: housekeeping prevents; explosion venting and sprinklers protect.
Sprinkler K-factor and flammable storage limits are favorite numbers.
topics.yates: Ch. 12 Fire Prevention and Protection, p. 350
subs: Fire prevention
Fire prevention keeps fires from starting by controlling ignition sources and fuel loads (NFPA 1 Fire Code). OSHA 1910.39 requires a fire prevention plan when an OSHA standard calls for one.

1910.39 plan contents: list of major fire hazards with proper handling/storage, potential ignition sources and their control, type of fire protection equipment for each hazard; names/job titles responsible for maintaining equipment and for controlling fuel source hazards; housekeeping procedures.
Written if more than 10 employees; oral if 10 or fewer; review with employees upon assignment.
Controls: hot work permits, housekeeping, electrical maintenance, static control, segregation of incompatibles, smoking rules.
Employers must provide a workplace free of recognized fire hazards (General Duty Clause).
Prevention = stop ignition (frequency). Sprinklers and alarms are protection, not prevention.
Fire protection

Fire protection is the systems and methods that detect, control or extinguish a fire and protect occupants (NFPA 72, NFPA 13, NFPA 101). It includes active systems (alarms, sprinklers, extinguishers) and passive features (fire-rated construction).
Active: needs detection/activation - sprinklers, extinguishers, alarm and detection systems, clean agent, foam, standpipes; needs ongoing ITM (NFPA 25, 72; OSHA 1910.157).
Passive: built-in, no action needed - fire-rated walls/doors/floors (NFPA 80, 101), fire dampers, smoke barriers, fireproofing on steel, firestopping, compartmentation, intumescent paint.
Layered approach: engineering (sprinklers, alarms, ventilation), administrative (prevention plans, permits, drills), protective equipment.
Annual program review and adjustment after audits, new hazards or code changes.
Fire doors propped open defeat passive protection - a frequent inspection finding.
Fire suppression
Suppression systems control or extinguish fire, from portable extinguishers to automatic sprinklers and special agent systems.
Wet pipe: water in pipes, most common, heated areas.
Dry pipe: pressurized air, for freezing areas (unheated warehouses, garages).
Deluge: all heads open, high-hazard areas (aircraft hangars, chemical processing).
Preaction: requires detection signal before water enters pipes (double interlock = two signals); data centers, museums, libraries.
Occupancy hazard classes for sprinkler design: light (offices), ordinary (warehouses, manufacturing), extra (flammable liquids); hydraulically calculated (NFPA 13).
Water-damage-sensitive area = preaction; freezing = dry pipe; rapid total flooding of water = deluge.
Fire science: triangle, tetrahedron, pentagon and phases
Fire is rapid exothermic oxidation (combustion). Removing any element of the fire model stops it.
Triangle: fuel, oxygen (~21% in air), heat. Tetrahedron adds the chemical chain reaction (interrupted by dry chemical and halogenated agents).
Dust explosion pentagon: fuel, oxygen, ignition, dispersion, confinement.
Deflagration = subsonic flame front (flash fire); detonation = supersonic.
Fire phases: incipient, growth, fully developed, decay.
Incomplete combustion produces more CO and soot.
Flash point, fire point, autoignition and flammable limits
Key properties that classify liquids and define when vapors can ignite.
Flash point: lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off enough vapor to form an ignitable mixture with an ignition source (closed-cup method for OSHA).
Fire point: vapors sustain burning for at least 5 s; typically about 10-30 deg C above flash point.
Autoignition temperature (AIT): ignites with no external ignition source (NFPA 497, SDS).
LEL/UEL: below LEL too lean, above UEL too rich; flammable range lies between. Gasoline about 1.4%-7.6%.
Hot work not allowed where atmosphere is within flammable range; confined space entry limit is 10% LEL.
Flash point = vapors CAN ignite; fire point = fire KEEPS burning; AIT = no ignition source needed.
Heat transfer in fires
Fire spreads by conduction, convection and radiation; understanding them predicts fire spread.
Conduction: through solids by direct contact (steel beam through a fire wall ignites the other side).
Convection: movement of hot gases/liquids (smoke rising through stairwells, shafts, ducts to upper floors).
Radiation: electromagnetic (infrared) waves, no medium needed (burning building ignites a neighbor across an alley).
Spread to upper floors via shafts = convection; across a gap to another building = radiation.
Flammable and combustible liquid classification and storage (NFPA 30 / OSHA 1910.106)
Liquids are classed by flash point and boiling point; the lower the class number, the stricter the storage and handling.
Class IA: FP < 73 deg F, BP < 100 deg F (ethyl ether). IB: FP < 73, BP >= 100 (acetone, gasoline, toluene). IC: FP 73-100 (xylene, turpentine).
Class II: 100-140 deg F (diesel, mineral spirits); IIIA: 140-200 (the guide lists kerosene here, but kerosene is usually Class II, FP about 100-150 deg F); IIIB: >= 200 (vegetable oil, glycerol).
OSHA 1910.106 now uses GHS Categories 1-4 (Cat 4 = FP > 140 to 199.4 deg F); NFPA 30 still uses classes.
Cabinets: no more than 60 gal of Category 1-3 (Class I/II) or 120 gal of Category 4/Class III per cabinet; max 3 cabinets in one fire area.
Storage rooms: 1-hour (or 2-hour) fire rating, self-closing doors, curbs/sumps; ventilation at least 1 cfm/ft2 of floor area (NFPA 30); keep vapors below 10% LEL.
Bond and ground containers when transferring Class I liquids (NFPA 77).
Know how to classify a liquid from flash point and boiling point and then pick the control.
Electrical and static ignition sources
Faulty wiring, overloaded circuits, arcing and static discharge are leading ignition sources.
Grounding connects to earth; bonding equalizes potential between conductive objects - both used for flammable liquid transfer (NFPA 77).
Static controls also: humidity control, anti-static flooring, non-sparking tools.
Hazards: overloaded circuits, damaged insulation, loose connections (arcing), unlisted equipment, misused extension cords.
Controls: AFCIs, explosion-proof equipment in classified locations, infrared thermography, NFPA 70E program.
Electrical fires: Class C agents (CO2, dry chemical); de-energize before using water. Heat detectors are better than smoke detectors in dusty electrical rooms.
Hot work safety (NFPA 51B / OSHA 1910.252)
Welding, cutting, brazing, grinding and soldering are major ignition sources; outside designated hot work areas they require a permit.
Permit: date, location, nature of job, authorization signature, fire watch assigned, precautions checklist.
Move combustibles at least 35 ft away or protect with fire-resistant covers/shields.
Fire watch during work and at least 30 min after (OSHA 1910.252); NFPA 51B (2019 and later editions) requires at least 1 hour after, followed by further fire monitoring - the guide states 30 minutes.
Test atmosphere with LEL detection in enclosed or poorly ventilated areas.
Fire watch must know how to use extinguishers and sound the alarm; designated permanent hot work areas preferred.
Combustibles that cannot be moved 35 ft must be covered - and a fire watch is required.
Combustible dust
Finely divided solids that present a fire or explosion hazard when dispersed in air - even materials not normally flammable (sugar, flour, aluminum, wood).
Stages: accumulation, dispersion, confinement, ignition, primary explosion, secondary explosion (secondary usually causes most damage and deaths).
NFPA 652 requires a Dust Hazard Analysis (DHA); NFPA 654 prevention; OSHA uses General Duty Clause and the Combustible Dust NEP (CPL 03-00-008).
Housekeeping trigger: dust layer over 1/32 in. (paper clip thickness) over 5% of floor area; vacuum with approved equipment, avoid dry sweeping and compressed air.
Electrical: Class II locations; Group E metal, F carbonaceous, G grain/organic; Div 1 normal operations, Div 2 abnormal.
Tests: Kst (deflagration index; St1 0-200, St2 200-300, St3 > 300 bar-m/s), MIE, MEC, go/no-go screening.
Engineering: explosion venting (NFPA 68), isolation and inerting (NFPA 69), spark detection; cases: Imperial Sugar 2008 (14 deaths).
Secondary explosion prevention = housekeeping of settled dust.
Fire detection and alarm systems (NFPA 72)
Detection provides early warning, starts evacuation and can trigger suppression and shutdowns.
Ionization smoke detectors: fast-flaming fires; photoelectric: smoldering fires.
Heat detectors: fixed temperature (e.g., 135 or 190 deg F) or rate-of-rise; used where smoke detectors false-alarm (kitchens, dusty areas).
Flame detectors: UV fastest (also triggered by welding arcs), IR for hydrocarbon fires, UV/IR dual for accuracy.
Gas detectors alarm before LEL is reached.
FACP supervises power and circuits; notification appliances meet ADA/NFPA 72; mass notification per NFPA 72 Ch. 24; records available to the AHJ.
Interlocks: sprinklers, gas shutoff, HVAC smoke dampers, emergency power (NFPA 110).
Smoldering fire = photoelectric; flaming fire = ionization; dusty room = heat detector.
Portable fire extinguishers (NFPA 10 / OSHA 1910.157)
Extinguishers are classed by fire type and must be selected, located, inspected and maintained for the expected hazard.
Classes: A ordinary combustibles; B flammable liquids/gases; C energized electrical; D combustible metals (dry powder); K cooking oils (wet chemical, potassium acetate).
Max travel distance: A 75 ft; B 30 or 50 ft depending on rating; D 75 ft; K 30 ft; C based on the A or B hazard.
Monthly visual inspection; annual maintenance (records kept 1 year or until next maintenance).

Hydrostatic test every 5 years (water, CO2, wet chemical) or 12 years (dry chemical) - the guide lists '6-year and 12-year'; 6 years is the internal maintenance interval for stored-pressure dry chemical.
Training on initial hire and annually if employees are expected to use them.
Special suppression systems
Gaseous and foam systems protect areas where water is unsuitable.
Clean agents (NFPA 2001): FM-200 (HFC-227ea), Novec 1230, inert gases (Inergen, Argonite) - no residue, non-conductive; for data centers, electrical rooms, museums.
CO2 (NFPA 12): smothers by displacing oxygen; lethal at design concentrations - pre-discharge alarm, delay, lockout for entry; use in normally unoccupied areas (transformers, generators).
Foam (NFPA 11, 16): AFFF and AR-AFFF for Class B fires (hangars, fuel racks); alcohol-resistant foam for polar solvents. PFAS-containing AFFF is being phased out.
Clean agent inspection: semiannual cylinder weight/pressure checks and functional tests without discharge.
Sprinkler inspection, testing and maintenance (NFPA 25)
Water-based systems must be inspected and tested on fixed schedules to remain reliable.
Monthly: control valves (sealed/locked) and gauges (dry, preaction, deluge).
Quarterly: alarm devices (waterflow, supervisory).
Annually: visual sprinkler inspection, main drain/flow tests.
Every 5 years: internal pipe inspection.
Sprinkler head testing: dry sprinklers every 10 years; standard-response heads at 50 years then every 10; fast-response at 20 years then every 10.
Keep at least 18 in. clearance below sprinkler deflectors; do not hang items from piping.
Closed control valve = most common reason sprinklers fail - valves must be supervised or locked open.
Segregation and separation
Separate incompatible or flammable materials and control building design and ventilation to prevent fires and limit their spread.
Oxygen cylinders separated from fuel-gas cylinders or combustibles by 20 ft or a 5-ft-high noncombustible barrier with at least 1/2-hour fire rating (1910.253).
NFPA 400 segregation by hazard class (oxidizers away from flammables); NFPA 30 Ch. 9 container storage; 1910.1450 lab segregation procedures.
Separate full and empty containers; store chemicals below eye level; secondary containment; keep fire department access clear.
Outdoor storage: minimum distances to buildings, property lines and public ways per NFPA 30 tables.
Fire safety housekeeping
Good housekeeping reduces fuel load, prevents ignition and keeps exits and fire equipment accessible (1910.22, NFPA 1, 101, 13).
Remove trash, scrap and oily rags daily; oily rags in covered metal containers.
Keep aisles, exits, extinguishers, alarms and electrical panels clear (36 in. working clearance at panels per NEC).
No storage in stairwells, exits or mechanical rooms; maintain 18 in. below sprinklers.
Written checklists, assigned duties, documentation and surprise audits.
mcq: A safety professional notes that a Class BC extinguisher has been placed near the range hood of a deep fat fryer in the cafeteria. The manager says a Class BC extinguisher is fine for a kitchen. Who is correct?
The manager, because a BC agent both cools grease and displaces oxygen
The safety professional, because one extinguisher never holds enough agent for a fryer fire
Neither, because a Class A water extinguisher should be used
The safety professional, because a Class K extinguisher is required for cooking oil and fat fires
NFPA 10 requires Class K (wet chemical) extinguishers for cooking media; the agent saponifies and cools hot oil to prevent reignition. Water on grease causes violent spattering.
A combustible dust explosion requires which two elements in addition to the fire tetrahedron (fuel, heat, oxygen, chain reaction)?
Fuel and confinement
Dispersion and confinement
Dispersion and ignition
Oxygen and pressure
The dust explosion pentagon adds dispersion (a dust cloud) and confinement to fuel, ignition and oxygen. Fuel, ignition and oxygen are already part of the base elements.
Which detector is MOST appropriate for fast-developing flammable-liquid fires in an open process area?
Optical flame detector (UV/IR)
Rate-of-rise heat detector
Photoelectric smoke detector
Fixed-temperature heat detector
UV/IR flame detectors respond in seconds to radiant energy and work outdoors, where smoke and heat dissipate before reaching smoke or heat detectors.
A contractor will weld near a combustible wood-framed wall. According to NFPA 51B, what is the BEST course of action before starting hot work?
Cover the wall with a plastic tarp to prevent damage
Keep a fire extinguisher nearby and start welding immediately
Move combustibles at least 35 feet away or protect them with approved fire-resistant shields or blankets
Post a 'Caution: Hot Work in Progress' sign and proceed
NFPA 51B and OSHA 1910.252 require removal of combustibles within 35 ft or protection with fire-resistant guards, plus a permit and fire watch. Plastic tarps are combustible.
When nearby combustible materials cannot be removed or guarded during welding, a fire watch must be maintained for at least how long after the work is completed?
15 minutes
30 minutes
45 minutes
90 minutes
OSHA 1910.252(a)(2)(iii) requires the fire watch for at least 30 minutes after hot work ends to detect smoldering fires. NFPA 51B (2019+) extends this to 60 minutes, so read what the question cites.
Which NFPA standard specifies the inspection, testing, and maintenance requirements for water-based fire protection systems such as sprinklers?
NFPA 25
NFPA 13
NFPA 72
NFPA 70E
NFPA 25 covers ITM of water-based systems; NFPA 13 covers sprinkler installation and design, NFPA 72 fire alarms, NFPA 70E electrical safety.
An employee uses a portable fire extinguisher on an office fire, but the flames continue to grow. What is the MOST appropriate next action?
Move flammable materials away from the fire
Open windows to allow smoke to escape
Retrieve a larger extinguisher from another floor
Sound the fire alarm and evacuate immediately
Portable extinguishers are for incipient fires only. If the fire grows, the employee should leave, alert others and let trained responders take over.
A renovated attic is being fitted with fire detection. The space is dusty, has wide temperature swings, and no HVAC. What should the safety engineer recommend?
Install combination smoke/CO detectors
Defer installation until the dust settles
Install heat detectors instead of smoke detectors
Calibrate the smoke detectors with open-flame testing
Dust and environmental extremes cause nuisance alarms and failures in smoke detectors; heat detectors are suited to dirty or unconditioned spaces.
Which element was added to the traditional fire triangle to form the fire tetrahedron?
Dispersion
Chemical chain reaction
Confinement
Vaporization

The tetrahedron adds the uninhibited chemical chain reaction to fuel, heat and oxygen; agents such as dry chemical and halon work by interrupting it. Dispersion and confinement belong to the dust pentagon.
What is the required inspection and maintenance frequency for portable fire extinguishers under OSHA 1910.157 and NFPA 10?
Weekly visual check only
Semi-annual inspection only
Inspection every 3 years
Monthly visual inspection and annual maintenance
OSHA 1910.157(e) requires monthly visual inspection and annual maintenance checks; hydrostatic testing occurs at longer intervals (5 or 12 years).

topics.title: Hazardous Materials Transportation and Security
topics.bp: Prepare procedures for the safe transportation and security of hazardous materials
topics.definition: Hazardous materials transportation is regulated by the U.S. DOT Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR 171-180) and internationally by the UN Model Regulations, IMDG Code (sea), IATA DGR (air) and ADR (road, Europe). Security requirements address theft, sabotage and terrorism risks (49 CFR 172 Subpart I security plans; DHS CFATS for facilities).
topics.easy: Before hazmat moves, you must classify it, package it correctly, label and placard it, prepare shipping papers, train the people involved and keep it secure so it cannot be stolen or misused.
points: Nine hazard classes: 1 explosives, 2 gases, 3 flammable liquids, 4 flammable solids, 5 oxidizers/organic peroxides, 6 toxic/infectious, 7 radioactive, 8 corrosives, 9 miscellaneous.

Shipper responsibilities: classify, select UN-specification packaging, mark (proper shipping name, UN number), label, prepare shipping papers with emergency response information and 24-h telephone number, placard information, certify.

Placards (172.504): Table 1 materials (e.g., Division 1.1-1.3, 2.3, 4.3 dangerous when wet, 6.1 PIH, 7 radioactive yellow III) - any quantity; Table 2 materials - when the aggregate gross weight is 1,001 lb or more.
Shipping papers must be within the driver's immediate reach (or in the door pocket when out of the vehicle).

Hazmat employee training (172.704): general awareness, function-specific, safety, security awareness, in-depth security (if a security plan is required) - within 90 days of hire and at least every 3 years.
Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG): first responders' guide - initial isolation and protective action distances; SDS gives detailed chemical information.
Security plans: personnel security (background checks), unauthorized access controls, en-route security (routes, stops, GPS tracking).
Other modes: IMDG Code (sea), IATA (air), pipelines (PHMSA).
topics.example: A plant ships drums of flammable solvent weighing 1,200 lb in total by truck. The shipping coordinator prepares shipping papers with the UN number and emergency phone, applies Class 3 labels, provides Class 3 placards because the aggregate weight exceeds 1,000 lb, and confirms that the driver has hazmat training and keeps the papers within reach.
tips: Table 1 = placard any quantity; Table 2 = 1,001 lb aggregate.
Hazmat training every 3 years; new employees within 90 days.
ERG is for first responders; SDS for detailed chemical data.
Class 8 = corrosive; Class 2 = gases; Class 3 = flammable liquids.
topics.yates: Ch. 27 Hazardous Materials Management, p. 616; Ch. 32 Site Security, p. 731
subs: Hazmat transportation (DOT 49 CFR 171-180)

DOT's Hazardous Materials Regulations govern classification, packaging, marking, labeling, placarding, shipping papers, training and incident reporting for hazmat in commerce - from loading through transit to unloading.

Nine hazard classes: 1 explosives, 2 gases (2.1 flammable, 2.2 non-flammable, 2.3 toxic), 3 flammable liquids (FP <= 140 deg F / 60 deg C), 4 flammable solids, 5 oxidizers (5.1) and organic peroxides (5.2), 6 toxic (6.1) and infectious (6.2), 7 radioactive, 8 corrosives, 9 miscellaneous.
Packing groups: I great danger, II medium, III minor.
Shipping paper basic description order: UN ID number, proper shipping name, hazard class, packing group; plus 24-hour emergency response phone number.
Placards: any quantity of Table 1 materials (e.g., 1.1-1.3, 2.3, 4.3, 7 Yellow-III); Table 2 materials when aggregate gross weight is 1,001 lb or more.
PHMSA (DOT) enforces; FMCSA covers motor carrier rules; incidents reported by phone to the National Response Center immediately (within 12 hours) and in writing on DOT Form 5800.1 within 30 days.
DOT applies during transport; EPA RCRA applies to hazardous waste management and disposal; OSHA HazCom applies in the workplace.
Hazmat security
Hazmat security prevents theft, sabotage and terrorist misuse of hazardous materials in transport and at facilities.
DOT security plans (49 CFR 172.800, Subpart I) required for higher-risk shipments (e.g., placarded quantities, Division 1.1-1.3, select agents, large bulk toxic inhalation hazards).
Plan must address personnel security, unauthorized access and en-route security, based on a security risk assessment.
Facility security: access control, inventory reconciliation, cameras, lighting, background checks, cybersecurity of process controls.
DHS CFATS (6 CFR 27) covered high-risk chemical facilities; its statutory authority lapsed in July 2023. EPA RMP (40 CFR 68) and PSM still apply.
Integrate security planning with emergency response planning.
DOT hazmat employee training (49 CFR 172.704)
Every hazmat employee (anyone who loads, unloads, packages, marks, prepares shipping papers or transports hazmat) must be trained, tested and certified.
Content: general awareness/familiarization, function-specific, safety, security awareness, and in-depth security training if a security plan is required.
Initial training within 90 days of employment or job change (may work under direct supervision meanwhile).
Recurrent training at least every 3 years; records kept for the preceding 3 years and 90 days after employment ends.
Driver training also required for those operating motor vehicles carrying hazmat.
DOT = every 3 years; contrast with HAZWOPER annual refresher.
Marking, labeling, placarding and the Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)
Communication of hazard during transport lets responders identify materials quickly.
Labels go on packages (4-in. diamonds); placards go on vehicles, bulk containers and rail cars (10.8-in. diamonds) on all four sides.
UN/NA number displayed on placards or orange panels for bulk shipments.
ERG: yellow pages (ID number index), blue pages (material name index), orange pages (response guides), green pages (initial isolation and protective action distances for toxic inhalation hazards).
Shipper certifies shipment is properly classified, described, packaged, marked and labeled.
CHEMTREC and other services can provide the required 24-hour emergency response number.
Green ERG pages = isolation and protective action distances.
Packaging and loading/segregation in transport
Packaging must be authorized for the material and packing group, and incompatible classes must be segregated in vehicles.
UN specification packaging is performance-tested (drop, stack, leakproofness) and marked with the UN packaging code.
Segregation table (49 CFR 177.848) prohibits loading certain classes together (e.g., oxidizers with flammables, cyanides with acids).
Secure packages against movement; bulk containers need closures and venting as specified.
Hazardous waste shipments also need an EPA uniform hazardous waste manifest (cradle-to-grave tracking).
Hazmat transportation incident response
Transport incidents require isolation, identification and notification before action.
Approach from upwind, uphill and upstream; isolate the area; identify the material from placards, shipping papers (in the cab within reach of the driver) and the ERG.
Use ERG initial isolation distance first, then protective action (evacuate or shelter in place).
Only trained HAZWOPER responders take offensive action.
Report to NRC and DOT as required; CERCLA reportable quantities trigger federal notification.
Shipping papers are kept within the driver's reach (or in the door pocket) so responders can find them.
mcq: A company driver is transporting several 55-gallon drums of flammable liquid. At a roadside inspection, the officer notes that a placard is missing and the shipping papers are in the glove compartment under personal items. What is the MOST appropriate corrective action?
Place the shipping papers within the driver's immediate reach and replace the missing placard before proceeding
Continue the trip because the drums themselves are sealed and labeled
Have the shipper send new documents while the trip continues
Replace the placard with a handwritten sign
49 CFR 177.817 requires shipping papers within the driver's immediate reach (or in the door pouch), and required placards must be displayed before transport continues.
A truck transporting compressed gas would display which DOT hazard class placard?
Class 1
Class 3
Class 2
Class 8
DOT Class 2 = gases (2.1 flammable, 2.2 non-flammable, 2.3 toxic). Class 1 = explosives, Class 3 = flammable liquids, Class 8 = corrosives.

A new employee will serve as a hazardous materials technician, responding to uncontrolled releases to stop them but not doing post-emergency cleanup. Under 29 CFR 1910.120(q), what is the MINIMUM initial training?
8 hours
24 hours
40 hours
48 hours
1910.120(q)(6)(iii): HAZMAT technicians need at least 24 hours of training equal to the operations level plus specific competencies. 40 hours applies to general site workers at cleanup sites.

A HAZMAT team member enters an area to retrieve soil samples wearing safety glasses, steel-toe boots, coveralls, gloves, and a hard hat, with no respiratory protection. What EPA protection level is this?
Level D
Level A
Level B
Level C
Level D is a work uniform with no respiratory protection and minimal skin protection. Level C adds an air-purifying respirator; B adds SCBA; A is fully encapsulating.

A tanker truck overturns near a facility gate, spilling an unknown liquid. Employees smell a strong chemical odor, and one feels dizzy. The facility has a trained HAZWOPER team on-site. What is the MOST appropriate action?
Call the fire department while employees wait near the spill
Have all employees approach the spill wearing available PPE
Attempt to contain the spill with sandbags right away
Evacuate the area upwind and allow only trained HAZWOPER responders to assess the spill
With an unknown material and symptoms already present, untrained workers must evacuate; only trained responders with proper PPE should identify and control the release.
A truck carries Table 2 hazardous materials (for example Class 3 flammable liquids) in non-bulk packages. When are placards required?
For any quantity
Only above 10,000 lb
When the aggregate gross weight of Table 2 materials is 1,001 lb or more
Never for non-bulk packages
49 CFR 172.504: Table 1 materials (e.g., Division 1.1-1.3 explosives, poison inhalation hazards) need placards in any quantity; Table 2 materials at 1,001 lb or more aggregate gross weight.
Where can first responders find generic hazard and initial response information for materials regulated in transportation?
Incident Command Guide
DOT Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)
The shipper's corporate website
OSHA Hazard Communication standard
The ERG gives generic guidance by UN/NA number and guide page (isolation distances, fire and spill response). The SDS gives product-specific detail.
What is the primary purpose of the International Maritime Dangerous Goods (IMDG) Code?
To establish rules for preventing collisions at sea
To regulate the discharge of pollutants from ships
To set standards for ship construction and design
To provide requirements for safely transporting dangerous goods by sea
The IMDG Code (IMO) governs sea transport of dangerous goods; IATA DGR covers air, and 49 CFR covers US ground transport.
A company ships placarded quantities of hazardous materials by highway. Under 49 CFR 172 Subpart I, its written security plan must address which elements?
Personnel security, unauthorized access, and en route security
Fire extinguisher placement and sprinkler coverage
Driver hours-of-service logs and vehicle fuel economy
Insurance coverage and customer billing
DOT security plans must include an assessment of transportation security risks and measures for personnel security, unauthorized access and en route security, plus security training.
Under DOT hazmat training rules (49 CFR 172.704), which training must ALL hazmat employees receive in addition to general awareness and function-specific training?
40-hour HAZWOPER training
Commercial driver's license training
Safety and security awareness training
Incident commander training

All hazmat employees need general awareness, function-specific, safety and security awareness training, with recurrent training at least every 3 years. In-depth security training applies when a security plan is required.

topics.title: Workplace Violence Prevention
topics.bp: Implement a workplace violence prevention program
topics.definition: Workplace violence is any act or threat of physical violence, harassment, intimidation or other threatening disruptive behavior at the work site. A prevention program combines management commitment, worksite analysis, hazard prevention and control, training and recordkeeping/evaluation (OSHA 3148 guidelines; ANSI/ASIS/SHRM WVPI standard).
topics.easy: Violence at work usually has warning signs. Assess where and how it could happen, design the workplace to deter it, train people to recognize and report warning signs, respond quickly to threats and support those affected.
points: Types: Type I criminal intent (robbery, no relationship - leading cause of workplace homicide), Type II customer/client/patient (healthcare, social services), Type III worker-on-worker, Type IV personal relationship (domestic violence spilling into work).
Risk factors: handling cash, working alone or at night, contact with the public, delivering services in community settings, high-crime areas, guarding valuables.

Program elements: written policy (zero tolerance, no retaliation for reporting), threat assessment team (HR, security, legal, EHS, management), worksite analysis and security survey, controls, training, reporting, post-incident response (medical and psychological support, EAP, investigation), evaluation.

Controls: engineering (access control, lighting, cameras, panic alarms, drop safes, barrier windows, metal detectors), administrative (two-person staffing, cash-handling limits, visitor policies, de-escalation procedures), CPTED (crime prevention through environmental design).

Warning signs: threats, talk of weapons or violence, intimidation, escalating anger, sudden behavior change, isolation, substance abuse. Aggression continuum: anxiety → intimidation → crisis → violence (stages vary by model).

Response: report concerns immediately to supervisor/HR/security; for an imminent threat, call security/911 and follow emergency procedures (Run-Hide-Fight for active shooter). Do not confront or physically intervene.
Security concepts: deter, detect, delay, respond.
topics.example: A former employee sends emails hinting that people 'will understand' his anger. The threat assessment team reviews the messages the same day, notifies security and local police, updates the visitor and badge system, briefs reception staff with a photo, and offers EAP support to the targeted supervisors.
tips: Immediate response to threats: report to HR/security; do not ignore, confront or forward to coworkers.
Know the four violence types and the main risk factors.
Engineering vs administrative: metal detectors and drop safes = engineering; weapon bans and visitor rules = administrative.
Post-incident: medical and psychological support first, then investigation and review of controls.
topics.yates: Ch. 32 Site Security, p. 731
subs: Workplace violence prevention program

A written program that commits management, involves employees, analyzes the worksite, controls hazards, trains staff and records and evaluates incidents. OSHA has no specific standard but enforces under the General Duty Clause (directive CPL 02-01-064).

OSHA program elements (OSHA 3148): management commitment and employee participation; worksite analysis; hazard prevention and control; safety and health training; recordkeeping and program evaluation.
Written policy: zero tolerance, clear reporting procedures, no reprisal for reporting.
Threat assessment team (HR, security, safety, legal, management, EAP) to assess and manage threats.
California requires most employers to have a written Workplace Violence Prevention Plan (Labor Code 6401.9, from July 2024).
Consensus standard: ANSI/ASIS/SHRM WVPI.1 (workplace violence and active assailant prevention, intervention and response).
Management commitment and employee involvement come first; 'install cameras' alone is not a program.
Types of workplace violence
Workplace violence is classified by the relationship between the perpetrator and the workplace (NIOSH / UIIPRC typology).
Type I criminal intent: no legitimate relationship (robbery) - most workplace homicides.
Type II customer/client: patients, customers, students, inmates - most common in healthcare and social services.
Type III worker-on-worker: current or former employee.
Type IV personal relationship: domestic violence that spills into the workplace.
Patient assaulting a nurse = Type II; ex-spouse attacking at work = Type IV.
Risk factors and high-risk occupations
Certain job conditions increase the likelihood of violence and should drive the worksite analysis.

Risk factors: exchanging money with the public, working alone or in small numbers, late night/early morning hours, high-crime areas, guarding valuables, contact with unstable or volatile persons, alcohol served, delivering passengers/goods/services.
High-risk sectors: healthcare and social assistance, retail/late-night retail, taxi/rideshare, law enforcement and corrections.
Worksite analysis: records review (OSHA 300, incident and security reports), employee surveys, security audits.
Engineering and administrative controls for workplace violence
Apply the hierarchy: design out opportunity, then procedures, training and staffing.

Engineering: controlled access, badge systems, bullet-resistant barriers, good lighting, cameras, panic/duress alarms, drop safes and limited cash, curved mirrors, furniture arrangement preventing entrapment, escape routes.
Administrative: adequate staffing, no working alone at night, visitor management, cash-handling limits, check-in procedures for field staff, flagging of violent patients/clients.
Training: recognizing warning signs, de-escalation, reporting, emergency procedures, Run-Hide-Fight.
Warning signs and threat assessment
Most perpetrators show observable concerning behavior beforehand; a trained team assesses and manages threats.
Warning signs: verbal threats, intimidation, fascination with weapons or prior violent incidents, sudden behavior changes, substance abuse, severe stress, paranoia, violation of protective orders.
Threat assessment: gather facts, assess credibility and capability, decide interventions (EAP referral, discipline, security, law enforcement, protective orders).
Treat all threats seriously and document them.
Report and assess threats early - waiting for an overt act is the wrong answer.
Active shooter response and post-incident response
Employees must know what to do during an attack and the organization must support victims afterward.
DHS Run, Hide, Fight; when police arrive, keep hands visible and follow commands.
NFPA 3000 (ASHER) - integrated active shooter/hostile event preparedness, response and recovery with unified command.
Post-incident: medical care, report and investigate, critical incident stress debriefing, EAP/counseling, legal support.
Record injuries from workplace violence on the OSHA 300 log if recordable criteria are met; evaluate the program after each incident.
mcq: A hospital emergency department nurse is assaulted by a patient's relative. Which type of workplace violence is this?
Type I - criminal intent (no relationship)
Type II - customer/client/patient
Type III - worker-on-worker
Type IV - personal relationship
Type II involves customers, clients, patients, students or their families and is most common in healthcare. Type I is criminal intent, such as robbery by a stranger.

An employee reports that a co-worker has been making aggressive comments about supervisors and slammed equipment after a performance review. The company has a written workplace violence prevention program. What should the supervisor do FIRST?
Report the concern to HR or the safety/threat assessment team for immediate assessment under the program
Ignore the behavior until it escalates into a physical incident
Confront the worker publicly to discourage further aggression
Tell employees to avoid the worker but take no formal action
Warning signs should be reported early so a trained team can assess the threat; public confrontation can escalate and ignoring it misses the chance for prevention.
A recently terminated employee is sending hostile, vaguely threatening emails to your team, saying he might do something to 'make everyone understand.' How should the team respond?
Reply to explain the reasons for his termination
Ignore the emails, assuming he will cool down
Forward the emails to coworkers to gather opinions
Report the emails to security and human resources as soon as possible
Veiled threats from a former employee are a recognized risk factor; preserve the emails and report them to security and HR for threat assessment and protective measures.

Before construction begins, management convenes architects, safety experts, police, and fire officials to design security into a new facility (lighting, sight lines, controlled entrances). Which approach is this?
Safe construction through environmental design
Planned protection through environmental engineering
Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED)
Planned construction through environmental engineering
CPTED uses natural surveillance, access control, territorial reinforcement and maintenance to reduce crime opportunities; it is the security analog of prevention through design.
In a workplace violence prevention program, which element BEST demonstrates management commitment?
Installing CCTV cameras without any policy updates
A written zero-tolerance policy signed by top leadership and communicated to all employees
Conducting unannounced drills only
Providing counseling only after incidents
OSHA's program elements begin with management commitment and employee participation, shown by a visible, leadership-endorsed written policy backed by resources.
What is the MOST appropriate post-incident action following a workplace violence event?
Provide medical and psychological support, then investigate and review controls
Return operations to normal immediately
Focus only on legal reporting requirements
Suspend all security staff involved
OSHA guidance calls for immediate care, trauma counseling and debriefing, followed by investigation and corrective action to prevent recurrence.
Which four basic security concepts should be included in a facility security program?
Deter, detect, train, respond
Read, react, identify, respond
Deter, detect, delay, dial
Deter, detect, delay, respond
Layered security aims to deter attempts, detect intrusions, delay the intruder long enough for a response, and respond.
According to NSC data, what is the greatest risk factor for homicide at work?
A disgruntled coworker
A random shooter
Robbery
A recently fired worker
Most workplace homicides are Type I, committed during robberies, which is why late-night retail and taxi work are high-risk. Coworker violence is far less frequent.
What can a company do to help employees avoid the bystander effect if an active shooter enters the workplace?
Permit employees to carry concealed firearms
Train employees in advance on what to do (e.g., run, hide, fight) and how to report
Establish a clear hierarchy of communication
Develop stress management programs
Prior training and drills reduce freezing and diffusion of responsibility, so people act quickly instead of waiting for others.
A worksite analysis of a 24-hour convenience store shows that most incidents occur late at night during robberies. Which control is MOST effective at reducing this risk?
Require employees to work faster during night shifts
Post a zero-tolerance policy in the break room
Limit cash on hand with a drop safe, keep windows clear for visibility, and provide bright lighting with posted signs
Provide annual training only for day-shift workers

Engineering and administrative controls that reduce the reward and raise visibility (drop safes, low cash, clear sight lines, lighting) are proven robbery deterrents. A policy alone does not deter outsiders.

topics.title: Environmental Protection and Pollution Prevention
topics.bp: Describe environmental protection and pollution prevention programs (e.g., spill containment, abatement, best practices)
topics.definition: Environmental protection programs prevent or control releases to air, water and land. Pollution prevention (P2) reduces pollution at its source rather than treating it after it is created (Pollution Prevention Act of 1990). Key U.S. laws include the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act (NPDES, SPCC), RCRA, CERCLA, EPCRA and TSCA.
topics.easy: It is cheaper and safer not to make pollution in the first place. When you must store oils or chemicals, put a second container around them so a leak cannot reach drains, soil or rivers.
points: P2 hierarchy: source reduction → recycling/reuse → treatment → disposal (last resort).

SPCC (40 CFR 112): facilities with > 1,320 gal aggregate aboveground oil storage capacity (containers ≥ 55 gal) or > 42,000 gal underground that could discharge to navigable waters; secondary containment for the largest container plus freeboard for precipitation; plan certified by a PE (or self-certified if qualified); annual training for oil-handling personnel.
Secondary containment design: 110% of the largest tank is a common rule; RCRA container storage: 10% of total volume or 100% of the largest container, whichever is greater.
Clean Water Act: NPDES permits for point-source discharges; stormwater (SWPPP), construction site erosion and sediment controls (silt fence, inlet protection).

Clean Air Act: NAAQS for six criteria pollutants (CO, lead, NO₂, ozone, PM, SO₂); NESHAP for hazardous air pollutants; Title V operating permits; abatement equipment - baghouses (particulates), cyclones, electrostatic precipitators, wet scrubbers (acid gases), thermal oxidizers (VOCs), carbon adsorption.

EPCRA (SARA Title III): emergency planning (Section 302 threshold planning quantities of extremely hazardous substances), release notification (304), Tier II inventory reporting (311/312), Toxics Release Inventory (313). CERCLA (Superfund): cleanup of contaminated sites and release reporting of reportable quantities (RQ).
Best practices: inventory minimization, closed-loop systems, leak detection and repair, housekeeping, spill kits and drills, environmental aspects/impacts review (ISO 14001).
topics.example: A trucking terminal stores three 1,000-gallon diesel tanks. Its aggregate capacity (3,000 gal) exceeds 1,320 gal, so it needs an SPCC plan regardless of how much fuel is actually in the tanks. Double-walled tanks, a curbed fueling pad draining to an oil-water separator, and annual spill-response training are added.
tips: SPCC applicability is based on storage CAPACITY, not the amount on hand.
Source reduction beats recycling, treatment and disposal.
Match law to topic: EPCRA = community right-to-know; CERCLA = Superfund; RCRA = hazardous waste cradle to grave; TSCA = chemical inventory (PCBs, asbestos, lead).
topics.yates: Ch. 34 Environmental Management, p. 754; Ch. 33 Sustainability
subs: Spill containment

Spill containment prevents the uncontrolled release of oil, fuel, chemicals or waste into soil, water or air. It combines primary containment (tanks, drums, pipes), secondary containment (berms, double walls, spill pallets), floor and drain protection, and procedures and training.
Spills come from overfilling, equipment failure, corrosion, improper handling and transfer accidents.
Primary containment = the container holding the material under normal conditions; must be sound and compatible with contents.
Secondary containment = catches a primary failure: concrete/earthen berms, double-walled tanks, spill pallets, portable trays.
Floors in spill-prone areas: chemical-resistant, non-slip coating, sloped to sumps; storm drains covered or plugged during transfers.
Overfill prevention: high-level alarms, automatic shutoff valves, backup float systems (tank filling is a common spill source).
Containment is a system (design + technology + procedures + training), not just a berm.
SPCC rule (40 CFR 112)

EPA's Spill Prevention, Control and Countermeasure rule requires a written plan at non-transportation facilities that store oil above threshold amounts and could reasonably discharge to navigable waters.
Thresholds: more than 1,320 gal aggregate aboveground oil storage (counting containers 55 gal or larger) or more than 42,000 gal completely buried.
Plan includes site diagrams, drain maps, containment, inspection checklists, emergency contacts, training records.
Certified by a Professional Engineer and reviewed at least every 5 years (qualified facilities with 10,000 gal or less may self-certify).
Oil-water separators and secondary containment are typical SPCC controls.
SPCC is about OIL (EPA, water protection); HAZWOPER is about worker protection during response.
Secondary containment sizing (calculation)
Containment volume is sized from the largest container and the total stored volume. The guide states the rule as 110% of the largest container or 10% of total volume, whichever is greater.
RCRA container storage (40 CFR 264.175): 10% of total volume or 100% of the largest container, whichever is greater - the guide states 110%.
SPCC: hold the largest container plus freeboard for precipitation; 110% of the largest tank is the common design practice for outdoor dikes.
Example: four 55-gal drums = 220 gal total; 10% = 22 gal; largest = 55 gal (110% = 60.5 gal) -> size for the larger value (55-60.5 gal).
Example: 500-gal diesel tank -> 110% = 550 gal minimum; a 1,100-gal berm complies.
Dike volume = L x W x H (ft3) x 7.48 gal/ft3; subtract volume displaced by other tanks inside the dike.
Always compute BOTH values (percent of largest and percent of total) and choose the greater.
Spill response equipment and readiness
Spill kits must be located near potential spill points, matched to the hazard, and fully stocked.
Oil-only kits: hydrophobic pads/socks (repel water). Universal kits: water-based and non-aggressive chemicals. Hazmat kits: acids, bases, unknowns.
Contents: pads, socks, pillows, neutralizers, gloves/goggles/aprons, disposal bags and labels, emergency contacts.
Absorbent must be compatible - oil absorbents may be unsuitable for strong acids.
SDS Section 6 (accidental release measures) gives spill guidance.
Wrong absorbent for the chemical (e.g., combustible absorbent on an oxidizer) is a classic distractor.
Spill-related regulatory frameworks
Several overlapping rules govern spill prevention and response.
RCRA tank rules (40 CFR 264/265 Subpart J): secondary containment, leak detection, daily inspections with records.
SWPPP (40 CFR 122.26): stormwater controls such as berms, drain protection and covers.
OSHA HAZWOPER 1910.120: tiered responder training (awareness, operations - defensive, technician - offensive/hands-on, specialist, incident commander).
OSHA HazCom 1910.1200: SDS Section 6 and label/SDS training.
NFPA 30: storage spacing, containment and drainage for flammable/combustible liquids; ISO 14001 clause 8.2: emergency preparedness including environmental releases.
Operations level = defensive actions from a safe distance; technician level = approach the release to stop it.
Abatement (pollution abatement overview)

Pollution abatement captures, treats or reduces pollutants before they reach air, water or soil, ideally at the point of generation. It uses engineering controls plus administrative procedures to meet CAA, CWA, NESHAP and SWPPP requirements.
Proactive - controls pollution at the source rather than reacting to effects.
Media: air emissions, water discharges, stormwater runoff, soil.
Benefits: legal compliance, lower operational risk, worker safety, public image, sustainability metrics.
Multistage control is common (e.g., cyclone pre-cleaner then baghouse).
Memory set: Baghouse = dust; Scrubber = acid gas; VRU = VOC; Separator = oil; pH system = acid/base; SWPPP = sediment.
Air regulations: CAA, NAAQS, Title V, NESHAP
The Clean Air Act authorizes EPA to regulate air pollutants from stationary and mobile sources.
NAAQS criteria pollutants: PM (PM10, PM2.5), SO2, NOx (NO2), CO, ozone, lead.
Title V operating permits (40 CFR 70) required for major sources.
New Source Review: BACT for new or modified major sources (PSD areas); LAER in nonattainment areas.
NESHAP (40 CFR 63) controls hazardous air pollutants (benzene, formaldehyde, methylene chloride) by industry sector using MACT.
Nonattainment area = region not meeting a NAAQS; stricter controls for ozone precursors (VOC, NOx).
BACT = new/modified sources under NSR; MACT = HAPs under NESHAP.
Air pollution control devices
Device selection depends on pollutant type (particulate vs gas), particle size, industry and permit limits.
Baghouse (fabric filter): fine PM10/PM2.5, over 99% efficiency; watch bag rupture/bypass.
Wet scrubber: acid gases (SO2, HCl, HF) with alkaline liquid; needs mist eliminator; makes wastewater (CWA).
Dry scrubber/dry sorbent injection: acid gases with lime or sodium bicarbonate; no wastewater, lower cost, good for arid areas and retrofits; solids caught by baghouse/ESP.
Cyclone: coarse particles by centrifugal force, 70-90% for particles over 10 microns; pre-cleaner only.
Electrostatic precipitator (ESP): fine/submicron particles, up to 99.9%; affected by moisture and sticky particles.
Vapor recovery unit (VRU): VOCs at tank vents and loading; condenser, adsorber or compressor; required under NESHAP for bulk terminals.
Submicron particles -> ESP or baghouse; coarse only -> cyclone; acid gas -> scrubber; VOC -> VRU/carbon/thermal oxidizer.
Water pollution abatement (CWA, NPDES, pretreatment)
The Clean Water Act regulates discharges to waters of the U.S. Direct dischargers need NPDES permits; indirect dischargers to a POTW must meet pretreatment standards.
NPDES (40 CFR 122): effluent limits, monitoring, stormwater controls.
Pretreatment (40 CFR 403) for industrial users of municipal sewers; effluent guidelines 40 CFR 400-471.
Oil-water separator: oil rises and is skimmed, solids settle; sized for flow and oil type; required under SPCC/many NPDES permits.
pH neutralization: automated dosing (lime, caustic, acid) to typical discharge range 6.0-9.0.
Clarifiers/settling tanks: gravity removal of suspended solids, often with coagulants/flocculants.
Activated carbon: adsorbs trace organics, VOCs, chlorine, color; polishing step; monitor breakthrough; spent carbon may be hazardous waste.
Electroplating acidic rinsewater to a city sewer -> pH neutralization + industrial pretreatment permit.
Stormwater controls (SWPPP BMPs)
Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plans under 40 CFR 122.26 use best management practices to keep sediment and pollutants out of runoff.
BMPs: silt fences, retention/detention ponds, inlet protection (filter socks, drain baskets), vegetative swales and buffers.
Controls must be maintained; clogged filters and damaged fences are ineffective.
Visual monitoring and sampling during rain events are often required.
Prevent illicit discharges of chemicals or wash water to storm drains.
Soil pollution abatement
Soil abatement mitigates or removes hazardous substances (metals, hydrocarbons, pesticides, solvents, lead paint dust) under CERCLA, RCRA corrective action, TSCA and brownfield programs.
Excavation and off-site disposal: fast and definitive but costly; RCRA waste classification and DOT 49 CFR transport.
