Stabilization/solidification: cement, fly ash or lime binders immobilize metals; does not remove contamination; verify with TCLP (Method 1311).
Bioremediation: microbes degrade hydrocarbons; needs oxygen, nutrients, proper pH; months to years (land farming, biopiles).
Soil vapor extraction: vacuum removes VOCs from dry permeable soil; off-gas treatment required (CAA); often paired with air sparging.
Phytoremediation: plants (sunflowers, willows, mustard) for low-level metals; cheap but slow.
Heavy metals -> stabilization; VOCs in dry soil -> SVE; fuel spills -> bioremediation; urgent/near receptors -> excavation.
Best practices in pollution prevention
Best practices combine the pollution prevention hierarchy with administrative controls: plans, training, inspections, compatibility checks and drills.
Pollution Prevention Act 1990 hierarchy: source reduction > recycling > treatment > disposal/release.
Train spill responders per HAZWOPER with hands-on drills; awareness training for all employees.
Weekly inspection of tanks, hoses, valves and containment (best practice); log findings and track corrective actions.
Keep drain valves on containment closed and locked; inspect rainwater before release.
Integrate into an ISO 14001 EMS for continual improvement.
Source reduction (prevent at origin) beats any end-of-pipe abatement on 'BEST' questions.
mcq: Which regulation requires facilities with more than 1,320 gallons of aboveground oil storage capacity to prepare a Spill Prevention, Control, and Countermeasure (SPCC) Plan?
Clean Air Act
Resource Conservation and Recovery Act
EPA Oil Pollution Prevention rule (40 CFR 112)
Toxic Substances Control Act

The SPCC rule (40 CFR 112, issued under the Clean Water Act) applies to non-transportation facilities with over 1,320 gal aboveground (or 42,000 gal buried) oil capacity that could reach navigable waters.
Under EPA's SPCC rule, secondary containment for bulk oil storage containers must hold:
The capacity of the largest single container plus sufficient freeboard for precipitation
50% of the total stored volume
Exactly 100% of all containers combined
10% of the largest container
40 CFR 112.8(c)(2): containment for the entire capacity of the largest single container plus freeboard for precipitation (commonly designed as 110%).
A hazardous waste container storage area holds twenty 55-gallon drums of liquid waste. Under RCRA (40 CFR 264.175), what is the MINIMUM secondary containment capacity?
55 gallons
60.5 gallons
1,100 gallons
110 gallons
Containment must hold 10% of total volume or 100% of the largest container, whichever is greater: 10% x (20 x 55 = 1,100) = 110 gal, which exceeds 55 gal. Trap: using only the largest container.
What is the main goal of a pollution abatement program?
To record environmental data for audits
To capture or reduce pollutants before they are released to the environment
To clean up chemical spills after release
To eliminate the need for any waste treatment
Abatement means controlling or reducing emissions and discharges (e.g., scrubbers, filters, treatment) before release; cleanup after release is remediation.
Which control is a Best Management Practice (BMP) for stormwater pollution prevention at a construction site?
Silt fences and sediment traps
HEPA filtration
Baghouse filters
Cyclone separators
Stormwater BMPs such as silt fences, sediment basins and inlet protection keep sediment out of runoff. The other choices are air pollution controls.
Which action ranks HIGHEST in the EPA pollution prevention hierarchy?
Treating waste before discharge
Recycling spent solvent off-site
Disposing of waste in a permitted landfill
Changing the process to use a water-based coating that produces no hazardous waste
The Pollution Prevention Act hierarchy is source reduction > recycling > treatment > disposal. Eliminating the waste at the source is best.
Which air pollution control device is MOST suitable for removing coarse particles (greater than 10 microns), often as a pre-cleaner?
Baghouse filter
Electrostatic precipitator
Cyclone separator
Wet scrubber for acid gases
Cyclones use centrifugal force and are efficient and cheap for large particles; baghouses and ESPs are used for fine particulates.
Under the Clean Air Act, what type of permit is required for major stationary emission sources?
RCRA Part B permit
Title V operating permit
CERCLA clearance certificate
NPDES permit
Title V operating permits consolidate all CAA requirements for major sources. NPDES permits cover point-source water discharges under the CWA.
A facility neutralizes acidic process wastewater to meet pH limits before discharging it to the municipal sewer (POTW). Which pollution-control approach is this?
Pretreatment
Solidification
Recycling
Filtration
Industrial users must pretreat wastewater to meet POTW and CWA pretreatment standards; pH adjustment is a common pretreatment step.
Under EPCRA Section 302, what is a 'threshold planning quantity' (TPQ)?
The minimum quantity of any chemical that can be stored without reporting
The quantity of an extremely hazardous substance (EHS) on site that triggers emergency planning notification
The maximum amount of any chemical that may be released without consequence
The quantity of waste a company must dispose of yearly to avoid EPA oversight
When an EHS is present at or above its TPQ, the facility must notify the state and local emergency planning bodies and take part in local emergency planning.

topics.title: Hazardous Materials Management
topics.bp: Identify procedures used to manage hazardous materials (e.g., GHS classification system, storage and handling, policy, security, hazardous waste storage and disposal)
topics.definition: Hazardous materials management covers the whole life of hazardous chemicals at a site: purchasing approval, hazard classification and communication (GHS/HCS), safe storage and handling, security, and the storage and disposal of hazardous waste under RCRA.
topics.easy: Know what chemicals you have, label them clearly, store incompatible ones apart, keep them secure, and when they become waste, follow the RCRA rules from the moment the waste is generated until final disposal.
points: GHS/HCS 2012 (1910.1200, updated 2024): classification into physical, health (and environmental) hazard classes and categories; labels with product identifier, signal word (Danger or Warning), hazard statements, precautionary statements, pictograms, supplier information; 16-section SDS (Sec. 2 hazard ID, Sec. 7 handling and storage, Sec. 8 exposure controls/PPE, Sec. 10 stability and reactivity).

Nine HCS pictograms (eight OSHA-required): flame, flame over circle (oxidizer), exploding bomb, gas cylinder, corrosion, skull and crossbones (acute toxicity severe), exclamation mark (irritant, sensitizer, less severe), health hazard (carcinogen, mutagen, reproductive, respiratory sensitizer), environment (not required by OSHA).
Category 1 is the most severe in GHS (opposite of NFPA 704, where 4 is most severe).
Written HazCom program: chemical inventory list, labeling, SDS access, training (initially and when new hazards are introduced), non-routine tasks, contractor communication.

Storage and handling: segregation by compatibility (oxidizers away from flammables, acids away from bases, water-reactives dry), secondary containment, ventilation, flammable cabinets, quantity limits, inspections.
Security: chemical security (CFATS), inventory control, locked storage, access lists.

RCRA hazardous waste: listed (F - non-specific sources such as spent solvents; K - specific industries; P - acutely hazardous discarded commercial chemicals; U - toxic discarded commercial chemicals) or characteristic (ignitable, corrosive, reactive, toxic - TCLP).

Generator categories: VSQG ≤ 100 kg/month; SQG > 100 to < 1,000 kg/month (180 days storage, 270 if > 200 miles); LQG ≥ 1,000 kg/month or > 1 kg acute (90 days). Satellite accumulation up to 55 gal (1 qt acute). Containers closed, labeled 'Hazardous Waste' with hazard indication and accumulation start date; weekly inspections; uniform hazardous waste manifest; LQG annual training.
topics.example: An inspector finds unlabeled spray bottles of a solvent cleaner and containers of waste solvent with no dates. The safety professional labels the bottles with GHS workplace labels, adds the solvent to the chemical inventory, dates the waste containers with the accumulation start date, moves them to the central accumulation area, and schedules weekly inspections.
tips: SDS Section 8 = PPE and exposure limits; Section 2 = hazard identification.
GHS Category 1 = most hazardous.
Generator category thresholds and accumulation times are high-yield numbers.
Flame over circle = oxidizer.
topics.yates: Ch. 4 Regulations (HazCom/GHS comparison), p. 55; Ch. 27 Hazardous Materials Management, p. 616
subs: GHS classification system
The UN Globally Harmonized System standardizes chemical classification, labels and SDSs. OSHA adopted it in the Hazard Communication Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1200 (2012, updated 2024).
Three hazard groups: physical, health, environmental (OSHA does not enforce environmental classes).
Each hazard class is split into categories; Category 1 is the most severe (Flammable Liquid Cat 1 is worse than Cat 3).
Physical: flammables, gases under pressure, explosives, oxidizers, pyrophorics, self-heating.
Health: acute toxicity, skin corrosion, respiratory sensitization, carcinogenicity, reproductive toxicity, STOT.
EPA uses hazard categories for EPCRA Tier II; DOT uses its own 9 classes; NFPA 704 is a separate 0-4 system (4 = most severe).
GHS: Category 1 = MOST hazardous. NFPA 704: 4 = MOST hazardous. The numbers run opposite.
GHS labels: signal words, pictograms and statements
A shipped-container label has six elements: product identifier, signal word, pictogram(s), hazard statements, precautionary statements and supplier information.
Only two signal words: Danger (severe) and Warning (less severe); only one per label - Danger overrides.
Nine pictograms (red diamond border); OSHA requires eight - the environment pictogram is not mandatory in U.S. workplaces.

Flame = flammables; flame over circle = oxidizers; exploding bomb = explosives/self-reactives; gas cylinder = gases under pressure; corrosion = skin burns/metal corrosion; skull and crossbones = acute toxicity (fatal/toxic); health hazard = carcinogen, mutagen, respiratory sensitizer; exclamation mark = irritant, skin sensitizer, narcotic effects.
Hazard statements are standardized and cannot be altered (e.g., 'May cause cancer').
Precautionary statements give handling, storage, PPE and emergency instructions.
Respiratory sensitizer = health hazard pictogram; skin sensitizer = exclamation mark.
Safety Data Sheets (16 sections)
The SDS replaced the MSDS and must follow a fixed 16-section format. Employers must keep SDSs readily accessible to workers on every shift and update them when new hazard information arrives.
1 Identification, 2 Hazard identification, 3 Composition, 4 First aid, 5 Fire-fighting, 6 Accidental release, 7 Handling and storage, 8 Exposure controls/PPE.
9 Physical/chemical properties, 10 Stability and reactivity, 11 Toxicological information.
12 Ecological, 13 Disposal, 14 Transport, 15 Regulatory - included for GHS consistency but not enforced by OSHA.
16 Other information, including date of last revision.
Electronic access is acceptable if there are no barriers to immediate access.
Spill guidance = Section 6; PPE and exposure limits = Section 8; incompatibles = Section 10.
Storage of hazardous materials
Storage must prevent fires, toxic releases and reactions by using proper cabinets/rooms, segregation, ventilation and containment, under OSHA 1910.106, NFPA 30/400/45 and RCRA.
Flammable cabinets (NFPA 30/OSHA): max 60 gal Class I/II (120 gal Class III) per cabinet; labeled 'FLAMMABLE - KEEP FIRE AWAY'; doors closed; away from ignition sources.
Corrosives: chemically resistant (polyethylene or epoxy-coated) cabinets with trays; acids and bases separate.
Toxics/poisons: locked, access-restricted, inventoried.
Compressed gas cylinders: upright, capped, secured; full and empty separated; oxygen and fuel gas separated by 20 ft or a 5-ft-high, 1/2-hour fire-rated wall (1910.253).
Inside storage rooms for flammables: ventilation of at least six air changes per hour; explosion-proof electrical where required.
Oxygen cylinders stored next to acetylene with no 20 ft / 5 ft wall separation is a classic violation.
Segregation of incompatible materials
Incompatible chemicals must be physically separated so a leak cannot cause fire, explosion or toxic gas.
Acids away from bases; oxidizers away from flammables/combustibles.
Cyanides never near acids (hydrogen cyanide gas); hypochlorite away from acids (chlorine gas).
Water-reactives isolated from sinks, sprinklers and humid areas.
Segregate with separate cabinets, distance or fire-rated barriers - not just different shelves of one cabinet.
Check SDS Section 10 and compatibility charts.
Handling and transfer of hazardous materials
Transfers are high-risk; controls focus on static, splashes and container breakage.
Bond and ground flammable liquid transfers to prevent static ignition (NFPA 77).
Use closed dispensing systems (pumps, nozzles) instead of open pouring.
Never carry breakable containers by hand - use carriers, spill trays and carts.
Select PPE from the SDS; eyewash/shower within 10 seconds travel (ANSI Z358.1) where corrosives are handled.
Containers kept closed, compatible and in good condition; secondary containers labeled.
Bonding equalizes potential between containers; grounding drains charge to earth - both are needed for Class I transfers.
Security of hazardous materials
Hazmat security protects against intentional misuse - theft, sabotage or terrorism - through access control, physical barriers, information protection and emergency integration.
Access control: authorized trained staff only, key cards/PINs/biometrics, sign-in logs, restricted-area signage.
Physical: locked cabinets/cages, steel doors, fencing, CCTV, motion detectors, lighting, intrusion alarms.
Bulk tanks: locked hatches and remote fill points, screened vents, fenced dikes, tamper-evident seals.
Protect inventory data: limit database access, secure Tier II reports and chemical maps, no public posting of tank contents.
Plan for theft, sabotage and suspicious items; drill with police, fire and LEPC.
Insider threat and missing inventory scenarios: first secure/control access and investigate, then report.
CFATS (DHS Chemical Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards)
CFATS covered facilities holding screening threshold quantities of Chemicals of Interest (e.g., ammonium nitrate, chlorine, hydrogen peroxide).
Top-Screen survey submitted to DHS; high-risk facilities assigned Tiers 1-4 (Tier 1 = highest risk).
Tiered facilities implement a Site Security Plan: perimeter security, personnel vetting, cybersecurity, incident response coordination.
Note: CFATS statutory authority lapsed in July 2023; verify current status. EPA RMP and DOT security plans still apply.
DOT security plans (49 CFR 172 Subpart I) apply to shippers/carriers of certain hazmat quantities.
Hazardous materials policy and program
A written, management-approved hazmat program defines how chemicals are acquired, stored, used and disposed of, integrating HazCom, EPA emergency planning and NFPA codes.
Chemical inventory: names, quantities, container sizes, locations, linked SDSs; supports EPCRA Tier II (40 CFR 370) and emergency planning.
Policy elements: procurement controls, labeling, handling/PPE, spill and first aid, storage assignments, inspections.
SOPs for receiving, transfers, disposal/decontamination, equipment cleanup.
HazCom training at initial assignment and whenever a new hazard is introduced; document it.

Inspections (weekly/monthly) for container condition, labels, containment, expired/unknown materials. Note: the guide cites 3-year retention under 1910.1020, but exposure records under 1910.1020 must be kept 30 years.
'When is retraining required?' - when a NEW hazard is introduced, not when a new product with the same hazards arrives.
DOT hazard classes (49 CFR 171-180)
DOT's Hazardous Materials Regulations govern hazmat in transport (loading, transit, unloading) using nine hazard classes that drive packaging, labels and placards.
1 Explosives; 2 Gases (2.1 flammable, 2.2 non-flammable non-toxic, 2.3 toxic).
3 Flammable liquids (flash point not over 60 C / 140 F); 4 Flammable solids (4.1, 4.2 spontaneously combustible, 4.3 dangerous when wet).
5 Oxidizers (5.1) and organic peroxides (5.2); 6 Toxic (6.1) and infectious (6.2).
7 Radioactive; 8 Corrosives; 9 Miscellaneous (lithium batteries, dry ice, magnetized materials).
Hazmat employees need DOT training (49 CFR 172.704) at least every 3 years.
GHS governs the workplace label; DOT governs the transport label/placard - they can legitimately differ on the same drum.
Hazardous waste
Once a hazardous material is no longer usable and is discarded, it becomes waste governed cradle-to-grave by RCRA Subtitle C (40 CFR 260-273), with DOT for transport and HAZWOPER for workers.
Hazardous materials are regulated in use; hazardous waste is regulated after use or disposal.
Store on impervious surfaces with secondary containment, in central or satellite accumulation areas.
Containers: compatible, closed, undamaged, labeled 'Hazardous Waste', hazards indicated, accumulation start date (central areas).
Inspect container storage areas weekly; keep spill kits, PPE and emergency info nearby.
States (e.g., California DTSC) may be more stringent than federal RCRA.
Hazardous waste identification
Generators must determine whether a waste is hazardous by listing or by characteristic, using testing or process knowledge.
Ignitability D001: liquid flash point below 140 F (60 C).
Corrosivity D002: aqueous pH 2 or less, or 12.5 or more (or corrodes steel).
Reactivity D003: unstable, water-reactive, explosive, generates toxic gas.
Toxicity D004-D043: TCLP extract exceeds limits (e.g., lead, benzene, mercury).
Listed wastes: F (non-specific sources, e.g., F003 spent solvents), K (specific industries), P (acutely hazardous discarded chemicals), U (toxic discarded chemicals).
pH 2 or less OR 12.5 or more = corrosive (D002). pH 12 is NOT a characteristic hazardous waste.
Generator categories, manifests and TSDFs
Generator status depends on monthly quantity and sets accumulation time and paperwork.
VSQG: 100 kg/month or less (and 1 kg or less acute); no federal time limit, but 1,000 kg on-site cap.
SQG: more than 100 and less than 1,000 kg/month; 180 days (270 if TSDF is over 200 miles); 6,000 kg cap.
LQG: 1,000 kg/month or more (or over 1 kg acute); 90 days; contingency plan and annual training.
Ship to a permitted TSDF via registered transporter (EPA ID) with the Uniform Hazardous Waste Manifest (EPA Form 8700-22) / e-Manifest; keep copies 3 years.
Example: 1,200 kg/month spent solvent -> LQG -> 90-day limit.
The guide's table lists SQG as 100-1,000 kg; federal rule is more than 100 and less than 1,000 kg; 1,000 kg exactly is LQG.
mcq: A facility generates 600 kg of hazardous waste per month (no acute hazardous waste). What is its RCRA generator category?
Very Small Quantity Generator
Small Quantity Generator
Large Quantity Generator
Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facility
VSQG: 100 kg/month or less; SQG: more than 100 and less than 1,000 kg/month; LQG: 1,000 kg/month or more (or more than 1 kg acute). 600 kg falls in the SQG range.
A supplier's SDS for a new solvent shows a flame pictogram and the hazard statement 'Flammable liquid, Category 2.' What is your FIRST action before allowing the material on site?
Verify that proper flammable storage and ventilation controls are available
Require the supplier to train all employees in SDS reading
Approve the purchase since the supplier provided an SDS
Have employees store it in the nearest open area
Pre-purchase review should confirm that storage (cabinets, quantity limits), ventilation and ignition controls exist before the material arrives.

An international project site receives a drum of toluene marked only with US DOT hazard labels. A European subcontractor refuses to use it, citing labeling noncompliance. What is the MOST appropriate corrective action?
Repackage the drum into smaller unlabeled containers
Explain that DOT labels are sufficient for workplace use
Provide an SDS only if a worker asks for it
Apply a GHS label with the product identifier, pictograms, signal word, and hazard and precautionary statements
DOT labels communicate transport hazards; workplace use requires GHS/HazCom labeling and an accessible SDS.
Under GHS, which elements are required on a shipped container label?
Chemical formula, warnings, and pictograms only
pH, boiling point, flash point, and pictograms
Product identifier, pictogram, signal word, hazard statement, precautionary statement, and supplier information
SDS number, pictograms, and training date
HazCom 1910.1200(f) requires product identifier, signal word, hazard statements, pictograms, precautionary statements, and the supplier's name, address and phone.
During an inspection, you find a drum of acid cleaner (corrosive pictogram) stored next to a pallet of bleach. What is your MOST urgent concern?
The chemicals could react to release toxic chlorine gas
The drum label is missing the manufacturer's phone number
The pictogram is somewhat faded
The bleach lacks a transport placard
Acids mixed with sodium hypochlorite liberate chlorine gas; incompatible materials must be segregated in storage (SDS Sections 7 and 10).
An SDS for a parts-cleaning solvent lists: 'Keep away from heat/sparks/open flame. Use explosion-proof equipment.' In which SDS section are these precautionary statements found?
Section 2 - Hazard Identification
Section 4 - First-Aid Measures
Section 7 - Handling and Storage
Section 10 - Stability and Reactivity
Precautionary statements are label elements and are listed in Section 2 along with signal word, hazard statements and pictograms. Section 7 gives detailed handling practices.
A safety professional is reviewing an SDS before training employees. Which section contains personal protective equipment recommendations?
Section 2 - Hazard Identification
Section 4 - First-Aid Measures
Section 8 - Exposure Controls/Personal Protection
Section 10 - Stability and Reactivity
Section 8 lists exposure limits (PEL, TLV), engineering controls and PPE.
Which area may accumulate up to 55 gallons of non-acute hazardous waste at or near the point of generation without the full central storage requirements?
Central Accumulation Area (CAA)
Universal Waste Area
Hazardous Storage Room
Satellite Accumulation Area (SAA)
SAAs at or near the point of generation, under operator control, may hold up to 55 gal (or 1 qt acute); containers must be closed and marked 'Hazardous Waste' with the hazards indicated.
During a spill response, a new worker reaches for a container labeled with a flame-over-circle pictogram. What should the supervisor remind the worker?
This symbol means the chemical is flammable
This symbol identifies an oxidizer, which can cause or intensify a fire
This symbol identifies explosive chemicals
This symbol warns of corrosion of skin and metals
Flame over circle = oxidizer; plain flame = flammable; exploding bomb = explosive; corrosion = skin and metal damage. Keep oxidizers away from combustibles.
A facility stores ammonium nitrate and other theft-attractive hazardous materials. Which measure BEST addresses hazardous materials security?
Store the materials near the loading dock for faster shipping
Restrict access to authorized personnel, conduct regular inventory reconciliation, and report unexplained losses
Rely on GHS labels to deter theft
Keep the storage area unlocked so emergency responders can enter
Hazmat security combines access control, inventory accountability and reporting of losses so diversion is prevented or detected quickly. Labels communicate hazards but do not secure them.

topics.title: Waste Management
topics.bp: Identify procedures used to manage waste (e.g., universal, recycling, spill clean-up, labeling, remediation)
topics.definition: Waste management covers how all wastes are characterized, segregated, labeled, stored, recycled, transported and disposed of, how spills are cleaned up, and how contaminated sites are remediated.
topics.easy: Sort waste correctly, label it, recycle what you can, clean up spills safely, and fix contaminated soil and water using the right technology.
points: Universal waste (40 CFR 273): batteries, pesticides (recalled), mercury-containing equipment, lamps (and aerosol cans federally since 2019). Simplified rules: label 'Universal Waste - [type]', accumulate up to 1 year, train handlers, send to a destination facility. Used oil is managed under 40 CFR 279, not as universal waste.
Other categories: non-hazardous solid waste (municipal landfill), medical/regulated waste (state rules, sharps containers), radioactive waste (NRC; decay-in-storage for short half-lives), e-waste.
Recycling and reuse: solvent reclamation, scrap metal, pallets; legitimate recycling vs 'sham recycling'.

Spill cleanup: assess (SDS, size, hazards) → protect people (evacuate if needed, PPE) → stop the source if safe → contain (dikes, absorbents, drain covers) → clean up and decontaminate → dispose of cleanup materials as waste → report if above a reportable quantity → review. Incidental vs emergency spills (HAZWOPER).
Labeling: hazardous waste labels ('Hazardous Waste', hazard indication, start date), DOT labels for transport, universal waste labels.

Remediation technologies: pump-and-treat (groundwater), soil vapor extraction (VOCs in unsaturated soil), air sparging, bioremediation, phytoremediation, excavation and disposal, capping/containment (does not remove contamination), in-situ chemical oxidation, monitored natural attenuation.
CERCLA: potentially responsible parties (strict, joint and several liability), National Priorities List; brownfield redevelopment; Phase I/II environmental site assessments.
topics.example: A facility generates spent fluorescent lamps, used batteries, used oil and waste paint. The safety professional sets up universal-waste containers for the lamps and batteries (labeled, dated, kept less than one year), sends used oil to a used-oil recycler under Part 279, and characterizes the paint waste as ignitable hazardous waste.
tips: Used oil is NOT universal waste - a common 'which is NOT' trap.
Capping limits migration but does not remove contaminants.
Universal waste accumulation limit: one year.
topics.yates: Ch. 34 Environmental Management, p. 754; Ch. 27 Hazardous Materials Management
subs: Waste management regulatory overview
Waste management covers identifying, segregating, labeling, storing and disposing of all waste streams (hazardous and non-hazardous) from operations, spills, expired chemicals and maintenance.
RCRA 40 CFR 260-273: definitions, generator rules, labeling, storage, manifests.
DOT 49 CFR 171-180: packaging, marking and transport of hazardous waste.
OSHA HAZWOPER 1910.120: workers handling hazardous waste or cleaning up releases.
State programs may be stricter than federal rules.
Non-hazardous solid waste falls under RCRA Subtitle D.
Universal waste
Universal waste (40 CFR 273) is a streamlined category for common, lower-risk hazardous wastes so they are easier to collect and recycle.
Federal types: batteries, recalled/unused pesticides, mercury-containing equipment (thermostats, thermometers), lamps (fluorescent, HID), aerosol cans (added 2019); some states add electronics.
Label 'Universal Waste - [type]' (or 'Waste/Used [type]') and show accumulation start date.
Accumulation limit: 1 year.
Containers closed, intact and compatible; employees trained on handling and emergency procedures.
Universal waste does not count toward generator status.
Fluorescent lamps in a fiber drum labeled 'Universal Waste - Lamps' with a start date = compliant. 'Hazardous Waste' label is not required.
Recycling of industrial waste
Recycling reduces disposal cost and liability while supporting sustainability, provided materials are kept clean and recyclers are legitimate.
Common streams: used oil (40 CFR 279), scrap metal, distillable solvents, cardboard and plastic drums.
Label containers (e.g., 'Used Oil'), avoid contamination, verify recycler licensing and keep documentation proving recycling.
Closed-loop recycling: material reclaimed and returned to the same process may be excluded from RCRA.
Used oil mixed with hazardous waste can become hazardous waste - keep streams separate.
Documentation proving material was actually recycled (not sham recycling) is the CSP's protection.
Spill cleanup
Spills must be handled quickly and safely using a formal response plan. HAZWOPER applies when cleanup involves an uncontrolled release of a hazardous substance.

Sequence: 1 recognize the material (SDS/label), 2 alert and evacuate (EAP), 3 select PPE, 4 contain (absorbents, booms, dikes), 5 clean and decontaminate/neutralize, 6 dispose of debris (often as hazardous waste), 7 document and report.
Incidental spills handled by trained area employees are not HAZWOPER emergency response.
Oil spill planning: SPCC (40 CFR 112).
Cleanup debris from a hazardous chemical spill is generally hazardous waste.
FIRST step questions: identify the material and protect people before containment.
Release reporting (CERCLA and EPCRA)
Releases of hazardous substances at or above a Reportable Quantity must be reported to the National Response Center.
CERCLA RQ release: notify the NRC immediately upon knowledge (the guide says within 24 hours).
The RQ is measured as the amount released within any 24-hour period.
EPCRA Section 304 also requires notice to state and local emergency planning bodies (SERC/LEPC).
Oil discharges producing a sheen on water are reportable under the CWA.
Document the release and follow-up written reports as required.
Labeling
Labeling is one of the most-cited EPA/OSHA areas; containers must be labeled, compatible and closed at all times.
Hazardous waste: 'Hazardous Waste', indication of hazards, EPA waste codes (e.g., D001) before shipment, accumulation start date, clear contents.
Universal waste: type and accumulation start date.
Used oil: 'Used Oil'.
Shipping: DOT marking, labels and placards plus the manifest.
Satellite accumulation areas
An SAA lets generators accumulate waste at or near the point of generation under reduced requirements.
Up to 55 gal of hazardous waste (or 1 qt liquid / 1 kg solid acute) per SAA.
Must be under control of the operator; containers closed, labeled 'Hazardous Waste' with hazard indication.
Once the limit is exceeded, excess moves to the central area within 3 consecutive days and is dated.
Central accumulation area clock (90/180 days) starts when waste enters it.
Remediation
Remediation cleans up contaminated soil, water or structures under CERCLA (Superfund) or RCRA corrective action.
Techniques: excavation, solidification/stabilization, bioremediation, soil vapor extraction, pump and treat (groundwater).
Phase I ESA: records review, site visit, interviews (no sampling; ASTM E1527).
Phase II ESA: sampling and analysis to confirm contamination.
Brownfield programs support redevelopment of contaminated land.
CERCLA liability is strict, joint and several, and retroactive for potentially responsible parties.
Phase I = no sampling; Phase II = sampling.
mcq: A consultant proposes installing a cap over contaminated soil on company property. What is a key LIMITATION of capping as a remediation method?
A cap increases water infiltration and speeds plume movement
A cap makes the property unattractive
A cap does not remove the contamination; it only minimizes exposure and migration
A cap prevents any reuse of the property
Capping is containment: it reduces infiltration and direct contact but leaves contaminants in place, requiring long-term monitoring and maintenance.
Under 40 CFR 279, containers and tanks of used oil stored for recycling must be labeled:
'Used Oil'
'Hazardous Waste - Oil'
'Universal Waste - Oil'
'Recyclable Waste Only'
Used oil managed for recycling falls under the used oil standards, not hazardous waste rules; containers must be labeled with the words 'Used Oil'.
What marking is required on a container of universal waste lamps?
'Hazardous Waste - Lamps' with an EPA waste code
'Used Oil for Recycling'
'Flammable - Keep Fire Away'
'Universal Waste - Lamp(s)' (or 'Waste Lamps'/'Used Lamps'), with the accumulation start date demonstrated
40 CFR 273 requires the universal waste marking and a way to show how long it has been accumulated (one-year limit).
A worker must segregate four waste streams into 55-gallon drums: wastewater, lithium metal, toluene, and halogenated hydrocarbons. What is the GREATEST concern?
Mixing lithium metal and toluene
Mixing lithium metal and water
Mixing halogenated hydrocarbons and toluene
Mixing wastewater and toluene
Lithium is a water-reactive metal that releases flammable hydrogen and heat on contact with water; waste segregation must keep reactives apart.
Volatile organic compounds are found in unsaturated (vadose zone) soil above the water table. Which remediation technology is MOST suitable?
Pump and treat
Phytoremediation of groundwater
Capping only
Soil vapor extraction
SVE applies a vacuum to the unsaturated zone to remove volatile contaminants. Pump and treat addresses groundwater, and capping does not remove contaminants.
While inspecting a small facility, you find several containers labeled 'corrosive waste' in the central accumulation area with no dates. What is your BEST course of action?
Notify the facility manager that the containers are noncompliant and must be marked with the accumulation start date
Remove the containers immediately without telling anyone
Have workers put on PPE and move the waste elsewhere
Call the fire department to dispose of the waste
Generators must mark containers 'Hazardous Waste', indicate the hazards, and record the accumulation start date to track time limits (40 CFR 262.16/262.17).
How long may a universal waste handler accumulate universal waste (e.g., spent lamps, batteries) on site?
90 days
180 days
1 year from the date it became a waste
Indefinitely
Universal waste may be accumulated up to one year (longer only if needed to collect quantities for proper recovery). 90 and 180 days are LQG and SQG hazardous waste limits.
Which action represents the LOWEST (least preferred) level of the waste management hierarchy?
Redesigning a process to eliminate hazardous chemical use
Disposing of hazardous waste in a permitted landfill
Reusing scrap material in the same process
Sending waste solvent off-site for recycling
Hierarchy: source reduction > reuse/recycling > treatment > disposal. Landfill disposal is the last resort.
Which characteristic identifies a waste as EPA hazardous waste code D001?
Ignitability (e.g., liquid with flash point below 140 F / 60 C)
Corrosivity (pH 2 or less, or 12.5 or more)
Reactivity (unstable or explosive)
Toxicity (TCLP metals such as lead or mercury)
D001 = ignitable, D002 = corrosive, D003 = reactive, D004-D043 = toxicity characteristic.
Employees clean up a spill of a listed hazardous solvent using absorbent pads. How should the used absorbent be managed?
In the regular trash once it has dried
By rinsing it in a floor drain and reusing the pads
As universal waste, since it came from a spill
As hazardous waste, properly containerized, labeled, and disposed of through a permitted facility
Spill cleanup materials contaminated with a listed hazardous waste carry that listing (contained-in principle) and must be managed as hazardous waste. Absorbents are not a universal waste category.

topics.title: Sustainability
topics.bp: Determine sustainability principles and practices (e.g., supply chain; reduce, reuse, recycle)
topics.definition: Sustainability means meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs (Brundtland, 1987). In business it is often framed as the triple bottom line - people, planet, profit - and includes supply-chain responsibility, resource efficiency and life-cycle thinking.
topics.easy: Use less, reuse what you can, recycle the rest, and choose suppliers who also work safely and responsibly. Sustainability and safety support each other because waste, inefficiency and unsafe work all cost money and harm people.
points: Waste hierarchy: refuse/reduce → reuse → recycle → recover (energy) → dispose.
Life-cycle assessment (ISO 14040/44): impacts from raw material extraction through manufacturing, use and end of life ('cradle to grave' or 'cradle to cradle').

Supply chain: supplier codes of conduct, audits, conflict minerals, responsible sourcing, diversified suppliers to reduce disruption risk, green procurement (recycled content, low-VOC materials, energy-efficient equipment).
Green building: LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design) - energy, water, materials, indoor environmental quality.
Sustainability reporting: GRI, SASB, integrated reporting; safety metrics (fatalities, TRIR) appear in sustainability reports.
Links to safety: substitution of less hazardous chemicals reduces both exposure and hazardous waste; energy efficiency reduces emissions; worker well-being is the 'social' pillar.
topics.example: A construction company changes its purchasing policy to require recycled concrete aggregate, low-VOC paints and LED lighting. The safety professional notes that low-VOC paint also reduces worker solvent exposure, and the switch is reported in both the safety and the sustainability report.
tips: Source reduction is the best sustainability answer.
LEED = Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design.
Diversifying suppliers = supply-chain risk reduction.
topics.yates: Ch. 33 Sustainability and Sustainability Principles, p. 743
subs: Sustainability frameworks
Sustainability means operations that are environmentally sound, socially responsible and economically viable across the product life cycle and supply chain.
ISO 14001: EMS with legal compliance, continual improvement and a life-cycle perspective.
EPA: CAA, CWA, RCRA and the Pollution Prevention Act (source reduction first), green chemistry, LCA support.
OSHA: green jobs and renewable-technology hazards (solar, battery storage), IAQ, ergonomics.
Triple bottom line: people, planet, profit.
UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
The 17 UN SDGs are non-binding global goals; several align directly with EHS work.
Goal 3 Good health and well-being (injury/illness prevention).
Goal 6 Clean water and sanitation; Goal 7 Affordable clean energy.
Goal 9 Resilient infrastructure; Goal 12 Responsible consumption and production; Goal 13 Climate action.
Not legally binding - a voluntary vision.
Supply chain sustainability
Sustainable supply chain management extends EHS expectations upstream and downstream to suppliers, contractors and logistics partners.
Supplier audits cover environmental compliance (ISO 14001), labor practices (ILO, SA8000), resource efficiency and hazmat handling.
Conflict minerals (3TG: tin, tantalum, tungsten, gold) - Dodd-Frank Section 1502.
SA8000: social accountability standard - health and safety, working hours, compensation, freedom of association.
Integrate procurement into ISO 14001 clause 8.1 (operational planning and control).
Supply chain emissions = Scope 3.
Auditing a supplier's labor and safety conditions in a developing region -> SA8000.
Green procurement and responsible sourcing
Green procurement adds environmental and social criteria to purchasing, not just cost and availability.
Specify recycled content, low-VOC/non-toxic materials, minimal/reusable packaging.
Prefer vendors with ISO 14001 or CDP ratings and low-carbon logistics.
EPA Environmentally Preferable Purchasing (EPP) is a model program.
Example: solvents in reusable stainless drums cut hazardous waste about 40%.
Reduce
Reduce (source reduction) eliminates waste and pollution before it is created and is the most effective of the 3Rs.
Strategies: lean process design, energy audits, material substitution (water-based for solvent), Design for Environment.
Matches the top of the hierarchy of controls (eliminate/substitute).
Pollution Prevention Act: source reduction is the preferred strategy.
Upstream redesign that removes a hazardous input = 'Reduce'.
Reuse
Reuse keeps products and materials in service without significant reprocessing, cutting raw material demand and disposal volume.
Examples: reusable totes, refillable chemical drums, launderable rags/absorbents, upcycled scrap, internal asset recovery.
Safety check: reused containers must be clean, compatible and not degraded (especially after corrosives/flammables).
Example: switching to reusable PPE totes cut plastic waste 60% and procurement cost 30%.
Recycle
Recycling turns waste into new material; it ranks below reduce and reuse but is vital when those are not practical.
Examples: cardboard baling, e-waste management, metal recovery, closed-loop recycling.
Can lower hazardous waste quantities and generator status (e.g., solvent recycling).
Hierarchy: Reduce > Reuse > Recycle > Treat/energy recovery > Dispose.
If a question asks which 3R is BEST, choose Reduce.
Life cycle assessment (LCA)
LCA quantifies environmental impacts across every stage of a product's life, cradle-to-grave or cradle-to-cradle, per ISO 14040/14044.
Stages: raw material extraction, manufacturing, distribution/transport, use, end of life.
ISO 14040/14044 phases: goal and scope, inventory analysis (LCI), impact assessment (LCIA), interpretation.
Tools: SimaPro, GaBi, OpenLCA, EPA Sustainable Materials Management tools.
Differs from a waste audit or carbon footprint - it covers all impacts across all stages.
Life cycle costing and total cost of ownership
Life cycle costing (LCC) weighs purchase price against long-term environmental, social and operational costs.
Include disposal fees, emissions penalties, water charges, reputational and supply-continuity risk.
TCO can justify paying more for a durable, certified product to avoid fines, failures and injuries.
LCA measures environmental impact; LCC measures money.
Sustainable design and green engineering
Design for Environment (DfE) and green engineering build environmental and safety considerations into the earliest design stage.
Aligns with the EPA P2 hierarchy, ISO 14001 clause 6.1.2 (environmental aspects) and Prevention through Design (ANSI/ASSP Z590.3; the guide cites Z10).
DfE: fewer raw materials, easy disassembly and recycling, low energy/water use, less waste.
Energy-efficient equipment: VFDs, compressed-air leak repair, LED lighting with motion sensors (also improves visibility).
Modular equipment and non-toxic paints/adhesives reduce IAQ problems and hazardous waste.
Safer chemical substitution
Substitution improves worker safety and environmental performance at the same time when evaluated holistically.
Use low-VOC solvents/coatings; lower GHS hazard categories (remove sensitizers and carcinogens).
Avoid substances restricted under TSCA or EU REACH.
Tools: EPA Safer Chemical Ingredients List (SCIL), GreenScreen.
Check new waste profile, process compatibility and PPE needs before switching.
A substitute that introduces a new, worse hazard is not a valid improvement.
Sustainability metrics and KPIs
Sustainability progress is tracked with environmental, economic and social indicators and benchmarked against recognized programs.
Environmental: water per unit, GHG (CO2e), hazardous waste per product.
Economic: life-cycle cost, return on sustainability investment, resource productivity.
Social: injury rates, engagement in green initiatives, fair labor certifications.
Benchmarking tools: ENERGY STAR, EPA WasteWise, GRI.
mcq: Which is the MOST effective step in the 'Reduce-Reuse-Recycle' hierarchy?
Reuse
Recycle
Reduce
Dispose
Reducing eliminates waste and resource use at the source, so no handling, reprocessing or disposal is needed; recycling still consumes energy.
Which sustainability practice manages suppliers and vendors based on their ethical, safety, and environmental performance?
Sustainable supply chain management
Energy audits
Waste minimization
Pollution abatement
Sustainable supply chain management sets supplier codes of conduct, screens and audits suppliers, and extends EHS expectations beyond the company's own sites.

A construction company changes its purchasing policy to require recycled concrete aggregate, energy-efficient lighting, and low-VOC materials on all projects. Which sustainability principle does this BEST represent?
Waste isolation
Pollution control after production
Compliance with local code minimums only
Source reduction and sustainable material selection
Specifying recycled, efficient and low-toxicity inputs at procurement reduces impacts before they occur (green purchasing).
A company replaces solvent-based paints with water-based coatings to lower VOC emissions. Which sustainability principle does this demonstrate?
Reuse
Source reduction (Reduce)
Recycling
Waste diversion
Substituting a less hazardous input prevents the pollution from being generated at all, which is source reduction.
What is the primary focus of LEED certification?
Sustainable building performance, such as energy efficiency and water conservation
Building aesthetics and architectural style
Minimizing short-term construction costs
Urban zoning and development approvals
LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design) rates buildings on energy, water, materials, indoor environmental quality and site sustainability.
A Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA) evaluates:
Worker performance over a career
Product pricing over its sales life
Regulatory compliance at a single facility
Environmental impacts of a product from raw material extraction through disposal
LCA is a cradle-to-grave (or cradle-to-cradle) analysis of materials, energy, emissions and waste across all life-cycle stages (ISO 14040/14044).
A manufacturer replaces single-use cardboard shipping boxes with durable plastic totes that suppliers return for refilling. Which principle does this represent?
Recycle
Reuse
Source reduction through product redesign
Energy recovery
Using the same item again for its original purpose without reprocessing is reuse. Recycling would break the material down to make new products.
A company finds that most of its environmental footprint comes from raw materials made by overseas suppliers. What is the BEST first step to improve supply chain sustainability?
Stop tracking supplier impacts because they are outside the company's control
Switch all suppliers immediately regardless of cost or quality
Establish a supplier code of conduct with sustainability criteria and assess suppliers against it
Publish a sustainability statement without supplier engagement
Setting clear expectations, then assessing and engaging suppliers, is the foundation of supply chain sustainability; ignoring or making unfounded claims (greenwashing) is weak.
The 'triple bottom line' approach to sustainability evaluates an organization's performance in which three areas?
People, planet, and profit
Quality, cost, and schedule
Plan, do, and check
Reduce, reuse, and recycle
The triple bottom line measures social (people), environmental (planet) and economic (profit) performance, a precursor to ESG reporting.
A plant collects scrap aluminum trimmings, sends them to be remelted, and buys back the resulting ingots for production. This is BEST described as:
Reuse
Source reduction
Landfill diversion by incineration
Closed-loop recycling
The material is reprocessed (remelted) and returned to the same product system, which is closed-loop recycling, a circular economy practice. Reuse would involve no reprocessing.

topics.title: Environmental Issues and ESG
topics.bp: Describe the impact of environmental issues (e.g., aging infrastructure, asbestos, air pollution, climate change, environmental, social, and governance)
topics.definition: This competency covers major environmental issues that affect organizations and communities - deteriorating infrastructure, legacy hazards such as asbestos and lead, air pollution, climate change - and ESG (Environmental, Social and Governance) frameworks used by investors and stakeholders to judge corporate performance.
topics.easy: Old pipes, tanks and buildings can leak or contain hazardous materials; dirty air and a changing climate affect health and operations; and investors now look at how companies manage environment, people and governance, not just profit.
points: Aging infrastructure: corroded pipelines, tanks, sewers and bridges increase release and failure risk; manage with risk-based inspection, integrity management programs and planned replacement.

Asbestos: friable vs non-friable; asbestosis, mesothelioma, lung cancer; OSHA PEL 0.1 f/cc (8-h TWA), excursion limit 1.0 f/cc (30 min); building survey before renovation/demolition; NESHAP notification 10 working days before work when RACM thresholds are exceeded (260 linear ft, 160 ft², 35 ft³); removal with containment, negative pressure, wet methods and HEPA; never dry-sweep suspect material.
Lead: renovation (EPA RRP rule for pre-1978 housing), OSHA lead standards (PEL 50 µg/m³, action level 30 µg/m³).
Air pollution: criteria pollutants, ozone, PM2.5, VOCs; health effects (respiratory, cardiovascular); indoor air quality links.

Climate change: greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, fluorinated gases); scope 1 (direct), scope 2 (purchased energy), scope 3 (value chain) emissions; physical risks to operations (heat stress, flooding, severe weather) and transition risks (regulation, markets).

ESG: Environmental (emissions, waste, water), Social (worker safety and health, human rights, community), Governance (board oversight, ethics, transparency). Frameworks: GRI, SASB/ISSB, TCFD. Safety performance is a core 'S' metric.
topics.example: Before renovating a 1960s office, the safety professional orders an asbestos survey. It finds 400 linear feet of friable pipe insulation, so the company files a NESHAP notification 10 working days ahead, hires a licensed abatement contractor using negative-pressure containment, and performs clearance air sampling before re-occupancy.
tips: Any suspect insulation in an old building: stop, do not sweep, assume asbestos until tested.
Scope 2 = purchased electricity.
ESG 'S' includes occupational safety and health.
topics.yates: Ch. 34 Environmental Management, p. 754; Ch. 33 Sustainability; Ch. 4 Regulations (asbestos)
subs: Aging infrastructure

Many facilities run past their design life; pipelines, tanks, structures and electrical systems 40+ years old face corrosion, fatigue and overload, raising failure risk under modern demands and extreme weather.
Common failures: corroded USTs/transfer lines (40 CFR 280 requires leak detection, corrosion protection, secondary containment for new USTs).
Fire sprinklers: scale-clogged galvanized pipe; inspect/test/maintain per NFPA 25; design to NFPA 13.
Structures: rusted fasteners, rotted supports (1910 Subpart D).
Electrical: degraded insulation, overloaded panels, no arc-flash labels, not lockable (1910.147, NFPA 70E).
HVAC: decayed ducts, mold - review ASHRAE 62.1.
Aging infrastructure is multi-disciplinary: compliance, life safety and business continuity.
Inspecting and managing aging assets
Risk-based inspection and asset management prioritize work by consequence and likelihood of failure.
Risk-based inspection: API 580/581.
NDT: ultrasonic thickness, radiography, magnetic particle, dye penetrant.
Infrared thermography (electrical hot spots, bearings), vibration and acoustic monitoring.
ISO 55000 asset management; CMMS, SCADA, structural health monitoring sensors.
Administrative: aging infrastructure register, retrofit timelines in capital plans, pre-task checks. Example: ultrasonic testing of tanks over 20 years old after a corrosion leak.
Wall thinning from corrosion -> ultrasonic thickness testing.
Asbestos

Asbestos is a group of fibrous silicate minerals once used in insulation, pipe wrap, flooring, roofing, gaskets and fireproofing. Disturbed fibers cause mesothelioma, asbestosis and lung cancer decades later; there is no known safe level.
OSHA PEL 0.1 f/cc 8-hr TWA; excursion limit 1.0 f/cc over 30 minutes (1910.1001; construction 1926.1101).
Above the PEL: regulated areas, respirators, training, signage, medical surveillance.
Buildings built before 1981 - presume thermal insulation and surfacing materials are ACM unless tested.
Latency of 20-40+ years; smoking multiplies lung cancer risk.
Exceeding the excursion limit (1.0 f/cc for 30 min) is a violation even if the 8-hr TWA is under 0.1.
Asbestos regulations, abatement and disposal
Several agencies regulate asbestos during work, demolition, schools and transport.

EPA NESHAP (40 CFR 61 Subpart M): survey before renovation/demolition; notify 10 working days before work involving at least 260 linear ft, 160 sq ft or 35 cu ft of regulated ACM (demolition always needs notice).
AHERA (schools): inspections, management plans, re-inspection every 3 years (surveillance every 6 months).
Controls: licensed contractors, negative-pressure enclosures, wet methods, glove bags, HEPA vacuums, decon units.
Clearance: PCM or TEM air sampling; often under 0.01 f/cc.
Waste: wetted, double-bagged in 6-mil leak-tight bags, labeled, transported to approved landfill with records.
Disturbed suspect ceiling insulation: FIRST stop work, evacuate and isolate the area, then sample.
Other legacy contaminants (lead, PCBs, USTs)
Legacy contaminants in pre-1980s buildings become hazardous when disturbed during maintenance, renovation or demolition.
Lead-based paint: OSHA 1926.62 (PEL 50 ug/m3, action level 30); EPA RRP rule for target housing.
PCBs (old transformers, ballasts, caulk): TSCA regulated.
Leaking underground storage tanks: 40 CFR 280.
Failure to manage can bring civil penalties, criminal prosecution or fatal exposures.
Air pollution
Industrial air pollution affects worker health, the community, regulatory standing and ESG scores.
Combustion: NOx and SO2 (acid rain and smog precursors).
Particulate matter: PM2.5 penetrates deep into lungs (diesel exhaust, grinding).
VOCs from paints, solvents and fuels form ground-level ozone.
Fugitive dust may carry silica or heavy metals.
Health effects: short-term irritation, headaches; long-term asthma, bronchitis, cardiovascular disease, lung cancer.
Air quality regulation, reporting and monitoring
EPA, OSHA and states regulate air emissions and exposures.
CAA: NAAQS, NSR/PSD permits, Title V permits when potential to emit exceeds major-source thresholds; state SIPs may be stricter.
Title V reports semiannually with CEMS data for key sources.
TRI (EPCRA 313): annual Form R when a listed chemical exceeds 25,000 lb manufactured/processed or 10,000 lb otherwise used (the guide cites only 10,000 lb).
Penalties: the guide states up to $50,000/day; inflation-adjusted CAA civil penalties now exceed $100,000 per day per violation.
Monitoring: fence-line stations, DustTrak (PM), PID (VOCs), MIRAN/infrared analyzers.
PID measures VOCs; DustTrak measures particulate - know which instrument fits the pollutant.
Climate change
Climate change is now a safety, health, operational and regulatory issue: hotter summers, extreme weather, shifting disease vectors and utility disruptions.
Heat stress for outdoor and hot indoor work; OSHA heat National Emphasis Program (launched 2022; the guide says 2023).
Extreme weather: floods, hurricanes, wildfires disrupt facilities and supply chains; EAPs (1910.38) must reflect new risks.
Vectors: ticks and mosquitoes spreading (Lyme, West Nile, dengue).
Grid strain and blackouts affect ventilation, cooling and communications; floods can release chemicals.
ISO 14001 (2024 amendment) requires considering climate change in context of the organization; TCFD for financial disclosure.
Heat illness prevention
A heat illness prevention program is expected under the General Duty Clause and the NEP.
Water: about 1 quart per hour (1 cup every 15-20 minutes).
Rest and shade on work-rest cycles based on heat index or WBGT (NIOSH RELs, ACGIH TLVs).
Acclimatization: new and returning workers ramp up over 7-14 days (20% first day rule).
Train workers and supervisors on symptoms; emergency plan for heat stroke (medical emergency - cool immediately, call 911).
Humidity raises heat index even at moderate air temperature.
Most heat deaths occur in the first days on the job - acclimatization is the key control.
Climate resilience and emergency planning
Facilities adapt to climate risk through resilience audits, updated ERPs and forward-looking climate risk assessment.
ERP updates: long blackouts, wildfire smoke (N95s, HVAC sealing), shelter-in-place for hurricanes/floods, resilient communications, drills with local agencies.
Resilience: backup power (generators, UPS), drainage capacity, anchored rooftop equipment, fire-resistant materials, supplier redundancy.
Climate risk assessment: identify regional trends (NOAA, IPCC), overlay on critical assets, score and control, add to aspects register or BCP.
Use ISO 31010 risk techniques; results inform capital projects and insurance.
ESG (Environmental, Social and Governance)
ESG evaluates how responsibly and sustainably an organization operates; it affects investment, insurance and public trust. Safety performance feeds every pillar.
Environmental: GHG emissions, resource efficiency, compliance record (fines, spills).
Social: worker health and safety (TRIR, DART, near misses), DEI, community engagement and environmental justice.
Governance: transparency and reporting, regulatory compliance, whistleblower protection, ethics.
A strong safety culture underpins the Social score.
GHG scopes and ESG reporting frameworks
ESG data is reported through recognized frameworks, and emissions are split into three scopes.
Scope 1: direct emissions from owned sources (boilers, fleet, forklifts, refrigerants).
Scope 2: indirect emissions from purchased electricity, steam, heat.
Scope 3: other value chain emissions (suppliers, transport, product use).
Frameworks: GRI, SASB (now under IFRS/ISSB), CDP, TCFD.
Management systems supporting ESG: ISO 14001, ISO 45001.
Purchased electricity = Scope 2; supplier emissions = Scope 3.
ESG KPIs
CSPs prove value by supplying measurable indicators for each pillar.
Environmental: % GHG reduction per revenue unit, tons diverted from landfill, water intensity.
Social: TRIR/DART trends, % workforce trained, safety perception survey results.
Governance: near misses reported, % audit findings closed on time, inspections without citations.
KPIs may link to bonuses, public reports and stock value.
mcq: A renovation will remove 300 linear feet of friable asbestos pipe insulation from a commercial building. Under the asbestos NESHAP, the owner/operator must notify the regulatory agency:
At least 10 working days before the work begins
After the work is complete
Only if workers complain
24 hours before the work begins
NESHAP (40 CFR 61 Subpart M) requires written notice 10 working days in advance when regulated ACM meets or exceeds 260 linear ft, 160 sq ft, or 35 cu ft.
A crew will remove damaged pipe insulation confirmed to contain asbestos. What is the MOST effective method to prevent workers from inhaling asbestos fibers?
Provide N95 respirators and ask workers to minimize disturbance
Cover the insulation with duct tape before removal
Use full containment with negative air pressure, wet methods, and appropriate respirators such as P100
Limit exposure time and ventilate the room with fans
Regulated asbestos removal relies on engineering controls (negative-pressure enclosure, HEPA, wet methods) supplemented by proper respirators; fans spread fibers.
According to OSHA's asbestos standard (1910.1001(k)(7)), which statement about sanding asbestos-containing flooring is correct?
Sanding is allowed if local exhaust ventilation captures fibers above the PEL
Sanding is allowed if the surface is first wetted or enclosed
Sanding is allowed if it is done in a wet state
Sanding of asbestos-containing flooring material is prohibited
OSHA prohibits sanding asbestos-containing flooring outright; floor care must use wet methods and low-abrasion pads at low speeds.
A CSP leads ISO 14001 and ISO 45001 programs, reports sustainability metrics to the board, and improves safety culture. Which ESG pillar does this work strengthen?
Environmental only
All three: Environmental, Social, and Governance
Social only
Governance only
ISO 14001 supports E, worker safety and culture support S, and board-level reporting and management systems support G.
In greenhouse gas reporting, emissions from electricity a company PURCHASES from the utility are classified as:
Scope 2
Scope 1
Scope 3
Not reportable
Scope 1 = direct emissions from owned sources (boilers, fleet); Scope 2 = indirect emissions from purchased energy; Scope 3 = other value-chain emissions.
What is the MOST common cause of chemical releases from aging infrastructure?
Software failure
Overtraining of personnel
Corrosion and metal fatigue of tanks, piping, and valves
Excessive electrical grounding
Over time corrosion, fatigue and wear thin walls and weaken joints, leading to leaks; mechanical integrity programs address this.
What is the OSHA Permissible Exposure Limit (PEL) for airborne asbestos?
0.5 fiber/cc as an 8-hour TWA
1.0 fiber/cc as an 8-hour TWA
0.05 fiber/cc as an 8-hour TWA
0.1 fiber/cc as an 8-hour TWA
OSHA's asbestos PEL is 0.1 f/cc (8-hr TWA) with an excursion limit of 1.0 f/cc over 30 minutes. Trap: confusing the excursion limit with the PEL.
In ESG frameworks, the 'S' (Social) pillar MOST directly includes which CSP-related metric?
GHG intensity (tons CO2e per unit)
TRIR and DART incident rates
Energy efficiency ratio
Hazardous waste recycling rate
Worker health and safety performance is a core Social metric; GHG, energy and waste metrics are Environmental.
A plant has 40-year-old underground process piping with no inspection history. What is the BEST approach to manage environmental release risk?
Wait for a leak to identify weak sections
Apply risk-based inspection: prioritize segments by likelihood and consequence of failure and inspect or replace accordingly
Replace all piping immediately regardless of cost
Increase insurance coverage
Risk-based inspection and integrity management focus resources where failure is most likely and most harmful. Waiting is reactive; insurance transfers cost but not the hazard.
Electrostatic precipitators (ESPs) are primarily used to control air pollution by:
Separating oil from water
Neutralizing acid gases
Removing fine particulates from exhaust gas using an electric field
Adsorbing VOCs on activated carbon
ESPs charge particles and collect them on plates, achieving high efficiency for fine particulates at power plants and smelters.

topics.title: Occupational Exposure: Anticipate, Recognize, Evaluate, Control
topics.bp: Anticipate, recognize, evaluate, and control occupational exposures by implementing techniques for measurement, sampling, and analysis (e.g., hazardous chemicals, SDS, radiation, noise, biological hazards, heat/cold, indoor air quality, ventilation, nanoparticles, combustible dust, heat systems, high pressure, silica, powder and spray applications, blasting, molten metals, hot work, cold and heat stress, laser)
topics.definition: Industrial hygiene is the science of anticipating, recognizing, evaluating and controlling workplace health hazards (chemical, physical, biological and ergonomic) that can cause illness or impaired well-being. Evaluation compares measured exposures with occupational exposure limits (OSHA PELs, ACGIH TLVs, NIOSH RELs).
topics.easy: Expect where exposures will be, spot them, measure how much people breathe, hear or absorb, compare that with the safe limit, and then reduce it - using engineering controls first.
points: Exposure limits: PEL (OSHA, legal), TLV (ACGIH, guideline, updated annually), REL (NIOSH); TWA (8-h), STEL (15-min), Ceiling (never exceed), IDLH (immediately dangerous to life or health). Action level usually ½ PEL.

Sampling: personal samples in the breathing zone; active (pump, calibrated before/after) vs passive (diffusion badges); media - filters (particulates), sorbent tubes (vapors), impingers; direct-reading instruments (4-gas meters, PIDs). Sample volume = flow rate × time. Concentration = mass ÷ volume.
Chemicals: ppm = mg/m³ × 24.45 ÷ MW (25 °C, 1 atm). TWA = Σ(C × T) ÷ 8. Mixtures with additive effects: Σ(C/T) must be ≤ 1.

Noise (1910.95): PEL 90 dBA (5-dB exchange rate); action level 85 dBA (50% dose) triggers hearing conservation program - monitoring, annual audiometric testing, hearing protectors, training, records. Standard threshold shift = average 10 dB shift at 2,000, 3,000 and 4,000 Hz. T = 8 ÷ 2^((L − 90)/5). Adding sources: L = 10 log Σ10^(L/10); doubling distance −6 dB (point source).

Radiation: ionizing (alpha - stopped by paper; beta - plastic/aluminum; gamma/X-ray - lead/concrete; neutron - water/hydrogen-rich materials). ALARA with time, distance (inverse square law I₂ = I₁(d₁/d₂)²), shielding. Dosimeters measure cumulative dose. OSHA/NRC occupational limit 5 rem (50 mSv)/year whole body. Half-life: A = A₀(½)^(t/T½). Non-ionizing: UV, IR, RF/microwave, lasers.
Lasers (ANSI Z136.1): Class 1, 2, 3R, 3B, 4; Class 3B and 4 require a Laser Safety Officer, nominal hazard zone, interlocks, eyewear with correct optical density.

Heat stress: WBGT outdoors = 0.7 NWB + 0.2 GT + 0.1 DB; indoors = 0.7 NWB + 0.3 GT. Heat stroke (core > 104 °F, confusion, may stop sweating) is a medical emergency; heat exhaustion (heavy sweating, weakness). Acclimatization: new workers 20% day 1, +20%/day. Cold stress: hypothermia, frostbite, trench foot; wind chill.

Ventilation: Q = V × A; V = 4005√VP; TP = SP + VP; local exhaust (capture at source - preferred for toxics) vs general/dilution ventilation (low-toxicity, low-volume, dispersed sources). Dilution Q = 403 × 10⁶ × SG × ER × K ÷ (MW × C). Air changes per hour = Q × 60 ÷ volume.

Respirators (1910.134): written program, medical evaluation, fit test (annually for tight-fitting), training; APFs - half-mask 10, full-face APR 50, PAPR loose hood 25, SAR/SCBA pressure-demand full face 1,000/10,000; MUC = PEL × APF; atmosphere-supplying respirators for IDLH or oxygen deficient (< 19.5%).
Biological hazards: bloodborne pathogens (1910.1030 - exposure control plan, universal precautions, hepatitis B vaccine within 10 working days), Legionella (cooling towers), molds, TB (BSL-3 labs).
Indoor air quality: CO₂ as a ventilation indicator (> ~700 ppm above outdoor), ASHRAE 62.1, sources (VOCs, mold, outdoor air intake location).

Specific hazards: respirable crystalline silica (PEL 50 µg/m³, AL 25; wet methods, LEV; Table 1 for construction), combustible dust (DHA, housekeeping), nanoparticles (high surface area, HEPA effective), abrasive blasting (substitute non-silica media, blast enclosures, Type CE respirators), molten metal (moisture → steam explosions, aluminized PPE), welding fumes (manganese, hexavalent chromium from stainless steel, zinc → metal fume fever), high-pressure systems (stored energy, injection injuries).
topics.example: Workers polishing stainless steel complain of sinus irritation. The hygienist first reviews SDSs, then takes task-based personal breathing-zone samples for hexavalent chromium and nickel. Results exceed the action level, so a downdraft table with local exhaust is installed, respirators are used while it is built, and follow-up sampling confirms exposures below the action level.
tips: Always start with SDS review and hazard recognition, then personal breathing-zone sampling.
Noise and radiation calculations (dose, adding dB, inverse square, half-life) are high-yield.
Local exhaust is preferred over dilution ventilation for toxic contaminants.
Mixture exposure can exceed the limit even if each chemical is individually below its own limit.
topics.yates: Ch. 6 Particulates and Gases, p. 228; Ch. 8 Industrial Hygiene Air Sampling, p. 273; Ch. 9 Ventilation, p. 294; Ch. 10 Noise, p. 314; Ch. 11 Biological Hazards, p. 332; Ch. 13 Thermal Stressors, p. 367; Ch. 14 PPE, p. 385; Ch. 28 Radiation Safety, p. 636
subs: OSHA hazard categories
Workplace health hazards are grouped into four categories: physical, chemical, biological and ergonomic. Recognizing the category tells you which standards, sampling methods and controls apply.
Physical: noise, vibration, heat/cold, ionizing and non-ionizing radiation, electricity, pressure.
Chemical: solvents, metals, dusts (silica, asbestos), gases, corrosives - governed by HazCom 1910.1200 and substance-specific standards.
Biological: bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, prions/toxins - e.g., Bloodborne Pathogens 1910.1030.
Ergonomic: force, repetition, awkward posture, contact stress, vibration - no OSHA ergonomics standard; enforced via the General Duty Clause 5(a)(1).
IH sequence: anticipate, recognize, evaluate, control (plus confirm). Recognition comes before measurement.
Occupational exposure limits (PEL, TLV, REL, STEL, Ceiling, IDLH)
Exposure limits set the airborne concentration most workers can tolerate without adverse effect. Know who publishes each and whether it is enforceable.
PEL = OSHA, legally enforceable (1910.1000 Z-tables and substance standards); many date from 1971 and are outdated.
TLV = ACGIH, advisory, updated yearly; REL = NIOSH, recommended (10-h TWA basis); WEL = UK; IOELV = EU.
TWA = 8-h average; STEL = 15-min average, max 4 times/day, at least 60 min apart; Ceiling (C) = never exceed.
Action level (AL) is usually 1/2 the PEL and triggers monitoring and medical surveillance.
IDLH (NIOSH) = concentration from which escape within 30 min is possible without irreversible effects; used for respirator selection (e.g., CO IDLH 1,200 ppm).
'Legally enforceable limit' = PEL; 'best practice' or 'most protective' usually = TLV or REL.
Measurement

Measurement quantifies exposure with direct-reading instruments or integrated sampling so it can be compared with an exposure limit. Instruments must be appropriate for the agent, calibrated and used by a competent person.
Direct-reading: multigas meters (O2, LEL, CO, H2S), PID for VOCs, FID, electrochemical sensors, colorimetric detector tubes, real-time aerosol monitors.
Combustible gas indicators are calibrated to a specific gas (e.g., methane or pentane); readings for other gases need a response/correction factor.
Bump test before each day's use; full calibration per manufacturer; pre- and post-calibrate sampling pumps (accept if within about 5%).
Noise: sound level meter (Type 1 precision, Type 2 general survey); dosimeter for personal dose; octave band analyzer for frequency content.
Heat: WBGT monitor; radiation: GM counter (survey), TLD/film badge (personal dose).
Direct-reading = immediate decision (entry, alarm); integrated personal sampling = compliance with a TWA.
Sampling
Air sampling collects contaminant from the worker's breathing zone over a known air volume. The strategy - who, when, how long, how many - matters as much as the method.
Personal breathing-zone samples (within about a 1-ft radius of nose/mouth) are required for compliance; area samples characterize sources.

Media: charcoal/sorbent tubes for vapors (about 0.01-0.2 L/min), filters/cassettes for particulates and metals (about 1-4 L/min), cyclone for respirable dust (10-mm nylon about 1.7 L/min), PCM cassette for asbestos fibers, bags/canisters for grab samples.
Concentration = mass collected / air volume. Example: 0.5 mg at 2.0 L/min for 240 min = 480 L = 0.48 m3, so C = 0.5/0.48 = 1.04 mg/m3.
Full-shift single sample or consecutive samples are preferred over grab samples for TWA comparisons; STEL samples are 15 min.
Include field blanks (commonly 10% of samples, at least 1-2 per set); sample similar exposure groups (SEGs) and the maximum-risk employee first.
Other types: bulk samples (identify material, e.g., asbestos in insulation), wipe/surface samples (lead, beryllium, hygiene), biological monitoring (BEIs).
Unit trap: 1 m3 = 1,000 L. Forgetting this gives answers off by 1,000.
Analysis
Analysis turns sample results into decisions: the lab quantifies the agent, and the safety professional compares the result with the limit using sound statistics.

Lab methods: gas chromatography (organics), AAS/ICP (metals), X-ray diffraction (crystalline silica), PCM (asbestos fibers, TEM to confirm type), gravimetric (total/respirable dust). Use an AIHA-accredited lab and NIOSH/OSHA methods.
OSHA compliance test: Y = result/PEL; UCL = Y + SAE, LCL = Y - SAE. UCL <= 1 compliance; LCL > 1 violation; otherwise 'possible overexposure'.
Example: result 105 ppm, PEL 100 ppm, SAE 0.10 -> Y = 1.05, LCL = 0.95 -> possible overexposure, not a citable violation.
Exposure data are usually lognormal: describe with geometric mean (GM) and geometric standard deviation (GSD) and judge the 95th percentile against the OEL.
Extended shifts (Brief and Scala): RF = (8/h) x ((24 - h)/16). 12-h shift: RF = (8/12)(12/16) = 0.5, so a 100 ppm limit becomes 50 ppm.
AIHA exposure categories compare the 95th percentile with the OEL (e.g., <10% highly controlled ... >100% poorly controlled).
One result just under the PEL does not prove compliance - variability means more samples or a lower AL are needed.
TWA and mixture calculations
The 8-hour time-weighted average combines different concentrations over a shift; mixtures of chemicals with similar effects are assessed with the additive formula.
TWA = (C1T1 + C2T2 + ... + CnTn) / 8 h. Unsampled time is assumed zero only if no exposure is known to occur.
Example: 3 h at 50 ppm, 2 h at 100 ppm, 3 h at 20 ppm -> (150 + 200 + 60)/8 = 51.25 ppm.
Additive mixture: Em = C1/L1 + C2/L2 + ... + Cn/Ln; Em > 1 means the mixture limit is exceeded.
Use the additive formula only for agents with the same target organ/effect (e.g., CNS-depressant solvents); independent effects are judged separately.
Always divide by 8 h for an 8-hr TWA, even if the worker was exposed for only 6 h.
Chemicals

Chemical hazards include toxic, flammable, corrosive and reactive substances in gas, vapor, mist, fume, dust or fiber form. OSHA's Hazard Communication standard (1910.1200, aligned with GHS) is the core program.
HazCom elements: written program, chemical inventory, labels, SDSs, employee training (before initial assignment and when a new hazard is introduced).
Shipped-container label elements: product identifier, signal word, hazard statements, pictograms, precautionary statements, supplier name/address/phone.
Signal words: 'Danger' (more severe) or 'Warning'; only one is used on a label.
Physical forms: gases/vapors (molecular), aerosols - dusts (mechanical), fumes (condensed metal vapor, < 1 um), mists (liquid droplets), fibers.
Substance-specific standards (1910.1001-1053) add AL, exposure monitoring, regulated areas, medical surveillance and hygiene rules (e.g., lead, benzene, Cr(VI), silica).
If a question gives a new chemical, the first step is to obtain and review the SDS.
SDS (Safety Data Sheet)
The SDS is the 16-section GHS document from the manufacturer that describes a chemical's hazards and safe handling. It must be readily accessible to workers on every shift.

Sections: 1 Identification, 2 Hazard(s), 3 Composition, 4 First aid, 5 Fire-fighting, 6 Accidental release, 7 Handling and storage, 8 Exposure controls/PPE, 9 Physical/chemical properties, 10 Stability and reactivity, 11 Toxicological, 12-15 Ecological, Disposal, Transport, Regulatory (not enforced by OSHA), 16 Other (revision date).
Section 8 = PEL/TLV and PPE; Section 10 = incompatibilities; Section 11 = LD50/LC50 and carcinogenicity; Section 9 = flash point, vapor pressure, vapor density.
Employers can rely on the supplier's SDS; electronic access is fine if no barriers exist (power outage backup).
1910.1020 treats SDSs (or a record of chemical identity, where used and when) as exposure records kept 30 years.
'Which SDS section lists incompatible materials?' = Section 10 (handling/storage segregation guidance is in 7).
Radiation

Radiation is energy emitted as particles or waves. Ionizing radiation (alpha, beta, gamma/X-ray, neutrons) can remove electrons and damage DNA; non-ionizing radiation (UV, visible, IR, microwave, RF) mainly causes heating, burns and eye damage.

Shielding: alpha - paper/skin (internal hazard if inhaled/ingested); beta - plastic, glass, aluminum (use low-Z first to limit bremsstrahlung); gamma/X-ray - lead, concrete, water; neutrons - water, polyethylene, concrete.
Protection = time, distance, shielding (ALARA). Dose = dose rate x time: 50 mrem/h for 30 min = 25 mrem.
Inverse square law: I1 x d1^2 = I2 x d2^2. Example: 100 mR/h at 2 ft -> at 10 ft: 100 x (2/10)^2 = 4 mR/h. Doubling distance cuts intensity to 1/4.
Half-life: A = A0 x (1/2)^(t/T). 100 mCi of I-131 (T = 8 d) after 24 d -> 12.5 mCi.
Non-ionizing: UV - photokeratitis (welder's flash), skin cancer, cataracts; IR - cataracts, burns (glassblowers, furnace work); RF/microwave - tissue heating.
Regulators: NRC (licensed nuclear material, 10 CFR 20), states (Agreement States), OSHA 1910.1096 (other sources, e.g., X-ray machines), EPA/DOE environmental and defense.
Inverse square law applies to point sources; for 'move from 3 ft to 6 ft' the answer is always 1/4 the original intensity.
Radiation units, dose limits and area classifications
Radiation quantities have traditional and SI units, and dose limits apply to workers, lens of eye, skin/extremities and the public.
Activity: curie (Ci) / becquerel (Bq; 1 Ci = 3.7 x 10^10 Bq). Exposure: roentgen (R). Absorbed dose: rad / gray (1 Gy = 100 rad). Dose equivalent: rem / sievert (1 Sv = 100 rem).
Dose equivalent = absorbed dose x quality (weighting) factor: alpha 20, neutrons 5-20, beta/gamma/X-ray 1.

Annual occupational limits (NRC 10 CFR 20): 5 rem (50 mSv) whole body TEDE, 15 rem lens of eye, 50 rem skin/extremities; public 0.1 rem (1 mSv); declared pregnant worker 0.5 rem over the pregnancy. The guide labels these OSHA limits; OSHA 1910.1096 itself uses 1.25 rem per calendar quarter whole body.
Areas (NRC): Radiation Area > 5 mrem/h at 30 cm; High Radiation Area > 100 mrem/h at 30 cm; Very High Radiation Area > 500 rad/h at 1 m.
Monitoring: TLD/OSL badges and film badges measure accumulated dose; GM counters survey contamination.
Overexposure reporting under 1910.1096: immediate/24-h notification depending on dose, written report within 30 days.
Gray/rad = energy absorbed; sievert/rem = biological effect. Pick rem/Sv when the question mentions 'biological damage'.
Radiation emergency response
Radiation incidents follow life-safety-first priorities, isolation, notification and ALARA-based protection of responders.
Rescue the injured first if safe - medical care outranks decontamination for serious injuries.
Isolate and post the area; notify NRC/state, DOE or EPA as applicable, and OSHA if limits are exceeded.
Responders use time, distance, shielding and worker rotation; wear dosimeters and respirators for airborne alpha/beta contamination.
Personal decon: remove clothing (removes about 90% of contamination), wash with mild soap and water, do not abrade skin.
Potassium iodide (KI) blocks thyroid uptake of radioactive iodine only; shelter-in-place if evacuation is unsafe.
Contaminated PPE is radioactive waste; store until decayed per half-life or ship to licensed disposal.
'First action' at a radiation spill with an injured worker = life-safety rescue/medical care, then control contamination.
Noise
