Noise is unwanted sound; prolonged exposure above 85 dBA destroys cochlear hair cells and causes permanent noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL). OSHA 1910.95 sets the PEL and Hearing Conservation Program triggers.
OSHA PEL 90 dBA 8-h TWA (5-dB exchange rate); Action Level 85 dBA (dose 50%) triggers the HCP; impulse noise should not exceed 140 dB peak.
NIOSH REL and ACGIH TLV: 85 dBA 8-h with 3-dB exchange rate (more protective).
Human hearing 20-20,000 Hz; most sensitive 1,000-4,000 Hz; NIHL first appears as a notch at 3,000-6,000 Hz (classic 4 kHz notch).
dBA weighting mimics the ear and is used for compliance; dBC/peak (flat) for impulse and low-frequency noise.
Instruments: SLM for area spot checks, integrating SLM for variable noise, dosimeter for personal dose (compliance).
PEL 90 vs AL 85: at 87 dBA TWA the employer is under the PEL but must run a hearing conservation program.
Noise calculations (dB addition, dose, distance)
Decibels are logarithmic, so sound levels cannot be added arithmetically. Dose and TWA calculations follow OSHA 1910.95 Appendix A.
Adding levels: L = 10 log10(sum of 10^(Li/10)). Two equal sources = +3 dB (90 + 90 = 93 dB); 90 + 95 = 96.2 dB.
Shortcut: difference 0-1 dB add 3; 2-3 add 2; 4-9 add 1; 10+ add 0 to the higher level.
Distance (point source, free field): L2 = L1 - 20 log10(d2/d1); drops 6 dB per doubling. 100 dB at 3 ft -> 88 dB at 12 ft.
Halving exposure time under OSHA allows +5 dB; under NIOSH only +3 dB. Do not mix exchange rates.
Hearing conservation program and hearing protectors
1910.95(c)-(o) requires a hearing conservation program when the 8-h TWA reaches 85 dBA. Engineering and administrative controls are required above 90 dBA; HPDs are interim/last line of defense.
Elements: monitoring, audiometric testing, HPDs at no cost (mandatory over 90 dBA or with an STS), training annually, recordkeeping.
Baseline audiogram within 6 months of first exposure at/above AL (1 year with mobile van, HPDs required meanwhile); 14 h without workplace noise before baseline; annual audiograms thereafter.

Standard threshold shift (STS) = average change of 10 dB or more at 2,000, 3,000 and 4,000 Hz in either ear; OSHA-recordable if also 25 dB or more above audiometric zero. Notify employee in writing within 21 days.
NRR derating (OSHA App. B, dBA): effective level = TWA - (NRR - 7). OSHA FOM also applies a 50% safety factor: TWA - (NRR - 7)/2. Example: 100 dBA, NRR 29 -> 100 - 11 = 89 dBA.
Records: noise exposure measurements 2 years; audiograms for duration of employment.
Hearing loss types: conductive (outer/middle ear, often treatable), sensorineural (cochlea/nerve - NIHL, permanent), mixed, central (brain). TTS is temporary; PTS and presbycusis (age) are permanent.
Calculation trap: subtract 7 from NRR before derating when the exposure is in dBA.
Biological hazards

Biohazards are microorganisms, their toxins and biological materials that cause infection, allergy or poisoning. Exposure is significant in healthcare, labs, agriculture, animal handling, sewage and waste work.

Categories: bacteria (TB, anthrax, Legionella), viruses (HBV, HCV, HIV, rabies, influenza), fungi (Aspergillus, Histoplasma, Candida), parasites (malaria, Giardia), prions and toxins (CJD, botulinum, aflatoxin).

Bloodborne Pathogens 1910.1030: exposure control plan reviewed annually, universal/standard precautions, engineered sharps, HBV vaccine offered within 10 working days at no cost (signed declination if refused), annual training, sharps injury log, post-exposure evaluation.
BBP records: medical records duration of employment + 30 years; training records 3 years.

Biosafety levels: BSL-1 teaching labs (E. coli K-12); BSL-2 clinical labs, Class II BSC (Salmonella, HBV, HIV samples); BSL-3 negative pressure, HEPA exhaust (TB, SARS-CoV-2, Coxiella); BSL-4 positive-pressure suits, isolated building (Ebola, Marburg).
Controls: elimination/substitution, engineering (BSCs, negative-pressure rooms, ventilation), vaccination, administrative (screening), PPE (N95 or higher for airborne agents).
Match the containment clue: 'negative pressure' = BSL-3; 'full-body positive-pressure suit' = BSL-4.
Heat/cold

The thermal environment (heat or cold) is assessed by measuring air temperature, humidity, air movement and radiant heat, together with work rate and clothing. The WBGT index is the standard heat-stress metric.
Outdoor with sun: WBGT = 0.7 NWB + 0.2 GT + 0.1 DB. Indoor/no solar load: WBGT = 0.7 NWB + 0.3 GT (NWB = natural wet bulb, GT = globe, DB = dry bulb).
Example: NWB 25 C, GT 40 C, DB 30 C -> outdoor WBGT = 17.5 + 8 + 3 = 28.5 C; indoor = 17.5 + 12 = 29.5 C.
Compare WBGT (adjusted for clothing) with ACGIH TLV/Action Limit tables by metabolic rate and work-rest regimen (e.g., continuous moderate work, acclimatized TLV about 28 C).
Heat index (temperature + humidity) is used for outdoor work planning; OSHA relies on the General Duty Clause and a heat NEP (a federal heat rule was proposed in 2024).
Cold: wind chill (air temperature + wind speed) drives frostbite risk; ACGIH cold TLV aims to keep core temperature at or above 36 C (96.8 F).
NWB carries 70% of the WBGT weight - humidity and evaporative cooling dominate heat stress.
Heat/cold stress
Heat and cold illnesses range from mild skin conditions to life-threatening emergencies. Recognize the signature symptom and the correct first response.
Heat rash - blocked sweat ducts; heat cramps - sodium/potassium loss (electrolyte drinks); heat syncope - blood pooling in legs (lie down, elevate legs).
Heat exhaustion - heavy sweating, nausea, rapid pulse, core temperature below 104 F (40 C); reversible with rest, cooling and fluids.
Heat stroke - core above 104 F (40 C), confusion/seizures, often hot dry skin; MEDICAL EMERGENCY: call EMS and cool rapidly (cold-water immersion).
Prevention: acclimatization (NIOSH: no more than 20% of usual exposure on day 1 for new workers, increasing about 20%/day), water about 1 cup every 15-20 min, shade, work-rest cycles, buddy system.

Cold: hypothermia (core below 95 F / 35 C, shivering then confusion), frostbite (frozen tissue, pale waxy skin), chilblains (non-freezing, red itchy patches), trench/immersion foot (cold and wet, 32-60 F), reduced dexterity from vasoconstriction.
Confusion/altered mental state + heat = heat stroke, regardless of whether the worker is still sweating.
Indoor air quality

IAQ problems arise from inadequate ventilation, indoor sources (VOCs, mold, combustion products) and outdoor air intake contamination. Investigations combine occupant surveys, walkthroughs and targeted measurements.
Tools: CO2 monitoring (surrogate for ventilation adequacy), direct-reading CO/VOC/particle meters, smoke tubes and anemometers for airflow, culture plates and spore traps for mold.
CO2 above about 1,000 ppm (or more than about 700 ppm above outdoor, ~400 ppm) suggests inadequate outdoor air.
Sick building syndrome (SBS): non-specific symptoms (headache, irritation, fatigue) that improve after leaving the building; no single cause.
Building-related illness (BRI): a diagnosable illness from an identified contaminant (Legionnaires' disease, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, CO poisoning); OSHA-recordable if work-related.
ASHRAE 55 = thermal comfort (about 68-76 F, RH about 30-60%); ASHRAE 62.1 = ventilation for acceptable IAQ.
Moisture control is key to mold; remediate water damage within 24-48 h.
SBS vs BRI: 'symptoms disappear when they leave' = SBS; 'confirmed diagnosis linked to a contaminant' = BRI.
Ventilation

Ventilation controls airborne contaminants either by diluting them with clean air (general/dilution ventilation) or by capturing them at the source (local exhaust ventilation, LEV). LEV is preferred for toxic contaminants and point sources.
Q = V x A (cfm = fpm x ft2). Example: 12-in duct (A = 0.785 ft2) at 3,000 fpm -> Q = 2,356 cfm.
Air changes per hour: ACH = Q (cfm) x 60 / room volume (ft3). Example: 2,000 cfm in 50 x 40 x 10 ft room (20,000 ft3) -> 6 ACH.
Plain-opening hood capture (DallaValle): Q = V(10X^2 + A); flanged hood Q = 0.75V(10X^2 + A). Example: 100 fpm at X = 1 ft, A = 0.5 ft2 -> Q = 1,050 cfm.
Velocity from velocity pressure (standard air): V = 4,005 x sqrt(VP in. w.g.); VP = 1 in. -> 4,005 fpm.
Dilution: Q = (403 x 10^6 x SG x ER x K)/(MW x C), ER in pints/min evaporated, K = mixing safety factor 1-10; only for low-toxicity contaminants with dispersed sources.

LEV components: hood, ductwork, air cleaner, fan, exhaust stack; provide make-up air; typical dust transport velocity about 3,500-4,500 fpm. ASHRAE 62.1 and ACGIH Industrial Ventilation manual are references.
Capture velocity falls off roughly with the square of distance - moving the hood closer is the cheapest improvement.
Nanoparticles
Engineered nanoparticles are smaller than 100 nm. Their very high surface-area-to-mass ratio makes them more reactive and lets them reach the alveoli and possibly the bloodstream.
Sources: nanotech labs, coatings/paints, electronics, drug delivery, carbon nanotubes/nanofibers, 3D-printing powders.
Hazards: lung inflammation and fibrosis, possible cancer, cardiovascular effects (translocation), skin/eye irritation; long-term toxicity data are limited - apply precautionary controls.
NIOSH RELs: carbon nanotubes/nanofibers 1 ug/m3 (respirable elemental carbon); ultrafine TiO2 0.3 mg/m3.
Controls: enclosure and LEV with HEPA filtration (HEPA captures nanoparticles efficiently by diffusion), wet methods, HEPA vacuums, no dry sweeping or compressed air, respirators with P100 filters.
References: NIOSH Approaches to Safe Nanotechnology; ISO/TR 12885.
Mass-based limits under-represent nano hazards - surface area and particle count matter more.
Combustible dust
Finely divided combustible solids can deflagrate when dispersed in air in a confined space. Secondary explosions from accumulated dust disturbed by a primary event cause most deaths.
Dust explosion pentagon: fuel, oxygen, ignition, dispersion, confinement (fire triangle + 2).
Materials: wood, grain/sugar/flour, plastics, coal, metals (aluminum, magnesium), pharmaceuticals.
Standards: NFPA 652 (fundamentals, Dust Hazard Analysis required), 654 (general), 61 (agricultural/food), 484 (metals), 664 (wood); OSHA Combustible Dust NEP; 1910.272 grain handling.
Kst (deflagration index) classes: St 1 up to 200, St 2 201-300, St 3 above 300 bar-m/s; higher = more violent.
Housekeeping: remove accumulations (historic NFPA 654 benchmark 1/32 in. over 5% of floor area); use approved vacuums; avoid compressed-air blowdown; inspect hidden surfaces.
Engineering: dust collection, explosion venting (NFPA 68), suppression/isolation (NFPA 69), Class II hazardous location equipment, bonding/grounding, spark detection.
The most effective prevention is controlling dust accumulation (housekeeping/containment), not just ignition control.
Heat systems (boilers, steam, thermal fluids, furnaces)
Process heating systems store large amounts of thermal and pressure energy. Failures cause burns, scalds, fires and boiler or furnace explosions.
Boilers and pressure vessels: ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, National Board inspection, state jurisdictional inspections.
Safeguards: safety relief valves, low-water fuel cutoffs, pressure/temperature limits, burner management systems and flame safeguards (NFPA 85/86), purge cycles before ignition.
Steam: scalding, water hammer, flashing condensate; lock out and depressurize/cool before opening; use proper steam-rated hoses.
Thermal fluid (hot oil) systems: leaks into insulation can autoignite below the fluid's normal autoignition temperature.
Controls also include insulation/guarding of hot surfaces (burn threshold about 140 F/60 C contact), heat-resistant PPE and trained operators.
Low-water condition in a boiler: never add cold water to a hot dry boiler - shut down the burner and let it cool.
High pressure (compressed air, hydraulics, gas cylinders, pressure testing)
High-pressure systems release stored energy violently through hose whip, projectiles, injection injuries and vessel rupture.
Compressed air for cleaning must be reduced below 30 psi with chip guarding and PPE (1910.242(b)); never use on skin or clothing.
Hydraulic/high-pressure fluid injection injuries look minor but are surgical emergencies; never locate leaks with hands - use cardboard.

Cylinders (1910.101, CGA P-1): store upright, secured, valve caps on; oxygen 20 ft from fuel gases or separated by a 5-ft, 1/2-hour fire-rated barrier; move with carts, not by rolling or lifting by caps.
Pressure testing: hydrostatic is preferred over pneumatic because gas stores far more energy; establish exclusion zones.
Whip checks on air hoses; relief valves on receivers; LOTO includes bleeding stored pressure.
Water jetting (very high pressure) requires trained operators, deadman controls and specific PPE.
Pneumatic test vs hydrostatic test: hydrostatic is safer because liquids are nearly incompressible.
Silica
Respirable crystalline silica (quartz, cristobalite) from cutting, grinding, drilling, blasting and foundry work causes silicosis, lung cancer, COPD, kidney and autoimmune disease.
OSHA 1910.1053 / 1926.1153: PEL 50 ug/m3 8-h TWA; action level 25 ug/m3. NIOSH REL 50 ug/m3; ACGIH TLV 25 ug/m3 (stricter, best practice).
Construction: follow Table 1 control methods (water, LEV, respirators) or do exposure assessment; competent person and written exposure control plan required.
Medical surveillance: general industry - exposure at/above AL for 30+ days/yr; construction - required respirator use 30+ days/yr; exams every 3 years.
Prohibited: dry sweeping and compressed-air cleaning where alternatives exist.
IARC Group 1 carcinogen; 'pneumoconiosis + autoimmune disease' points to silica.
Controls: substitution (non-silica abrasives), wet methods, LEV/vacuum shrouds, enclosed cabs, respirators.
Best practice limit = ACGIH TLV 25 ug/m3; enforceable limit = OSHA PEL 50 ug/m3.
Powder/spray applications (spray finishing, powder coating)
Spray painting and powder coating create flammable vapors, combustible dusts and toxic or sensitizing aerosols (isocyanates, Cr(VI) primers, solvents).
Standards: OSHA 1910.107 (spray finishing) and 1910.94(c) (spray booth ventilation); NFPA 33.
Booth interior and exhaust plenum are hazardous (classified) locations; no open flames or spark sources within 20 ft of spraying unless separated.
Keep vapor below 25% of LFL; exhaust fans interlocked with spray equipment; clean filters and residue regularly.
Electrostatic equipment and powder coating require bonding/grounding of parts and workers; powder coatings are combustible dusts.
Health: isocyanate (2-part urethane) asthma - supplied-air respirators often required; hexavalent chromium mist in aircraft painting.
Controls: high-transfer-efficiency (HVLP) guns, water-based coatings, enclosure, PPE (respirators, coveralls, gloves).
'Aircraft painting + chromate primer' = hexavalent chromium; 'auto-body clearcoat + asthma' = isocyanates.
Blasting (abrasive blasting)
Abrasive blasting cleans and prepares surfaces by propelling media at high pressure. It exposes workers to silica and toxic metals, noise, high-pressure injury and fire/explosion hazards.
Respirable silica (silicosis, lung cancer) - substitute non-silica media (steel grit, garnet, crushed glass, slag - check metals content).
Toxic metals from coatings: lead, cadmium, chromium, beryllium.
Noise often exceeds 100 dBA; high-pressure stream can inject or lacerate (deadman controls on nozzles).
OSHA 1910.94(a): blast cleaning enclosures with exhaust; abrasive-blasting respirators (Type CE supplied-air) for operators inside enclosures or where silica/toxic dust exists.
Dust-laden confined spaces raise fire/explosion risk; ground nozzles and hoses to prevent static.
Explosive blasting (demolition, quarrying) is separate: 1926 Subpart U and 1910.109 - blaster in charge, misfire procedures, radio-frequency precautions.
First control for silica in blasting is substitution of the abrasive, not a better respirator.
Molten metals
Foundry, smelting, casting and welding operations combine thermal, chemical and explosion hazards.
Burns from splashes and spills; aluminized/FR clothing, face shields, spats and leggings.
Steam explosions: molten metal contacting water or moisture (wet scrap, tools, molds, floors) expands violently - preheat and dry everything that contacts the melt.
Metal fumes: zinc/copper - metal fume fever; manganese - neurotoxic (manganism); Cr(VI) and others - respiratory/systemic toxicity.
Infrared radiation damages eyes (cataracts) and skin; use IR-rated eyewear and shielding.
Radiant heat causes heat stress; apply WBGT monitoring, work-rest cycles and cooling.
Additional: silica in foundry sand, CO from cupolas, noise, crane and ladle handling.
Most catastrophic molten-metal incidents involve water/moisture - the key preventive control is keeping everything dry.
Hot work
Hot work is any welding, cutting, brazing, grinding or other spark- or flame-producing work. It requires a permit system, fire prevention measures and control of welding fumes and radiation.
Standards: OSHA 1910.252 (and 1926 Subpart J), NFPA 51B. Prefer moving the work to a designated safe area.
Remove combustibles within 35 ft or protect them with covers/shields; cover floor and wall openings.
Fire watch during work and at least 30 min after (OSHA); NFPA 51B (2019 and later) requires 60 min followed by additional monitoring.

Permit authorizing individual inspects the area and issues a written permit; test atmosphere for flammables in confined spaces and around tanks (do not weld on containers that held flammables until cleaned/purged/inerted).
Health: welding fumes (Mn, Cr(VI) from stainless, Zn from galvanized), ozone, NOx, UV (welder's flash) - use LEV and correct filter shade numbers.
Cylinders, hoses and flashback arrestors inspected; separate oxygen and fuel gas in storage.
Where the work can be relocated to a shop, that beats any permit or fire-watch answer.
Lasers
Lasers emit coherent, highly collimated optical radiation that can damage the eye (retina for visible/near-IR, cornea for UV/far-IR) and skin. ANSI Z136.1 classifies lasers by hazard.

Classes: 1 and 1M safe (1M unless viewed with optics); 2 visible, protected by blink reflex (0.25 s); 2M hazardous with optics; 3R low risk; 3B direct and specular beam eye hazard; 4 eye, skin, fire and diffuse-reflection hazard.
A Laser Safety Officer (LSO) is required for Class 3B and 4.

Engineering controls first: beam enclosures, interlocks, key switches, beam stops, shutters; administrative: SOPs, training, 'Laser On' illuminated signs, restricted access, nominal hazard zone (NHZ).
Eyewear must match the laser's wavelength and have adequate optical density: OD = log10(H0/MPE). Example: exposure 10 W/cm2, MPE 0.001 W/cm2 -> OD = log10(10,000) = 4.
Class 4 lasers also create fire and laser-generated air contaminants (plume) - need FR materials and smoke evacuation.
The blink reflex protects only against Class 2 visible beams - never assume it protects against 3B or 4.
mcq: A worker's acetone exposure over an 8-hour shift was: 2 h at 300 ppm, 3 h at 200 ppm, and 3 h at 100 ppm. What is the 8-hour TWA?
202 ppm
163 ppm
221 ppm
TWA = sum(C x T)/8 = (600 + 600 + 300)/8 = 187.5 ppm. Trap: averaging the three concentrations without time weighting gives 200 ppm.
A worker is exposed to 95 dBA for 2 hours, 90 dBA for 4 hours, and 85 dBA for 2 hours. What is the worker's OSHA noise dose?
Allowed times (OSHA 5-dB rule): 95 dBA = 4 h, 90 dBA = 8 h, 85 dBA = 16 h. D = 2/4 + 4/8 + 2/16 = 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.125 = 112.5%, which exceeds the PEL.
A noise dosimeter reports a daily dose of 200% (OSHA criteria). What is the equivalent 8-hour TWA? (TWA = 16.61 log10(D/100) + 90)
90 dBA
93 dBA
95 dBA
100 dBA
TWA = 16.61 x log10(200/100) + 90 = 16.61 x 0.301 + 90 = 95 dBA. With a 5-dB exchange rate, doubling the dose adds 5 dB; 93 dBA is the 3-dB (NIOSH) trap.
A jackhammer produces 98 dB at 3 ft. Using the inverse square law (L2 = L1 - 20 log(d2/d1)), what is the approximate sound level at 12 ft?
86 dB
88 dB
92 dB
94 dB
Inverse square law for a point source: L2 = L1 - 20 log(d2/d1) = 98 - 20 log(12/3) = 98 - 12 = 86 dB. Each doubling of distance drops about 6 dB.

A radiography crew performs weld inspections with a gamma source. A helper normally works 4 ft from the source but steps back to 12 ft during exposures. How does the radiation intensity at 12 ft compare with that at 4 ft?
1/2 as much
1/9 as much
1/3 as much
The same amount
Radiation intensity follows the inverse square law: I2/I1 = (d1/d2)^2 = (4/12)^2 = 1/9. Trap: 1/3 assumes intensity drops linearly with distance.
Outdoors in direct sun, a heat stress survey records: natural wet bulb 25 C, globe 40 C, dry bulb 30 C. What is the WBGT? (Outdoor: WBGT = 0.7 NWB + 0.2 GT + 0.1 DB)
WBGT = 0.7(25) + 0.2(40) + 0.1(30) = 17.5 + 8 + 3 = 28.5 C. Trap: 29.5 C uses the indoor/no-solar-load formula (0.7 NWB + 0.3 GT).
Under OSHA's respirable crystalline silica standard, what are the PEL and action level (8-hour TWA)?
PEL 100 ug/m3; AL 50 ug/m3
PEL 50 ug/m3; AL 25 ug/m3
PEL 25 ug/m3; AL 10 ug/m3
PEL 10 mg/m3; AL 5 mg/m3
OSHA 1910.1053/1926.1153 set the respirable crystalline silica PEL at 50 ug/m3 and the action level at 25 ug/m3 (8-h TWA). The old 100 ug/m3 value is the trap.

A metal finishing shop uses a nickel-containing polishing compound. Workers complain of sinus irritation during buffing. No prior exposure data exists and ventilation effectiveness is unknown. What is the MOST appropriate first step in the exposure assessment?
Conduct full-shift dosimetry on all workers in the department
Rely on SDS information to estimate exposures without sampling
Assume exposures are below limits because symptoms are mild
Perform task-based personal air sampling on workers performing the buffing activity

With symptoms, no data, and unknown ventilation, the first step is task-based personal breathing-zone sampling of the buffing workers. Department-wide dosimetry is unfocused; SDS data alone cannot quantify exposure.

Ralph is assigned to sweep a dusty floor and asks for a filtering facepiece respirator (dust mask). Dust levels are well below regulatory limits. The supervisor refuses because Ralph has not been fit tested. Was the supervisor correct?
Yes, anyone wearing a tight-fitting respirator must be medically evaluated and fit tested prior to wearing one.
Yes, Ralph should not have asked for the respirator due to budget constraints.
No, fit testing is not required in this specific case.
No, the safety supervisor should have performed a fit test and issued the respirator.
Voluntary use of a filtering facepiece where exposures are below limits falls under 1910.134 Appendix D: give the user Appendix D information; fit testing and medical evaluation are not required.
An employee with facial hair that prevents a half-mask seal is assigned a powered air-purifying respirator (PAPR) with a loose-fitting hood. Which type of fit testing is required?
Fit testing is not required
Medical fit testing
Qualitative fit testing
Quantitative fit testing
Fit testing under 1910.134 applies to tight-fitting facepieces. A loose-fitting PAPR hood does not need a facial seal, so no fit test is required (medical evaluation is still required).

topics.title: Public Health and Epidemiology
topics.bp: Understand principles of public health as applicable (i.e., fundamentals of epidemiology, infectious disease, risk factors, statistics to interpret data)
topics.definition: Epidemiology is the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related events in populations and the application of that study to control health problems. Public health principles help the safety professional recognize disease patterns, infectious disease risks and risk factors in the workforce.
topics.easy: Epidemiology asks who gets sick, where, when and why. Comparing exposed and unexposed groups shows whether a workplace exposure raises the risk of disease.
points: Measures: incidence (new cases ÷ population at risk over time), prevalence (all existing cases ÷ population at a point/period), attack rate, mortality rate.

Study designs: cohort (follows exposed vs unexposed forward; relative risk), case-control (starts with cases vs controls, looks back at exposure; odds ratio), cross-sectional (snapshot; prevalence), ecological, randomized controlled trial.
Relative risk RR = incidence exposed ÷ incidence unexposed (RR > 1 = increased risk). Odds ratio OR = (a × d) ÷ (b × c). Attributable risk = Ie − Iu.

Causation criteria (Bradford Hill): strength, consistency, specificity, temporality (exposure before disease), dose-response, plausibility, coherence, experiment, analogy. Correlation is not causation; watch for confounding and bias (e.g., healthy worker effect).

Infectious disease chain of infection: agent → reservoir → portal of exit → mode of transmission (contact, droplet, airborne, vector, common vehicle) → portal of entry → susceptible host. Break the chain with vaccination, hygiene, ventilation, isolation, PPE.
Occupational infectious risks: bloodborne pathogens (HBV, HCV, HIV), TB, Legionella, zoonoses (brucellosis from animals/milk, anthrax, histoplasmosis), pandemic influenza/COVID-19 (pandemic plans).
Risk factors: modifiable (smoking, obesity, inactivity) vs non-modifiable (age, genetics); occupational vs non-occupational; Total Worker Health (NIOSH) integrates protection and health promotion.
Screening tests: sensitivity (true positive rate), specificity (true negative rate).
topics.example: A plant notices several cases of a rare respiratory disease. A cohort analysis shows 30 cases per 1,000 among workers exposed to a metalworking fluid versus 10 per 1,000 among unexposed workers - a relative risk of 3.0. The fluid system is found contaminated with bacteria; the system is cleaned, a biocide program and mist collectors are installed, and new cases stop.
tips: Cohort → relative risk; case-control → odds ratio.
Incidence = new cases; prevalence = existing cases.
Temporality (exposure before disease) is the one causation criterion that is required.
topics.yates: Ch. 11 Biological Hazards, p. 332; Ch. 15 Statistics for the Safety Professional, p. 408
subs: Epidemiology

Epidemiology studies the distribution (who, where, when) and determinants (why) of disease in populations and applies that knowledge to control health problems. In occupational health it links exposures to outcomes such as cancer or hearing loss.
Functions: prevention of disease, measuring frequency (incidence and prevalence) and describing distribution by person, place and time.
Descriptive studies generate hypotheses; analytic studies (cohort, case-control) test them.
Cohort study: start with exposed and unexposed groups and follow for disease (prospective or retrospective/historical); gives incidence and relative risk.
Case-control study: start with cases and controls and look back at exposures; good for rare diseases; gives odds ratio.
Cross-sectional: snapshot of prevalence; ecological: group-level data (ecological fallacy risk).
Bradford Hill causation criteria: strength, consistency, specificity, temporality (must have), dose-response, plausibility, coherence, experiment, analogy.
Rare disease, limited budget, look back at exposure = case-control. Following workers forward = cohort.
Infectious disease
Infectious disease spreads through the chain of infection. Breaking any link - at the agent, reservoir, transmission route or host - prevents spread.
Chain of infection: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host.
Modes: contact (direct/indirect), droplet (large particles, about 3-6 ft), airborne (droplet nuclei - TB, measles), vehicle (food/water - Hep A), vector (ticks, fleas, mosquitoes).
Standard precautions apply to all patients; transmission-based precautions add contact, droplet or airborne measures (airborne infection isolation rooms: negative pressure, 12+ ACH, N95 or higher).
Host defenses: vaccination (HBV, Hep A, rabies pre-exposure, Tdap), post-exposure prophylaxis (HBIG, rabies PEP, TIG).
Outbreak response: case definition, confirm diagnosis, count cases, describe by person/place/time, hypothesize, test, control, communicate.
Pandemic planning ties to business continuity: absenteeism planning, ventilation, PPE stockpiles, remote work.
TB transmission is airborne (droplet nuclei), not surface contact - controls are ventilation, isolation and respirators.
Risk factors
A risk factor is any attribute or exposure that increases the probability of disease or injury. Public-health thinking considers agent, host and environment together (the epidemiologic triangle).
Host factors: age, sex, genetics, immune status, pregnancy, pre-existing disease (diabetes, asthma), lifestyle (smoking, alcohol, obesity).
Agent factors: toxicity, infectivity, dose, duration; environmental factors: temperature, ventilation, crowding, sanitation, work organization.
Modifiable (smoking, PPE use, exposure level) vs non-modifiable (age, genetics).
Confounder: a factor linked to both exposure and outcome (e.g., smoking in a lung-cancer study of miners) - control by matching, stratification or adjustment.
Effect modification: smoking multiplies asbestos lung-cancer risk (synergy); healthy worker effect makes worker mortality look lower than the general population.
When a study ignores smoking in a lung disease outcome, the weakness is confounding.
Statistics (epidemiologic measures)
Public-health statistics express how often disease occurs and how strongly it is associated with an exposure.
Incidence rate = new cases / population at risk over a time period; prevalence = existing cases / total population at a point in time. Prevalence roughly = incidence x duration.
Relative risk RR = incidence exposed / incidence unexposed. Example: 30/1,000 vs 10/1,000 -> RR = 3. RR = 1 no association; > 1 increased risk.
Attributable risk = Ie - Iu = 0.03 - 0.01 = 20 per 1,000 exposed.
Odds ratio (case-control) = ad/bc. Example: exposed cases 40, unexposed cases 60, exposed controls 20, unexposed controls 80 -> (40 x 80)/(20 x 60) = 2.67.
SMR = observed deaths / expected deaths x 100. 15 observed vs 10 expected = 150 (50% excess).
Screening: sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN); specificity = TN/(TN + FP). 95% CI = mean +/- 1.96 x SD/sqrt(n); if a CI for RR/OR includes 1 the result is not statistically significant (p >= 0.05).
Odds ratio comes from case-control studies; relative risk comes from cohort studies.
Zoonotic and occupational bacterial diseases
Several bacterial diseases are acquired from animals, animal products, soil or water in specific occupations. Exam questions pair an occupation and a signature symptom.
Anthrax (Bacillus anthracis): wool, hides, livestock; cutaneous = black eschar (95% of cases); inhalation = 'woolsorter's disease' (most lethal); not person-to-person; CDC Category A agent.
Leptospirosis (Leptospira): animal urine in water/soil - rice-field, sewage, flood workers; severe form (Weil's disease) = jaundice + kidney failure.
Brucellosis (Brucella): meat packing, dairy, unpasteurized milk; 'undulant fever'; no human vaccine - pasteurization is key.
Q fever (Coxiella burnetii): inhalation of aerosols from animal birth products; pneumonia + hepatitis; chronic = endocarditis; BSL-3.
Psittacosis (Chlamydia psittaci): bird droppings/feather dust - pet shops, poultry; atypical pneumonia.

Tularemia (rabbit/deer-fly fever), plague (Yersinia pestis; rodent-flea-human; pneumonic form spreads person-to-person), tetanus (Clostridium tetani; lockjaw; Td booster every 10 years), cat scratch fever (Bartonella), RMSF (Rickettsia; tick-borne; rash starts at wrists/ankles).
Category A bioterrorism agents in the guide: anthrax, plague, tularemia.
Viral and fungal occupational diseases
Viral and fungal infections in the workplace follow distinct transmission routes that determine the control.
Hepatitis A: fecal-oral (food handlers, daycare, sewage); self-limiting, no chronic infection; vaccine available.
Hepatitis B: blood/body fluids (needlesticks, splashes); can become chronic (cirrhosis, liver cancer); 3-dose vaccine; HBIG + vaccine post-exposure. HBV survives on surfaces up to 7 days.
Hepatitis C and HIV: bloodborne; no vaccine; needlestick transmission risk roughly HBV 6-30% (unvaccinated) > HCV about 1.8% > HIV about 0.3%.
Rabies: bite/saliva of dogs, bats, raccoons; hydrophobia; nearly always fatal once symptoms appear - immediate wound washing and PEP.

Orf (sheep/goats - painful hand nodules); Histoplasmosis (bird/bat droppings - demolition, bridge work); Aspergillosis (construction dust, compost - HEPA in hospitals during renovation); Candidiasis (opportunistic, moist PPE, ICU).
Legionella: aerosols from cooling towers, hot water systems; prevented by water management programs (ASHRAE 188).
Hep A = fecal-oral and acute only; Hep B = bloodborne and can be chronic.
Total Worker Health
Total Worker Health (NIOSH) integrates protection from work-related hazards with promotion of injury and illness prevention and worker well-being.
Hazard prevention comes first; health promotion supplements, never replaces, controls.
Addresses work organization: scheduling, stress, fatigue, workload, supervision.
Integrates programs such as fitness, nutrition, smoking cessation, mental health and financial well-being.
Participatory approach - workers help design programs; evidence-based evaluation.
Reference: NIOSH Fundamentals of Total Worker Health Approaches.
Question stresses 'integration of OSH with health promotion' = Total Worker Health.
mcq: Which statement correctly distinguishes incidence from prevalence?
Incidence counts all existing cases; prevalence counts new cases
Incidence counts NEW cases over a period; prevalence counts ALL existing cases at a point or period in time
They are the same
Prevalence applies only to infectious disease
Incidence = new cases over a period among those at risk (measures risk); prevalence = all existing cases at a point or period (measures burden).
In a cohort study, 30 of 1,000 exposed workers and 10 of 1,000 unexposed workers develop a disease. What is the relative risk?
RR = incidence in exposed / incidence in unexposed = (30/1,000)/(10/1,000) = 3.0. Exposed workers are three times as likely to develop the disease.
In a case-control study, 40 cases were exposed and 60 were not; 20 controls were exposed and 80 were not. What is the odds ratio?
OR = (a x d)/(b x c) = (40 x 80)/(60 x 20) = 3,200/1,200 = 2.67. Case-control studies yield odds ratios; cohort studies yield relative risks.
A cohort study reports a relative risk of 1.4 for solvent exposure and liver disease, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.8 to 2.4. What is the BEST interpretation?
The association is not statistically significant at the 0.05 level because the interval includes 1.0
Solvent exposure is proven to cause a 40% increase in liver disease
Solvent exposure is protective against liver disease
Solvent exposure reduces liver disease risk by 40%
A 95% CI for a ratio that includes 1.0 (no effect) means the result is not statistically significant. Trap: reading the point estimate of 1.4 as proof of causation.
Foundry workers show a higher lung cancer rate than office workers, but the foundry workers also smoke at a much higher rate. In this study, smoking is BEST described as a:
Outcome variable
Primary exposure
Random sampling error
Confounding variable
A confounder is linked to both the exposure group and the outcome and can distort the apparent association. It must be controlled by stratification, matching or adjustment.
At the start of a year, 25 of a plant's 400 workers already have occupational dermatitis. During the year, 15 new cases occur. What is the annual incidence rate per 100 workers at risk?
Incidence = new cases / population at risk = 15/(400 - 25) = 15/375 = 4.0 per 100. Trap: 3.75 wrongly includes existing cases in the denominator; 10.0 counts all 40 cases (prevalence).
What is the primary route of transmission for Tuberculosis (TB)?
Airborne droplets
Skin contact
Blood transfusion
Contaminated water
Tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) spreads by inhaling airborne droplet nuclei expelled when an infected person coughs or sneezes, so controls focus on airborne isolation and respirators.
Which indoor contaminant is primarily responsible for Legionnaires' disease outbreaks?
Asbestos
Molds
Legionella bacteria in cooling towers and water systems
Ozone
Legionella pneumophila grows in poorly maintained warm-water systems such as cooling towers and is spread by inhaled aerosols. Water management programs are the main control.
Brucellosis is commonly known as:
Undulant fever
Blackwater fever
Weil's disease
Rabbit fever

Brucellosis, spread through contact with infected animal tissues and fluids (meat packers, dairy and abattoir workers), is called undulant fever because the fever comes and goes. Weil's disease is leptospirosis and rabbit fever is tularemia.
Which occupation is at highest risk of Leptospirosis infection?
Electricians
Rice-field workers
Office staff
Painters
Leptospira spreads through water and soil contaminated with animal urine, so rice-field, sewer and farm workers are at highest risk.

topics.title: Toxicology
topics.bp: Apply toxicology principles to create exposure control plans and develop risk mitigation plans (e.g., using sampling equipment, symptoms of an exposure, LD50, LC50, mutagens, carcinogens, teratogens, ototoxins)
topics.definition: Toxicology is the study of the adverse effects of chemical, physical and biological agents on living organisms. The dose makes the poison (Paracelsus): the effect depends on dose, route of entry, duration and frequency of exposure and individual susceptibility.
topics.easy: Every chemical can be harmful at a high enough dose. Know how it gets into the body, what it attacks, how much it takes, and the signs that someone has been exposed - then plan controls to keep the dose low.
points: Routes of entry: inhalation (most important occupationally), skin absorption, ingestion, injection.

Dose-response: NOAEL/LOAEL, threshold; LD50 (lethal dose for 50% of test animals, mg/kg, oral/dermal) and LC50 (lethal concentration in air, ppm or mg/m³, over a stated time); lower LD50/LC50 = more toxic. Most OELs are derived from animal toxicology studies.
Acute (short-term, high exposure, immediate effects) vs chronic (long-term, low exposure, delayed effects); local vs systemic effects.
Interactions: additive (1 + 1 = 2), synergistic (1 + 1 = 5, e.g., asbestos + smoking), potentiation (0 + 1 = 3, non-toxic agent increases another's effect), antagonism (1 + 1 < 2).

Target effects: carcinogens (IARC Group 1 = carcinogenic to humans, 2A probably, 2B possibly, 3 not classifiable), mutagens (change DNA), teratogens (birth defects), reproductive toxicants, sensitizers (allergic reaction after repeated exposure - isocyanates, epoxies), neurotoxins, hepatotoxins (liver), nephrotoxins (kidney), ototoxins (hearing - solvents like styrene, toluene; lead, CO), asphyxiants (simple - displace O₂, e.g., N₂, CO₂; chemical - interfere with O₂ use, e.g., CO, H₂S, cyanide), irritants.
Particulate lung diseases: silicosis (silica), asbestosis, siderosis (iron oxide), byssinosis (cotton dust), black lung/anthracosis (coal), berylliosis; fibrosis = scarring of lung tissue.
Symptoms of exposure: solvents - dizziness, headache, narcosis, defatting dermatitis; CO - headache, cherry-red skin; H₂S - rotten egg odor then olfactory fatigue; metal fume fever (zinc) - flu-like.
Exposure control plan: identify agents and SEGs, sampling strategy and equipment, compare with OELs, controls by hierarchy, medical surveillance, training, reassessment.
topics.example: A furniture plant introduces a new isocyanate-based coating. The safety professional reviews the SDS (respiratory sensitizer, carcinogen category 2), sets up personal sampling with the correct coated filters, installs a ventilated spray booth, adds supplied-air respirators for spraying, starts medical surveillance for sensitization, and trains workers to report wheezing early.
tips: Lower LD50/LC50 = MORE toxic.
Synergism vs potentiation is a common definition trap.
Teratogen = birth defects; mutagen = DNA changes; carcinogen = cancer; ototoxin = hearing.
IARC Group 1 = known human carcinogen.
topics.yates: Ch. 7 Toxicology, p. 251; Ch. 6 Particulates and Gases, p. 228
subs: Routes of entry and dose
Toxic substances enter by inhalation, ingestion, skin/eye absorption or injection. The effect depends on the dose that reaches the target organ.
Inhalation is the most common and significant occupational route (gases, vapors, dusts, fumes, mists).

Ingestion from poor hygiene (lead dust on hands/food); absorption through intact skin for lipid-soluble chemicals (solvents, pesticides, phenol - 'Skin' notation); injection by needlesticks or high-pressure fluid.
Dose = concentration x time (Haber's rule); Paracelsus: 'the dose makes the poison'.
Inhaled dose = C x breathing volume x time (x retention). Light work about 10 m3 per 8-h shift: 2 mg/m3 x 10 m3 = 20 mg inhaled.
Resting minute ventilation about 5 L/min (guide: 4.3-5.7 L/min) and tidal volume about 500 mL; work raises both.
Acute vs chronic exposure and effects; local (at contact site) vs systemic (distributed to target organs).
'Most significant occupational route of entry' = inhalation.
Dose-response (NOAEL, LOAEL, threshold)
Dose-response describes how the magnitude of effect changes with dose. Thresholds and no-effect levels are used to set exposure limits.
Threshold: dose below which no effect occurs (assumed for most non-carcinogens; not for genotoxic carcinogens).
NOAEL = highest dose with no observed adverse effect; LOAEL = lowest dose with an observed adverse effect (always above NOAEL).
Limits are derived from NOAEL/LOAEL divided by uncertainty (safety) factors, e.g., 10 for animal-to-human, 10 for human variability.
Example (guide): benzene animal NOAEL 10 ppm and LOAEL 25 ppm, but OSHA PEL 1 ppm and NIOSH REL 0.1 ppm after safety factors and cancer data.
Potency: a steeper curve or lower ED50 means more potent; TD50/ED50 relate toxic to effective dose (therapeutic index).
NOAEL is the regulatory benchmark; LOAEL is used when no NOAEL could be determined.
LD50
LD50 is the dose that kills 50% of a test-animal population by a non-inhalation route (oral, dermal, injection), expressed in mg/kg of body weight. Lower LD50 means higher acute toxicity.
Units mg/kg body weight; always state species and route (e.g., oral rat).
Examples (guide): sodium cyanide oral LD50 about 5.7 mg/kg (Cat 1/2 border); caffeine about 190 mg/kg (Cat 3); table salt about 3,000 mg/kg (Cat 5 range).
Signal words: Cat 1-2 'Danger', Cat 3-4 'Warning'; skull-and-crossbones for Cat 1-3, exclamation mark for Cat 4. OSHA HazCom does not adopt Cat 5.
Scale-up: lethal dose for a 70-kg person at LD50 50 mg/kg = 3,500 mg (3.5 g) - animal data extrapolate only approximately.
Keywords oral, dermal, injection, mg/kg = LD50. A chemical with LD50 4 mg/kg is MORE toxic than one with 400 mg/kg.
LC50
LC50 is the airborne concentration that kills 50% of test animals over a stated exposure time (usually 4 h), used for gases, vapors, dusts, mists and fumes.
Units: ppm (gases/vapors) or mg/L (vapors, dusts/mists); exposure duration must be stated.
GHS inhalation (gases, ppmV, 4 h): Cat 1 <= 100, Cat 2 <= 500, Cat 3 <= 2,500, Cat 4 <= 20,000.
Lower LC50 = more toxic. Example (guide): solvent with LC50 500 ppm (4-h rat) and LD50 200 mg/kg oral.
LC50 is an acute measure; it says nothing about chronic, carcinogenic or reproductive effects.
Related: LCLo / LDLo = lowest reported lethal concentration/dose; TCLo = lowest toxic concentration.
Keyword 'inhalation' or 'airborne' = LC50, not LD50.
IDLH and acute exposure guidance
IDLH values (NIOSH) mark atmospheres that pose an immediate threat to life, irreversible health effects or impaired escape. They drive respirator selection and emergency planning.
IDLH basis: escape within 30 minutes without escape-impairing or irreversible effects (e.g., CO 1,200 ppm, benzene 500 ppm, H2S 50 ppm).
Oxygen-deficient atmospheres (< 19.5%) are treated as IDLH under 1910.134 unless the employer shows otherwise.
IDLH entry requires pressure-demand full-facepiece SCBA (APF 10,000) or supplied-air with auxiliary escape SCBA, plus standby persons outside.
Emergency planning also uses ERPGs (AIHA) and AEGLs (EPA) for community exposure tiers.
H2S causes olfactory fatigue at about 100 ppm - smell is not a warning.
Any unknown concentration or IDLH atmosphere = SCBA (pressure-demand), never an air-purifying respirator.
Exposure control
Exposure control applies the hierarchy of controls to chemical, physical and biological agents; respirators are the last line of defense and require a full program.
Order: elimination, substitution, engineering (enclosure, isolation, LEV, wet methods), administrative (rotation, scheduling, hygiene, training), PPE.

Respiratory protection program (1910.134): written program, program administrator, medical evaluation before fit testing, annual fit test, training, cartridge change schedule, voluntary-use provisions.
APFs: half-mask APR 10; full-facepiece APR 50; loose-fitting PAPR 25; full-face PAPR 1,000; supplied-air pressure-demand full face 1,000; SCBA pressure-demand 10,000.
Maximum use concentration MUC = APF x PEL. Example: half-mask APF 10, PEL 50 ppm -> MUC 500 ppm (but never above IDLH).
Required protection factor = measured concentration / PEL: 300 ppm with PEL 25 ppm needs APF >= 12 -> full-face APR (50).
Personal hygiene: no eating/drinking in work areas, change rooms, showers (lead, arsenic, cadmium).
Hazard factor = C/PEL; select the respirator whose APF is at least that number.
Sampling (biological monitoring and toxicological exposure assessment)
Toxicological sampling measures how much of an agent the body has absorbed from all routes. Biological monitoring complements air sampling, especially when skin absorption or ingestion matters.
Biological Exposure Indices (BEIs, ACGIH) = reference values in blood, urine or exhaled air corresponding to exposure at the TLV.

Examples: blood lead (OSHA medical removal at 60 ug/dL or average of last 3 >= 50 ug/dL in general industry; 50 ug/dL in construction), urinary cadmium and beta-2 microglobulin, urinary metabolites (hippuric acid for toluene, phenol/S-PMA for benzene), carboxyhemoglobin for CO, cholinesterase for organophosphates.
Sample timing matters: end of shift, end of work week, or prior to shift depending on the agent's half-life.
Medical surveillance (pre-placement, periodic, exit) is required by substance standards (lead, cadmium, benzene, silica, asbestos, beryllium).
Exposure and medical records retained duration of employment + 30 years (1910.1020); employees have access within 15 working days.
Air sampling misses skin absorption and ingestion - biological monitoring captures total dose.
Exposure symptoms (signature effects of common agents)
Many exam questions describe a worker's symptoms and occupation and ask for the likely agent. Learn the signature effects.
Benzene - bone marrow suppression, aplastic anemia, leukemia (IARC Group 1). Lead - anemia, wrist/foot drop, slowed reflexes, kidney damage, hypertension, reproductive harm.
Arsenic - skin lesions (hyperpigmentation, keratosis) + peripheral neuropathy; skin/lung/bladder cancer. Mercury - tremor, erethism, Minamata disease (methylmercury).
Cadmium - acute pulmonary edema; chronic kidney damage (proteinuria) and osteomalacia (Itai-itai). Cr(VI) - nasal septum perforation ('chrome holes'), skin ulcers, lung cancer.
Manganese - Parkinson-like manganism in welders (mask face, micrographia). Zinc/copper - metal fume fever (flu-like, resolves 24-48 h). Cobalt (carbide tool grinding) - occupational asthma.
Formaldehyde - eye/airway irritation, nasopharyngeal cancer (mortuaries, labs). Antimony - GI effects (diarrhea, vomiting). Aluminum - pulmonary fibrosis.
CO - headache, cherry-red skin, hypoxia; H2S - rotten eggs then olfactory paralysis; cyanide - cellular asphyxiant; n-hexane - peripheral neuropathy; methanol - blindness.
Read the occupation clue: 'welding stainless' = Cr(VI) or Mn; 'battery plant' = lead or cadmium; 'galvanized' = zinc.
Pneumoconioses and occupational lung disease
Pneumoconioses are lung diseases caused by inhaled mineral or organic dust. Some are fibrotic and disabling; others are benign.
Silicosis - crystalline silica (nodular fibrosis, autoimmune link, lung cancer). Asbestosis - asbestos (also mesothelioma and lung cancer; synergistic with smoking).
Berylliosis (chronic beryllium disease) - granulomas that mimic sarcoidosis; sensitization test (BeLPT); P100 filtration; aerospace, electronics, ceramics, nuclear.
Coal workers' pneumoconiosis ('black lung'); siderosis - iron oxide (welders), benign/non-fibrotic.
Byssinosis ('brown lung') - cotton, flax, hemp dust; chest tightness on the first day back after a break ('Monday fever').
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (farmer's lung - moldy hay); occupational asthma from isocyanates, cobalt, flour, latex.
'Cotton dust' = byssinosis; 'iron oxide, benign' = siderosis; 'granulomas, aerospace' = berylliosis.
Target organ toxicity (STOT)
Toxicants often act on a specific organ. GHS calls this specific target organ toxicity (single or repeated exposure).
Nephrotoxins (kidney): lead, cadmium (proximal tubule, proteinuria), mercury, halogens, ethylene glycol (oxalate crystals), high-dose NSAIDs.

Hepatotoxins (liver): carbon tetrachloride (fatty liver, centrilobular necrosis), chloroform, vinyl chloride (angiosarcoma), acetaminophen overdose (NAPQI), ethanol, aflatoxin (Group 1 liver carcinogen).
Neurotoxins: lead (cognition, neuropathy), methylmercury (Minamata disease), arsenic (nerve conduction), n-hexane, organophosphates (cholinesterase inhibition), manganese.
Hematotoxins: benzene (marrow), CO (carboxyhemoglobin), nitrites/aniline (methemoglobinemia); pulmonary toxins: silica, asbestos, NO2, phosgene (delayed edema).
Sensitizers (skin/respiratory): isocyanates, nickel, chromium, epoxy, latex - once sensitized, very low exposure triggers reaction.
Ethylene glycol = oxalate crystals; CCl4 = liver; cadmium = kidney - classic exam pairs.
Chemical interactions (additive, synergistic, potentiation, antagonism)
When two or more chemicals are present, their combined effect may differ from each acting alone.
Additive: 2 + 2 = 4 - e.g., toluene + xylene CNS depression (basis of the mixture formula).
Synergistic: 2 + 2 > 4 - smoking + asbestos multiplies lung-cancer risk (roughly 50-90x combined vs about 5x asbestos alone and 10x smoking alone).
Potentiation: 0 + 2 > 2 - isopropanol (non-hepatotoxic) increases CCl4 liver toxicity.
Antagonism: 4 + 4 < 8 or 3 + (-2) = 1 - chelating agents binding heavy metals, antidotes.
Ototoxic interaction: solvents (toluene, styrene) + noise cause more hearing loss than either alone.
'One chemical has no effect alone but increases the other's toxicity' = potentiation, not synergism.
Mutagens
Mutagens damage DNA and cause heritable genetic changes. Germ-cell mutations can pass to offspring; somatic mutations can lead to cancer.
GHS germ cell mutagenicity: Category 1A (known human evidence), 1B (presumed), 2 (suspected).
Examples: benzene (bone marrow, leukemia), ethylene oxide (sterilizers), vinyl chloride (liver angiosarcoma), ionizing radiation.
Tests: Ames test (bacterial reverse mutation) screens for mutagenicity; many mutagens are also carcinogens.
Control as non-threshold agents: minimize exposure (ALARA), closed systems, substitution.
Keywords 'DNA damage' and 'heritable' = mutagen; 'fetus during pregnancy only' = teratogen.
Carcinogens
Carcinogens cause or promote cancer. Several bodies classify them by strength of evidence; only OSHA's list is legally enforceable.

IARC: Group 1 carcinogenic (asbestos, benzene, silica, arsenic, formaldehyde, diesel exhaust since 2012), 2A probably (glyphosate, night-shift work), 2B possibly (RF-EMF, gasoline engine exhaust, chloroform), 3 not classifiable (caffeine). The guide lists Group 4 'probably not' (caprolactam) and diesel as 2A; IARC removed Group 4 in 2019 and diesel exhaust has been Group 1 since 2012.
ACGIH: A1 confirmed human, A2 suspected human, A3 confirmed animal (unknown human relevance), A4 not classifiable, A5 not suspected.
NTP Report on Carcinogens: 'known to be' vs 'reasonably anticipated to be' human carcinogens.
OSHA regulates specific carcinogens with substance standards (asbestos, benzene, formaldehyde, Cr(VI), vinyl chloride, coke oven emissions, 13 carcinogens standard 1910.1003).
GHS carcinogenicity Category 1A/1B (Danger, health hazard pictogram) and 2 (Warning).
Latency is long (10-40 years for asbestos-related cancers); most are treated as non-threshold.
Group 1 / A1 / 'known' = confirmed in humans; 2A = probable; 2B = possible. Enforceable = OSHA.
Teratogens
Teratogens harm the developing embryo or fetus during pregnancy, causing birth defects; unlike mutagens, their effects are not passed to later generations.
Examples: thalidomide (limb malformations), ethanol (fetal alcohol syndrome), methylmercury (fetal brain), lead, ionizing radiation, some anticancer drugs and anesthetic gases.
Most sensitive period: organogenesis, roughly weeks 3-8 of gestation - often before pregnancy is known.
Reproductive toxicants also include agents affecting fertility (lead, DBCP, ethylene glycol ethers).
Program approach: hazard communication, exposure minimization for all workers (not exclusion of women), NRC declared-pregnant-worker limit 0.5 rem over the pregnancy.
Fetal protection policies that bar women from jobs are illegal (UAW v. Johnson Controls, 1991) - control the exposure instead.
Ototoxins
Ototoxic chemicals damage the cochlea or auditory nerve and can cause hearing loss on their own or worsen noise-induced loss.
Solvents: toluene, styrene, xylene, ethylbenzene, n-hexane, trichloroethylene.
Asphyxiants: carbon monoxide, hydrogen cyanide; metals: lead, mercury, organotins.
Combined solvent + noise exposure produces greater-than-additive hearing loss.
OSHA/NIOSH (2018 SHIB) recommend audiometric testing for workers exposed to ototoxicants even below 85 dBA; ACGIH notes ototoxic agents in the noise TLV.
Controls: reduce both noise and chemical exposure; hearing protectors do not prevent ototoxic damage from inhaled/absorbed chemicals.
Painter exposed to toluene + noise with unexpected hearing loss = ototoxic synergy.
mcq: Chemical A has a 4-hour rat inhalation LC50 of 50 ppm; Chemical B has an LC50 of 5,000 ppm. Which is correct?
B is more acutely toxic because its number is larger
A is more acutely toxic by inhalation
LC50 measures carcinogenic potency
Neither can be compared without an LD50
LC50 is the air concentration lethal to 50% of test animals over a stated time. A LOWER LC50 means GREATER acute inhalation toxicity, so A (50 ppm) is more toxic.
A chemical has an oral LD50 of 4 mg/kg. What is its GHS acute toxicity category?
Category 1
Category 2
Category 3
Category 4
Under GHS, acute oral toxicity Category 1 is LD50 <= 5 mg/kg, so 4 mg/kg is Category 1 (the most severe). Lower category numbers mean higher toxicity.
Isopropyl alcohol, which is not itself hepatotoxic, greatly increases the liver toxicity of carbon tetrachloride. What is this interaction called?
Additive
Synergistic
Antagonistic
Potentiation

Potentiation: a substance with no toxicity of its own (for example isopropanol) increases another's toxicity (carbon tetrachloride liver damage): 0 + 2 > 2. Synergism requires both agents to be toxic.
Smoking combined with asbestos exposure increases lung cancer risk far beyond the sum of the individual risks. What interaction is this?
Additive
Antagonistic
Synergistic
Potentiation
Synergism: two toxic agents together produce an effect much greater than the sum of their individual effects. Smoking plus asbestos multiplies lung cancer risk.
A worker is exposed to acetone at 300 ppm (TLV 500 ppm) and MEK at 100 ppm (TLV 200 ppm). Both affect the same target organs (additive). Is the mixture limit exceeded?
No - each is below its own TLV
Yes - the sum of ratios is 1.1
No - the sum of ratios is 0.8
Yes - the sum of ratios is 2.0
For additive mixtures, Em = C1/T1 + C2/T2 = 300/500 + 100/200 = 0.6 + 0.5 = 1.1. Because this exceeds 1.0, the mixture limit is exceeded even though each chemical alone is below its TLV.
What does a Group 1 classification by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) indicate about a substance?
The substance is not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans.
The substance is probably not carcinogenic to humans.
The substance is possibly carcinogenic to humans.
The substance is carcinogenic to humans.
IARC Group 1 = carcinogenic to humans (sufficient human evidence). 2A = probably, 2B = possibly, 3 = not classifiable.
A welder cutting galvanized steel develops fever, chills, a metallic taste and muscle aches several hours after the shift. Symptoms resolve within two days. Which fume is the MOST likely cause?
Iron oxide
Manganese
Tin oxide
Zinc oxide
Inhaling freshly formed zinc oxide fume (for example when welding galvanized steel) causes metal fume fever: flu-like fever and chills that resolve within 24-48 h.

Area noise levels average 82 dBA (below the 85 dBA action level), yet several workers in a fiberglass boat lay-up area that uses styrene resin show standard threshold shifts. What is the MOST likely contributing factor?
Normal age-related hearing loss only
An uncalibrated audiometer
Ototoxic styrene exposure acting together with noise
Overuse of hearing protection
Ototoxins such as styrene, toluene, lead and carbon monoxide can damage hearing on their own and add to the effect of noise, causing hearing loss below noise limits.
Section 11 of an SDS states that a solvent caused malformations in the offspring of pregnant test animals but showed no germ-cell mutations. How is this solvent BEST classified?
Teratogen
Mutagen
Sensitizer
Carcinogen
A teratogen causes birth defects in a developing embryo or fetus. A mutagen alters genetic material (DNA), and a carcinogen causes cancer. Exposure control plans should address pregnant workers.
An industrial hygienist must measure a painter's 8-hour exposure to toluene vapor. Which sampling method is MOST appropriate?
Activated charcoal sorbent tube on a low-flow personal pump in the breathing zone
Mixed cellulose ester (MCE) filter cassette
PVC filter with a cyclone pre-selector
Area grab sample taken at the room exhaust fan
Organic vapors such as toluene are collected on sorbent media (charcoal tube or passive badge) in the breathing zone. Filters collect particulates, and a cyclone is for respirable dust.

topics.title: Ergonomics and Human Factors
topics.bp: Evaluate principles related to ergonomics and human factors (e.g., visual acuity, body mechanics, lifting, vibration, anthropometrics, fatigue management)
topics.definition: Ergonomics (human factors engineering) is the science of fitting the job, equipment and environment to the worker's capabilities and limitations to prevent musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs), reduce error and improve performance.
topics.easy: Design the work to fit the person, not the person to fit the work. Reduce force, awkward postures, repetition, vibration and fatigue, and design controls and displays that people can see and use without mistakes.
points: MSD risk factors: force, repetition, awkward/static postures, contact stress, vibration, cold. Common MSDs: carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve at wrist), lateral epicondylitis ('tennis elbow'), De Quervain's tenosynovitis (thumb-side wrist), rotator cuff injuries, low back pain, trigger finger.

Ergonomics program elements: management commitment, employee involvement, job analysis (RULA, REBA, NIOSH lifting equation, Strain Index, Snook tables), controls (engineering first), training, medical management, evaluation.

Lifting: Revised NIOSH equation RWL = 51 × HM × VM × DM × AM × FM × CM (HM = 10/H in inches); LI = load ÷ RWL. Best lifting zone between knuckle and shoulder height, close to the body. Back belts are not proven effective (NIOSH).

Neutral posture: wrists straight, elbows close to body at about 90°, shoulders relaxed, knees about hip height, feet flat, lumbar support; monitor top at or slightly below eye level about an arm's length away.
Vibration: hand-arm (HAVS, Raynaud's phenomenon - white finger) and whole-body (low back, vehicles); A(8) = a × √(T ÷ 8); controls - low-vibration tools, reduced exposure time, warm hands.
Anthropometrics: body dimensions by percentile; design reach for the 5th percentile (small) user, clearance for the 95th percentile (large) user, adjustability for the 5th-95th range.

Visual acuity and displays: Snellen 20/40 = sees at 20 ft what normal sees at 40 ft; lighting levels, glare control, contrast; display/control compatibility (population stereotypes - clockwise to increase).
Human factors: human error types (slips, lapses, mistakes, violations), error-proofing (poka-yoke), workload, situational awareness.
Fatigue management: shift length and rotation (forward rotation), circadian rhythm, sleep debt, fatigue risk management systems, rest breaks, limits on consecutive night shifts.
topics.example: Warehouse workers lift 40-lb cases from floor-level pallets to a 36-in. conveyor 300 times a shift and report back pain. A NIOSH analysis gives LI ≈ 2.0. The company installs pallet lift tables that keep the top layer at waist height and a vacuum lift assist for heavy items; the LI falls below 1.0 and back complaints drop.
tips: Engineering redesign beats training, stretching and back belts in ergonomics questions.
LI = load ÷ RWL; LI > 1 means increased risk.
Reach → 5th percentile; clearance → 95th percentile.
Know where MSDs occur: epicondylitis = elbow; De Quervain's = thumb side of wrist; Raynaud's = fingers (vibration/cold).
topics.yates: Ch. 24 Ergonomics, p. 546; Ch. 13 Thermal Stressors (fatigue/heat)
subs: Visual acuity
Visual acuity is the sharpness of vision needed for accurate, safe work. Lighting, glare, contrast, display design and the aging workforce all affect it.
Snellen 20/20 = normal acuity; aging (presbyopia) reduces near focus and increases light needs - a 60-year-old needs about 2-3 times the light of a 20-year-old.

IES recommended illuminance (guide): offices/VDT 300-500 lux (30-50 fc); drafting 750-1,000 lux; labs 500-1,000; precision assembly/inspection 1,000-2,000 lux (100-200 fc); active warehouses 200-300 lux.
1 footcandle = 10.76 lux. Illuminance from a point source follows the inverse square law: E = I/d^2.
Glare: direct (light source in field of view) and reflected (screen, glossy surfaces); control with diffusers, indirect lighting, screen positioning perpendicular to windows.
Controls: task lighting, adjustable contrast, anti-glare screens, regular vision testing, prescription safety eyewear.
OSHA 1926.56 sets minimum illumination for construction (e.g., 5 fc general construction areas).
Increasing overall room light can worsen screen glare - task lighting and positioning are often the better answer.
Body mechanics
Good body mechanics keep the body in a neutral posture - straight spine, elbows close to the body, wrists straight - and minimize twisting, bending, overhead work and long reaches.
Neutral posture minimizes muscle effort and joint stress; awkward postures multiply the force on the spine and tendons.

Spinal disc compression rises sharply with load distance from the body (moment arm); L5/S1 is the most stressed disc. NIOSH action limit for disc compression is 3,400 N (770 lb); 6,400 N is the maximum permissible limit.
Use power zone: between mid-thigh and shoulder height, close to the body.
Pushing is preferred over pulling; avoid twisting - turn with the feet.
Controls: adjustable work heights, tool redesign, training on posture, job design to reduce static and repetitive positions.
A load held 20 in. from the spine stresses the back far more than the same load held at 10 in. - reduce horizontal distance.
Lifting (NIOSH lifting equation)
The revised NIOSH Lifting Equation computes a Recommended Weight Limit (RWL) for two-handed manual lifts; the Lifting Index compares the actual load to the RWL.
RWL = LC x HM x VM x DM x AM x FM x CM, with load constant LC = 51 lb (23 kg).
HM = 10/H (in.) [25/H cm], H 10-25 in.; VM = 1 - 0.0075|V - 30| (in.); DM = 0.82 + 1.8/D (in.); AM = 1 - 0.0032A (degrees); FM from frequency/duration table; CM from coupling (good/fair/poor) table.
Lifting Index LI = load / RWL. LI <= 1 nominal risk; LI > 1 increased risk; LI > 3 high risk for most workers.
Example: H = 20 in. (HM 0.5), V = 30 in. (VM 1.0), D = 10 in. (DM 1.0), A = 0, FM = CM = 1 -> RWL = 25.5 lb. A 30-lb box -> LI = 1.18 (increased risk).
Biggest lever: horizontal distance - halving H from 20 to 10 in. doubles the RWL.
Equation does not apply to one-handed, seated, kneeling, team lifts, high-speed lifting or unstable loads; consider Snook/Liberty Mutual tables or ACGIH lifting TLV.
If V is above 30 in. or below, VM drops; any multiplier is <= 1, so the RWL can never exceed 51 lb.
Vibration
Vibration transmitted to the hands (hand-arm) or whole body damages vessels, nerves and the spine. OSHA has no vibration PEL; ACGIH TLVs and ISO standards apply.

Hand-arm vibration (HAV) about 8-1,000 Hz (guide: 50-1,000 Hz) from grinders, chainsaws, jackhammers -> HAVS / vibration white finger (Raynaud's phenomenon): blanching in cold, numbness, loss of dexterity.
Whole-body vibration (WBV) about 0.5-80 Hz from trucks, forklifts, mining and construction vehicles -> low back pain, spinal degeneration, fatigue.
ACGIH (guide values): HAV TLV 5 m/s2 A(8), action level 2.5 m/s2; WBV about 0.5-1.0 m/s2 A(8). ISO 5349 = HAV; ISO 2631 = WBV.
Measured with accelerometers (frequency-weighted acceleration, m/s2).

Controls: low-vibration tools, tool maintenance/balancing, isolation mounts and suspension seats, limiting exposure time, keeping hands warm and dry, lighter grip; anti-vibration gloves have limited value.
'White fingers in winter + power tools' = HAVS; 'truck driver back pain' = WBV.
Anthropometrics
Anthropometrics is the measurement of human body dimensions used to design workplaces, tools and equipment that fit the user population.
Common design range: 5th percentile female to 95th percentile male (about 90-95% of users).
Reach distances and control forces: design for the smallest/weakest (5th percentile female).
Clearances (doorways, aisles, headroom) and tool handles/openings: design for the largest (95th percentile male).
Work surfaces and seats: make adjustable across the 5th-95th range; standing work height about elbow height (lower for heavy work, higher for precision).
Designing for the 'average' person fits almost nobody; use adjustability and universal design.
Reach = smallest user; clearance = largest user; height = adjustable.
Fatigue
Fatigue is reduced physical and mental capability caused by long hours, shift work, inadequate sleep, heavy or monotonous work. It increases errors, slower reactions and incidents.
Hazards: night and rotating shifts, extended overtime, long commutes, sleep disorders, circadian low point roughly 2-6 a.m.
About 17-19 hours awake impairs performance comparably to a BAC of about 0.05%; 24 hours about 0.10%.
IARC classifies night shift work as Group 2A (probably carcinogenic).

Controls: fatigue risk management system, forward-rotating shifts (day -> evening -> night), limit consecutive nights and 12-h shifts, guaranteed rest days, micro-breaks, task rotation, fatigue monitoring.
Transport: DOT/FMCSA hours-of-service and NRC 10 CFR 26 fatigue rules for regulated industries.
'Night shift' in a question should make you think of both performance decline and IARC 2A.
Musculoskeletal disorders and risk factors
Work-related MSDs (cumulative trauma disorders) are injuries to muscles, tendons, nerves and joints that develop over time from repeated stress.
Primary risk factors: force, repetition, awkward/static posture; secondary: contact stress, vibration, cold, inadequate recovery time; personal factors: diabetes, obesity, pregnancy, arthritis.
Carpal tunnel syndrome = median nerve compression at the wrist: numbness/tingling in thumb, index, middle and half of ring finger, worse at night, thenar atrophy when chronic.
Others: tendinitis, tenosynovitis, De Quervain's (thumb), trigger finger, epicondylitis (tennis elbow), rotator cuff injury, low back pain.
Assessment tools: RULA, REBA, Strain Index, ACGIH HAL TLV, Snook tables, checklists, symptom surveys and OSHA 300 log trends.
Controls: engineering (tool redesign, lift assists, workstation adjustment, automation), administrative (job rotation, rest breaks, pacing), training on neutral posture, early medical management.
Early reporting and medical management is a core ergonomics-program element - it catches MSDs before they become lost-time cases.
Ergonomics program and workstation design
An effective ergonomics program follows a systematic process and is enforced in the US through the General Duty Clause and industry guidelines.
Elements: management commitment, employee involvement, job hazard analysis, hazard prevention/control, training, medical management, program evaluation.
Computer workstation: monitor about an arm's length away with the top at or slightly below eye level; elbows about 90 degrees; wrists neutral; feet flat or on a footrest; ANSI/HFES 100.
Human factors design principles: follow population stereotypes (clockwise/up = increase, red = stop), make controls distinguishable, design out error (poka-yoke), keep displays simple.
Human error types: slips and lapses (skill-based), mistakes (rule- or knowledge-based), violations (intentional) - each needs a different control.
OSHA has industry guidelines (poultry, nursing homes, retail grocery, shipyards) but no general ergonomics standard (the 2000 rule was repealed in 2001).
Retraining fixes knowledge-based mistakes, not slips - slips need design changes.
Fitness for duty and return to work
Fitness for duty confirms a worker can safely perform the job; return-to-work programs bring injured or ill workers back gradually and safely.
Fitness for duty covers medical fitness (vision, hearing, strength), substance use testing (DOT, NRC 10 CFR 26) and psychological fitness (fatigue, stress).
Evaluations must be job-related and consistent with business necessity (ADA); use essential functions from job descriptions.
Return to work: medical clearance, transitional/light duty, written work restrictions, coordination among employer, provider, insurer and employee, follow-up monitoring.
Early RTW reduces lost workdays, claim costs and disability duration; modified duty converts lost-time cases to restricted cases on the OSHA 300 log.
'Worker capable of performing safely' = fitness for duty; 'gradual, monitored reintegration' = return to work.
mcq: A forklift driver's vision test shows 20/40 in each eye. What does this mean?
The driver sees at 40 ft what normal vision sees at 20 ft
The driver sees at 20 ft what a person with normal vision sees at 40 ft
The driver has double normal acuity
The driver is legally blind
Snellen 20/40 means the person must be at 20 ft to see what a person with normal vision sees at 40 ft, which is worse than normal. 20/200 is the usual legal-blindness threshold.
When designing a control panel, which anthropometric rule is MOST appropriate for REACH distances?
Design for the 5th percentile (small) user so nearly everyone can reach
Design for the 95th percentile male
Design for the 50th percentile (average) user
Anthropometrics do not apply to reach
Reach is designed for small users (5th percentile female) so about 95% of people can reach. Clearances are designed for large users (95th percentile male).
In anthropometric design, clearances such as door height are based on which percentile?
5th percentile female
50th percentile male
95th percentile male
100th percentile male
Clearances such as door height and legroom use the largest expected user (95th percentile male) so nearly everyone fits. A 100th percentile does not exist in design practice.
For a lifting task the load weight is 70 lb and the NIOSH Recommended Weight Limit (RWL) is 20 lb. What is the Lifting Index (LI = LW/RWL)?
LI = LW/RWL = 70/20 = 3.5. An LI above 1.0 means increased risk, and above 3.0 most workers are at high risk, so redesign is needed.

A NIOSH lifting analysis gives these multipliers: HM 0.625, VM 0.93, DM 0.91, AM 1.0, FM 0.88, CM 0.95. The load is 30 lb. What are the RWL and Lifting Index? (RWL = 51 lb x HM x VM x DM x AM x FM x CM)
RWL 22.6 lb; LI 0.75
RWL 22.6 lb; LI 1.33
RWL 51 lb; LI 0.59
RWL 30 lb; LI 1.00
RWL = 51 x 0.625 x 0.93 x 0.91 x 1.0 x 0.88 x 0.95 = 22.6 lb; LI = 30/22.6 = 1.33 (above 1.0, so the task needs redesign). Trap: dividing RWL by load gives 0.75.
At a fitness equipment plant, four back injuries this year involved lifting a 110-lb box from a 36-in-high conveyor to a 4-in-high pallet 36 in away. What is the BEST solution?
Rotate the task so each worker lifts the product only two hours a day
Lower the conveyor to 28 inches and ensure two workers lift the boxes
Provide the worker with safe lifting training and implement a stretching program
Provide a vacuum lift-assist device to lift the box to the pallet
Four injuries and a 110-lb box need an engineering control. A vacuum lift assist removes the manual lift. Rotation and training are administrative controls that leave the hazard in place.

On an assembly line, workers repeatedly reach more than 20 in in front of their bodies to grab parts from a supply bin, and several report shoulder fatigue late in the shift. Which improvement would MOST effectively reduce the shoulder strain?
Increase job rotation so workers switch positions every two hours
Provide anti-fatigue mats to reduce discomfort while standing
Move the parts bin closer to the worker to reduce extended forward reaches
Require workers to stretch before starting their shift
Reducing the reach distance (moving the bin into the primary reach zone) removes the risk factor at its source. Rotation, mats and stretching do not change the reach.
Hand-Arm Vibration Syndrome (HAVS) is also known as:
Raynaud's Phenomenon / Vibration White Finger
Siderosis
Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
Berylliosis
Hand-arm vibration syndrome (vibration white finger, a secondary Raynaud's phenomenon) comes from prolonged use of vibrating hand tools. It causes finger blanching, numbness and loss of dexterity.
Which fatigue-management measure is MOST effective in reducing the risk of human error in shift work?
Long shifts with fewer breaks
Rotating shifts forward with regular rest days
Fixed night shifts every week
Increasing overtime hours
Forward-rotating shifts (day to evening to night) with regular rest days fit the circadian rhythm and limit cumulative fatigue. Long shifts, fixed nights and overtime increase fatigue and error.
Workers in an assembly line are reporting back pain and discomfort. What initial step should you take to address potential ergonomic issues?
Conduct an ergonomic assessment to identify risk factors contributing to discomfort.
Provide training on proper lifting techniques and posture.
Redesign the workstation layout to minimize awkward postures and repetitive motions.
Implement job rotation to reduce the physical strain on workers.
The FIRST step is an ergonomic assessment (job hazard / risk-factor analysis) to identify causes. Controls such as redesign or rotation should follow from what it finds.

topics.title: Chemistry: Containment Volume and Storage Requirements
topics.bp: Apply chemistry principles to calculate required containment volumes and hazardous materials storage requirements
topics.definition: Applied chemistry for the CSP covers the properties of chemicals (states of matter, molecular weight, vapor pressure, flash point, pH, reactivity), gas laws, concentration conversions and the calculations needed to size secondary containment and comply with storage limits.
topics.easy: Know how chemicals behave - how fast they evaporate, whether vapors sink, whether they burn or react - and be able to calculate how big a dike must be and how much you are allowed to store.
points: Containment volume: required volume = % × largest container (e.g., 110%); convert gallons to ft³ (÷ 7.48) or liters to m³ (÷ 1,000); wall height = volume ÷ floor area; subtract volume displaced by other tanks inside the dike.
Geometry: cylinder V = πr²h; rectangle V = L × W × H; 1 ft³ = 7.48 gal; 1 gal = 3.785 L; 1 m³ = 264.2 gal.

Gas laws (use absolute temperature and pressure): Boyle P₁V₁ = P₂V₂; Charles V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂; Gay-Lussac P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂; combined P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂; ideal gas PV = nRT (R = 0.0821 L·atm/mol·K or 8.314 J/mol·K). K = °C + 273; °R = °F + 460; psia = psig + 14.7. 1 mole of gas = 24.45 L at 25 °C, 22.4 L at 0 °C.
Concentration: ppm = mg/m³ × 24.45 ÷ MW; % to ppm: 1% = 10,000 ppm; % LEL readings convert using the LEL (e.g., 10% of methane LEL 5% = 0.5% = 5,000 ppm).
pH = −log[H⁺]; 7 neutral; < 7 acid; > 7 base/caustic; each unit is a 10× change. Neutralization of strong acids and bases is highly exothermic.

Properties: vapor density (> 1 heavier than air, collects low), specific gravity (< 1 floats on water), vapor pressure (higher = evaporates faster), flash point, boiling point, LEL/UEL, autoignition temperature.

Storage requirements: flammable cabinets (60 gal Cat 1-3, 120 gal Cat 4, max 3 per fire area), container size limits by category, storage rooms (ventilation 6 ACH), separation of compressed gas oxygen and fuel gas cylinders by 20 ft or a 5-ft-high ½-hour fire-rated barrier, maximum allowable quantities per control area (IFC/NFPA 400), incompatibility segregation.
Balanced equations and chemical change (e.g., Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂; rusting is a chemical change).
topics.example: A dike must hold 110% of the largest of three tanks (10,000, 8,000 and 5,000 gal). Required volume = 11,000 gal ÷ 7.48 = 1,470.6 ft³. The dike floor is 40 × 30 ft (1,200 ft²), so the minimum wall height is 1.23 ft before allowing for the other tanks' displacement; the engineer specifies 1.6 ft to include displacement and freeboard.
tips: Containment questions use the LARGEST tank, not the total, unless the rule says otherwise.
Gas-law problems require absolute temperature and pressure - a frequent trap.
Higher vapor density means vapors flow to low points (pits, trenches).
topics.yates: Ch. 5 Math Review, p. 211; Ch. 6 Particulates and Gases, p. 228; Ch. 12 Fire Prevention (storage); Ch. 27 Hazardous Materials Management
subs: Containment-volume calculations
Secondary containment must hold the release from the largest container plus allowances. Calculate the required volume, then size the dike or berm.

Rule set: SPCC (40 CFR 112) - capacity of the largest container plus freeboard for precipitation (110% is the common design value); RCRA container areas (40 CFR 264.175) - 10% of total volume or 100% of the largest container, whichever is greater (the guide states 110% of the largest). NFPA 30 dikes - at least the capacity of the largest tank.
Conversions: 1 ft3 = 7.48 gal; 1 gal water = 8.34 lb; 1 m3 = 1,000 L = 264.2 gal.
Rectangular dike volume = L x W x H. Cylinder volume = pi x r^2 x h.
Example: largest tank 10,000 gal -> 110% = 11,000 gal / 7.48 = 1,470.6 ft3. Dike 30 ft x 25 ft (750 ft2) -> wall height = 1,470.6/750 = 1.96 ft (about 2 ft, plus freeboard).
Example: ten 55-gal drums (550 gal total) -> 10% = 55 gal vs largest 55 gal -> 55 gal required under RCRA (110% rule gives 60.5 gal).
