Subtract volume displaced by other tanks/foundations inside the dike below the wall height.
Always use the LARGEST container (not the sum) for the 100/110% rule, then compare with 10% of the total.
Hazardous-material storage requirements
Storage requirements limit quantities, separate incompatibles, control ignition sources and provide containment, ventilation and fire protection.

OSHA 1910.106 flammable liquid categories: Cat 1 FP < 73.4 F and BP <= 95 F; Cat 2 FP < 73.4 F and BP > 95 F; Cat 3 FP 73.4-140 F; Cat 4 FP 140-199.4 F. NFPA classes: IA, IB, IC (FP < 100 F), II (100-140 F), IIIA (140-200 F), IIIB (>= 200 F).

Flammable storage cabinets: max 60 gal Cat 1-3 or 120 gal Cat 4 per cabinet; no more than 3 cabinets in one fire area (more allowed in sprinklered areas per NFPA 30). Safety cans <= 5 gal with flame arrester and spring-closing lid.
Outside a room or cabinet in one area: max 25 gal Cat 1 in containers, 120 gal Cat 2-4 in containers, 660 gal Cat 2-4 in one portable tank (1910.106(e)).
Segregate incompatibles: oxidizers from flammables, acids from bases and cyanides/sulfides, water-reactives away from water/sprinklers; NFPA 400 hazardous materials code; SDS Sections 7 and 10.
Compressed gases: upright, secured, caps on; oxygen 20 ft from fuel gases or 5-ft half-hour barrier. Peroxide formers (ethers): date on receipt/opening, test or dispose per schedule.
Bond and ground when transferring Class I liquids; ventilation and Class I Div 2 electrical in storage rooms; NFPA 704 diamond (0-4, 4 = most severe; opposite of GHS where Cat 1 is most severe).
NFPA 704: 4 = worst. GHS category: 1 = worst. Know which scale the question uses.
Concentration units and ppm to mg/m3 conversion
Airborne concentrations of gases and vapors are expressed as ppm (by volume) or mg/m3 (by mass). Conversion uses the molar volume of an ideal gas.
mg/m3 = ppm x MW / 24.45; ppm = mg/m3 x 24.45 / MW (25 C, 1 atm; use 22.4 at 0 C).
Example: toluene (MW 92.14) at 100 ppm -> 100 x 92.14 / 24.45 = 376.9 mg/m3.
Example: 50 mg/m3 of acetone (MW 58.08) -> 50 x 24.45 / 58.08 = 21.0 ppm.
1% by volume = 10,000 ppm; 1 ppm = 0.0001%. Example: LEL 1.2% = 12,000 ppm.
Particulates and fibers cannot be expressed in ppm - use mg/m3 or fibers/cc.
Molar volume adjusts with temperature/pressure: V = 24.45 x (T/298) x (760/P).
24.45 is the magic number - if a question gives MW and asks to convert, this is the formula.
Flammability properties (flash point, LEL/UEL, vapor pressure, vapor density)
Fire and explosion hazard of a chemical is predicted from its physical properties on SDS Section 9.
Flash point: lowest temperature at which vapors ignite with an ignition source; fire point slightly higher; autoignition temperature ignites without a spark.
Flammable range LEL-UEL: gasoline about 1.4-7.6%, methane 5-15%, hydrogen 4-75%, acetylene 2.5-100% (wider range = more hazardous). Confined-space alarm at 10% LEL.
Mixture LEL (Le Chatelier): LEL_mix = 100 / (P1/LEL1 + P2/LEL2 + ...). Example: 50% methane (5%) + 50% propane (2.1%) -> 100/(10 + 23.8) = 2.96%.

Vapor pressure: higher = evaporates faster (more airborne exposure). Vapor density (air = 1): > 1 sinks to low areas (propane 1.55, H2S 1.19, gasoline vapors 3-4); < 1 rises (methane 0.55, hydrogen 0.07).
Specific gravity (water = 1): < 1 floats (most hydrocarbons - water spreads the fire); > 1 sinks. Weight = gallons x 8.34 x SG.
Water solubility determines whether water dilutes (alcohols) or spreads (hydrocarbons) a spill fire - use alcohol-resistant foam for polar solvents.
Vapor density > 1 means look for vapors at floor level, pits and trenches.
Gas laws and pressure
Gas laws predict how pressure, volume and temperature of a confined gas change. Always use absolute temperature and absolute pressure.
Combined gas law: P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2. Boyle (T constant): P1V1 = P2V2. Charles (P constant): V1/T1 = V2/T2. Ideal gas: PV = nRT.
Absolute temperature: K = C + 273; Rankine R = F + 460. Absolute pressure: psia = psig + 14.7.
Example: cylinder at 2,000 psig and 70 F heated to 150 F -> P2 = 2,014.7 x (610/530) = 2,318.8 psia = 2,304 psig.
Liquid-to-gas expansion ratios are large (e.g., liquid nitrogen about 1:694, LPG about 1:270) - oxygen-deficiency and BLEVE hazards.
Water pressure head: 0.433 psi per ft of water; 1 atm = 14.7 psi = 33.9 ft of water = 760 mm Hg.
Classic error: using F or psig directly in gas law ratios - convert to absolute units first.
Corrosives, reactivity and pH
Corrosives destroy tissue and materials; reactive chemicals can release energy or toxic products when mixed, heated, shocked or exposed to air or water.
pH scale 0-14: < 7 acidic, > 7 basic; each unit is a 10-fold change. GHS skin corrosion Cat 1 typically pH <= 2 or >= 11.5. RCRA corrosivity characteristic: pH <= 2 or >= 12.5.
Bases (caustics) penetrate deeper than acids (liquefaction necrosis); hydrofluoric acid needs calcium gluconate first aid.
Eyewash/shower (1910.151(c); ANSI Z358.1): reachable within 10 s (about 55 ft), flush 15 min, tepid water 60-100 F.
Dangerous combinations: bleach + acid -> chlorine; bleach + ammonia -> chloramines; acid + cyanide -> HCN; acid + sulfide -> H2S; oxidizer + organic -> fire.
Reactive classes: water-reactive (sodium, calcium carbide), pyrophoric (spontaneously ignite in air), peroxide formers, polymerizers, oxidizers (NFPA 400 classes 1-4).
Exothermic runaway reactions are controlled by cooling, inhibitors, relief systems and MOC (link to process safety).
Always add acid to water, never water to acid ('Do what you oughta, add acid to water').
mcq: A dike must contain 110% of the largest of three tanks (10,000, 8,000 and 5,000 gal). The dike floor is 40 ft x 30 ft. Ignoring the volume displaced by the other tanks, what minimum wall height is needed? (7.48 gal = 1 ft3)
Required volume = 1.1 x 10,000 = 11,000 gal / 7.48 = 1,470.6 ft3. Height = 1,470.6 / (40 x 30) = 1.23 ft. Trap: 2.56 ft wrongly sums all three tanks.

A RCRA hazardous waste container storage area holds twenty 55-gallon drums. Under 40 CFR 264.175, secondary containment must hold 10% of the total volume or 100% of the largest container, whichever is greater. What minimum containment capacity is required?
55 gal
110 gal
Total = 20 x 55 = 1,100 gal; 10% = 110 gal; largest container = 55 gal. The greater value is 110 gal. Trap: 55 gal applies only the largest-container rule.
A cylindrical tank storing a hazardous liquid is 10 ft in diameter and 20 ft high. What is its full capacity? (Use pi = 3.14)
1,570 cubic feet
3,140 cubic feet
6,280 cubic feet
7,850 cubic feet
V = pi r^2 h = 3.14 x 5^2 x 20 = 1,570 ft3 (about 11,750 gal at 7.48 gal/ft3). Trap: using the diameter (10) as the radius gives 6,280 ft3.
A compressed gas cylinder reads 2,000 psig at 70 F. It is left in the sun and reaches 140 F. Assuming constant volume, what is the new gauge pressure? (Use 14.7 psi for atmospheric and R = F + 460)
2,000 psig
2,400 psig
4,000 psig
2,266 psig
Gas law calculations need absolute units: P2 = 2,014.7 psia x (600 R / 530 R) = 2,280.8 psia = about 2,266 psig. Trap: using F directly (140/70) doubles the pressure to 4,000 psig.
An SDS lists the density of petroleum diesel as 6.943 lb/gal. What is the weight of diesel in a full 100,000-gallon tank?
Mass = volume x density = 100,000 gal x 6.943 lb/gal = 694,300 lb. This matters for foundation, floor loading and containment design.
A container holds 0.55 mol of gas at 105.7 kPa and 300 K. What volume does the gas occupy? (PV = nRT; R = 8.31 L kPa/mol K)
4 L
At constant pressure, a gas occupies 8.57 L at 273 K. What will its volume be at 355 K?
Charles's law at constant pressure: V2 = V1 x T2/T1 = 8.57 x 355/273 = 11.1 L. Temperatures must be absolute (K).

Under OSHA 1910.106, an approved flammable storage cabinet may hold no more than 60 gallons of Category 1, 2 or 3 flammable liquids. How many full 5-gallon safety cans of a Category 2 liquid may be stored in one cabinet?
60 gal / 5 gal per can = 12 cans. The 120-gal cabinet limit applies only to Category 4 (combustible) liquids, and no more than three cabinets are allowed per fire area.
Several flammable liquids in a paint shop have a flash point of 58 F (14 C). What does this mean for their handling and storage?
It can produce flammable vapors at normal room temperature and should be stored in a flammable cabinet
It is not hazardous below 100 F and can be stored with non-flammable liquids
Flash point only matters during combustion, not storage
Only liquids with a flash point below 32 F require special handling

A flash point of 58 F is below normal room temperature, so ignitable vapors form at ambient conditions (OSHA Category 2). Store the liquid in approved flammable cabinets or rooms away from ignition sources.
During an inspection, you find containers of nitric acid stored on the same shelf as containers of acetone. What should you do?
Approve the setup since both are common industrial chemicals
Suggest labeling the containers more clearly
Suggest diluting the nitric acid to make it less reactive
Move the acetone to a flammable cabinet and segregate it from the nitric acid

Nitric acid is a strong oxidizer and acetone is a flammable organic, so they are incompatible and can react violently. Segregate them: put acetone in a flammable cabinet and acids in a separate corrosive cabinet.

topics.title: Physics: Energy, Weight, Force and Stress
topics.bp: Apply core concepts in physics (e.g., forms of energy, weights, forces, stresses)
topics.definition: Applied physics (mechanics, hydrostatics and electricity) explains how energy causes injury and how structures, rigging and equipment resist loads. The CSP exam tests calculations of force, energy, velocity, pressure, stress and electrical quantities.
topics.easy: Injuries happen when energy reaches the body faster than it can absorb it. Physics lets you calculate how fast something falls, how hard it hits, how much force a sling or pressure vessel carries, and whether a part is strong enough.
points: Forms of energy: kinetic (KE = ½mv² - doubling speed quadruples energy), potential (PE = mgh), elastic (springs), thermal, chemical, electrical, radiant; energy is conserved (PE converts to KE in a fall).
Newton's laws: 1st - inertia (unsecured loads keep moving when a vehicle stops); 2nd - F = ma; 3rd - action-reaction. Weight W = mg (g = 9.81 m/s² or 32.2 ft/s²). 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².
Kinematics: v = √(2gh); d = ½gt²; v² = v₀² + 2ad; stopping distance = reaction distance (v × t) + braking distance (v² ÷ 2a). Momentum p = mv; impact force ≈ change in momentum ÷ time.
Friction: F = μN; static friction > kinetic friction (harder to start moving); slip resistance measured by coefficient of friction with a tribometer.

Stress and strength: stress σ = F ÷ A (psi or Pa); factor of safety = ultimate strength ÷ working stress (or breaking strength ÷ working load); tension, compression, shear, bending, torsion; fatigue failure under cyclic loading.
Pressure: P = F ÷ A, so F = P × A (force on a vessel door = pressure × area); hydrostatic P = ρgh (water: 0.433 psi per ft; 62.4 lb/ft³).
Mechanical advantage: levers, pulleys (effort = load ÷ number of supporting rope parts), inclined planes.
Electricity: Ohm's law V = IR; power P = VI = I²R; series and parallel resistance; current (not voltage) causes injury.
Work = force × distance; power = work ÷ time (1 hp = 550 ft·lb/s = 746 W).
topics.example: A 10-lb wrench falls 64 ft from a tower. Using v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 32.2 × 64) ≈ 64 ft/s, it hits the ground at about 44 mph with KE = ½ × (10/32.2) × 64² ≈ 636 ft·lb - far beyond what a hard hat is rated to absorb. The safety professional requires tool tethers and an exclusion zone below.
tips: Keep units consistent (pounds-mass vs slugs; convert lb to slugs by ÷ 32.2 when using F = ma in English units).
Doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy - why speed control matters.
Force on a door or plate = pressure × area (use radius, not diameter, in πr²).
Static friction > kinetic friction explains 'hard to start, easy to keep moving'.
topics.yates: Ch. 17 Mechanics, p. 454; Ch. 18 Hydrostatics and Hydraulics, p. 469; Ch. 16 Electrical Safety (Ohm's law); Ch. 5 Math Review
subs: Energy (kinetic and potential)

Energy is the capacity to do work; injuries occur when energy is released uncontrolled and transferred to the body. Kinetic energy depends on mass and the square of velocity; potential energy on weight and height.
KE = 1/2 m v^2 (joules with kg and m/s; ft-lb with slugs and ft/s, where mass in slugs = weight lb / 32.2).
PE = m g h = W x h. Example: 10-lb tool dropped 50 ft -> PE = 500 ft-lb; 1 J = 0.738 ft-lb.
Velocity after a free fall: v = sqrt(2gh). 16 ft -> sqrt(2 x 32.2 x 16) = 32.1 ft/s (time t = sqrt(2h/g) = 1.0 s).
Doubling speed quadruples KE: 3,000-lb car (93.2 slugs) at 44 ft/s (30 mph) -> KE = 0.5 x 93.2 x 44^2 = about 90,200 ft-lb; at 60 mph about 361,000 ft-lb.
Other forms: electrical, chemical, thermal, pressure, radiant - all must be controlled in LOTO (energy isolation and stored energy release).
Haddon's energy-release theory: prevent the build-up, reduce the amount, prevent release, separate in time/space, put barriers, modify surfaces, strengthen the target.
Speed matters more than mass for vehicle crash energy because velocity is squared.
Weight
Weight is the force of gravity on a mass: W = m x g. In US units the pound is a force, so weight in lb divided by g gives mass in slugs.
W = m g; g = 9.81 m/s2 = 32.2 ft/s2. Example: 100 kg -> 981 N; 1 kg weighs about 2.2 lb; 1 lb = 4.448 N.
Mass is constant; weight changes with gravity (and with acceleration - an accelerating hoist feels heavier).
Liquid weight: water 8.34 lb/gal, 62.4 lb/ft3; other liquids = 8.34 x SG. Example: 55 gal of liquid with SG 1.2 = 55 x 8.34 x 1.2 = 550 lb (plus drum).
Steel about 490 lb/ft3; concrete about 150 lb/ft3 - used to estimate rigging loads (weight = volume x density).
Center of gravity: the point where the weight acts; for lifting, the hook must be directly above the CG to avoid swing/tilt.
When rigging, estimate weight from dimensions and density if it is not marked - never guess.
Force
Force changes an object's motion: F = m x a. Force questions on the CSP exam include accelerations, impacts, fall arrest, friction and rigging tension.
Newton's 2nd law F = m a; units N (kg m/s2) or lb (slug ft/s2). Example: 2,000-kg forklift decelerating at 3 m/s2 -> 6,000 N.
Impulse-momentum: F x t = m x delta-v; increasing stopping time or distance reduces force (energy absorbers, airbags).
Fall arrest average force: F = W(h + d)/d. Example: 220-lb worker, 6-ft free fall, 3.5-ft deceleration -> 220 x 9.5 / 3.5 = 597 lb average (OSHA max arresting force 1,800 lb with harness).
Friction: F = mu x N. Walking surfaces: static COF about 0.5 commonly cited as slip-resistant (ANSI A1264.2).
Pressure-force: F = P x A. Example: 1,500 psi on a 4-in2 hydraulic piston -> 6,000 lb.
Stopping distance: d = v^2 / (2a). 60 mph (88 ft/s) braking at 0.7 g (22.5 ft/s2) -> 172 ft, plus reaction distance (1.5 s x 88 = 132 ft).
Shorter stopping distance = higher impact force: that is why a 2-ft free fall on a positioning device is limited.
Stress
Stress is internal force per unit area in a material: stress = F/A. Comparing working stress with material strength gives the safety factor used in rigging, scaffolds and structures.
Stress (psi or Pa) = force / cross-sectional area. Example: 2,000 lb on a 0.5-in2 rod -> 4,000 psi.
Types: tensile (pulling), compressive (pushing), shear (sliding), bending and torsion.
Strain = change in length / original length; Young's modulus E = stress/strain (elastic region). Beyond the yield point deformation is permanent; ultimate strength = failure.
Safety factor = ultimate (breaking) strength / working load. Wire rope 5:1 -> 10,000-lb breaking strength gives WLL 2,000 lb. Scaffolds: 4 times intended load; guardrail top rail 200 lb.
Fatigue failure: repeated cyclic stress below yield can crack metal over time - inspect cranes, hooks, pressure vessels.
Doubling the rod diameter quadruples the area and cuts the stress to 1/4.
Rigging and sling angles
Sling leg tension increases as the angle from horizontal decreases. Rigging calculations combine weight, number of legs and sling angle.
Leg tension T = (W / n) / sin(angle from horizontal). Load angle factor = 1/sin: 90 deg 1.000, 60 deg 1.155, 45 deg 1.414, 30 deg 2.000.
Example: 2,000-lb load, 2-leg bridle at 60 deg -> each leg 1,000 x 1.155 = 1,155 lb; at 30 deg each leg 2,000 lb.
Sling angles below 30 deg from horizontal are not recommended (ASME B30.9).
Choker hitch reduces rated capacity (about 75-80% of vertical); basket hitch with vertical legs = 2 x vertical capacity.
Assume only 2 legs carry the load on a 3- or 4-leg bridle unless an equalizer is used.
Flatter sling = more tension. At 30 degrees, each leg carries the full load weight.
Work, power, torque and stability
Work and power quantify energy transfer and its rate; torque (moment) explains levers, wrenches, crane and forklift stability.
Work = force x distance (ft-lb or J). Power = work / time; 1 hp = 550 ft-lb/s = 746 W. Example: lifting 500 lb 10 ft in 5 s = 1,000 ft-lb/s = 1.82 hp.
Torque/moment = force x perpendicular distance. Example: 50 lb on a 2-ft wrench = 100 ft-lb.

Equilibrium: sum of moments about the fulcrum = 0. Forklift: load moment (load x distance from front axle) must not exceed counterweight moment - capacity drops as the load center moves out (e.g., rated at 24-in. load center).
Crane stability: tipping load and rated capacity charts (often 75% of tipping for crawlers, 85% for outriggers); capacity falls with longer radius.
Electrical: Ohm's law V = I x R; power P = V x I = I^2 x R. Example: 120 V across 1,000 ohm body resistance -> 0.12 A (120 mA) - potentially fatal.
Moving a forklift load forward beyond its rated load center reduces safe capacity even if the weight is unchanged.
mcq: A steel rod with a cross-sectional area of 0.5 in2 carries a tensile load of 2,000 lb. The material's ultimate strength is 60,000 psi. What is the working stress and factor of safety?
Stress = F/A = 2,000/0.5 = 4,000 psi. Factor of safety = ultimate strength / working stress = 60,000/4,000 = 15.
A 10-kg toolbox falls from a scaffold platform 2 m high. Ignoring air resistance, what is its approximate velocity just before it hits the ground? (v = sqrt(2gh), g = 9.8 m/s2)
v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 x 9.8 x 2) = sqrt(39.2) = 6.3 m/s. Mass does not affect free-fall velocity (it does affect impact energy).
A 1,500-kg vehicle travels at 10 m/s. What is its kinetic energy? (KE = 1/2 m v^2)
KE = 1/2 mv^2 = 0.5 x 1,500 x 10^2 = 75,000 J. Because KE depends on v^2, speed control is critical in fleet and forklift safety.
A 24-inch-diameter access door on a vessel is under 50 psig. What total force acts on the door?
Area = pi r^2 = pi x 12^2 = 452.4 in2; F = P x A = 50 psi x 452.4 = 22,620 lb. Trap: using the diameter as the radius gives 90,480 lb. Always depressurize before opening.
A steel crane cable has a cross-sectional area of 150 mm2 and an allowable tensile stress of 400 MPa (1 MPa = 1 N/mm2). What is the maximum tensile force it can safely support? (F = stress x A)
F = stress x area = 400 N/mm2 x 150 mm2 = 60,000 N (60 kN).
A delivery truck is traveling through a jobsite at 15 mph when it strikes a pedestrian. If the same truck had been traveling at 30 mph, how would the impact energy compare?
It would double
It would increase by 1.5 times
It would stay the same
It would increase by four times
KE = 1/2 mv^2, so doubling speed from 15 to 30 mph raises impact energy by 2^2 = 4 times. Trap: assuming energy scales linearly (doubles).
A 10-kg rubber block slides on a concrete floor (mu = 0.65). What is the friction force? (F = mu N; g = 9.8 m/s2)
Friction F = mu x N = 0.65 x (10 kg x 9.8 m/s2) = 0.65 x 98 N = 63.7 N.
A car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s over 10 seconds. How far does it travel? (a = (v2 - v1)/t; v2^2 - v1^2 = 2a d)
a = (30 - 10)/10 = 2 m/s2; distance = (v2^2 - v1^2)/(2a) = (900 - 100)/4 = 200 m. Check: average velocity 20 m/s x 10 s = 200 m.
A worker says a heavy cart is hard to start moving but easier to keep moving. Which physics concept BEST explains this?
Kinetic energy
Static friction
Gravitational potential
Thermal expansion
Static friction (resistance to starting motion) is greater than kinetic friction (resistance to continued sliding), so a cart takes more force to start than to keep moving.
A 10-lb wrench slips from a platform 20 ft above a worker who is wearing a hard hat. Which physical principle BEST explains why the wrench still poses a serious injury risk?
Gravitational potential energy converting to kinetic energy
Frictional resistance
Conservation of momentum
Electromagnetic interference
The 10-lb wrench's potential energy (mgh) at 20 ft becomes kinetic energy as it falls and can exceed what a hard hat is designed to absorb. Prevent drops with tool tethers, toe boards and barricades.

topics.title: Training Needs Assessment
topics.bp: Describe the needs assessment process to determine worker training, competencies, and qualifications
topics.definition: A training needs assessment (TNA) is a systematic process to identify gaps between current and required knowledge, skills and abilities (KSAs) and to decide whether training is the right solution. It defines the competencies and qualifications required for each job.
topics.easy: Before you train, find out what people need to know and do, what they already know, and whether the problem is really a lack of skill. If they can already do the job but don't, more training will not fix it.
points: Levels: organizational analysis (goals, regulations, incident trends), task/job analysis (what the job requires - task inventory, JHA), person analysis (who needs training - assessments, observation, performance data).
Data sources: injury/incident data, audits, regulatory requirements, JHAs, observations, interviews, surveys, focus groups, performance appraisals, new equipment/processes (MOC), task matrix.

Mager and Pipe performance analysis: 'Could they do it if their life depended on it?' If yes → not a skill deficiency (fix consequences, obstacles, feedback, equipment, supervision). If no → training, practice or job aids.

Competency = demonstrated ability to perform to a standard (knowledge + skills + behavior). Qualification = formal credential, certificate or license. Competent person (OSHA) = can identify hazards and has authority to correct them; qualified person = has a degree/certificate or extensive knowledge to solve problems.

Regulatory training requirements: e.g., forklift (evaluation every 3 years), HAZWOPER (40 h/24 h/8 h refresher annually), confined space, LOTO, HazCom (initially and when new hazards), respirators (annually), bloodborne pathogens (annually), hearing conservation (annually), crane operator certification.
Prioritize training needs by risk (severity and consequence of failure), legal requirements and number of workers affected.
Output: training plan with objectives, audience, methods, resources, schedule, evaluation.
topics.example: Forklift near-misses rise at a warehouse. Operators score 95% on written tests and perform inspections correctly when observed, but three trucks have broken backup alarms and the night-shift supervisor rarely checks pre-use inspections. The needs assessment concludes training is not the main fix: alarms are repaired and supervisors are made accountable for inspection checks.
tips: The FIRST step in designing training is the needs assessment.
If workers know how but don't do it, the answer is not more training.
Prioritize training by safety impact and consequences of failure.
topics.yates: Ch. 19 Training, p. 483
subs: Worker training

Worker training gives employees the knowledge and skills to recognize hazards and perform tasks safely. It is driven by regulatory requirements, task hazards, incidents and changes in the workplace, and it is only the right solution when the gap is a knowledge or skill gap.
OSHA 1926.21(b)(2): employer must instruct each employee in recognizing and avoiding unsafe conditions.
Training triggers: new hire, new task or equipment, process change (MOC), incident/near miss, audit finding, regulatory refresher.
Common refresher frequencies: HAZWOPER 8 h annually; forklift evaluation at least every 3 years; PSM refresher at least every 3 years; bloodborne pathogens annually; respirator annually.
ANSI/ASSP Z490.1 = accepted practices for SH&E training (needs assessment, design, delivery, evaluation, records).
Training is NOT the fix when the problem is equipment design, lack of resources or motivation - use engineering, PtD or management actions instead.
If a performance problem exists even though workers can do the task correctly, more training is the wrong answer.
Competencies

A competency is a demonstrated combination of knowledge, skills and abilities (KSAs) needed to perform a task safely. Training needs are defined by comparing the competency a job requires with what the worker currently has.
Knowledge: regulations, SOPs, hazard recognition.
Skills: equipment operation, emergency response, PPE use.
Abilities: physical/mental readiness, decision-making under stress.
Example: a scaffold inspector must know 1926.451, demonstrate inspection skills and be able to stop unsafe work.
ISO 45001 clause 7.2 requires the organization to determine and ensure worker competence and retain documented evidence.
Competence must be demonstrated, not just attended - a sign-in sheet proves attendance, not competency.
Qualifications (competent vs. qualified person)

OSHA uses two distinct roles. A competent person can identify existing and predictable hazards and has authority to take prompt corrective action; a qualified person has a recognized degree, certificate or professional standing, or extensive knowledge, training and experience, and can solve problems in the subject area.
Competent person: 29 CFR 1926.32(f) - hazard recognition + authority to correct/stop work; no degree required.
Qualified person: 29 CFR 1926.32(m) - degree/certificate/professional standing or extensive knowledge, training and experience.
Competent examples: scaffold inspector, trench supervisor (soil classification, daily inspection), fall protection supervisor.
Qualified examples: PE designing an anchorage or trench protective system, electrician on electrical systems, industrial hygienist.
Rule of thumb: qualified = designs; competent = inspects and corrects on site.
Key discriminator: AUTHORITY to take corrective action belongs to the competent person definition.
Training needs assessment (ADDIE Analyze phase)

A needs assessment identifies who must be trained, on what, and to what level before any course is designed. It is the Analyze step of ADDIE and answers who the learners are, their current skill level and what gaps exist.
Sources: JHA/JSA, incident and near-miss data, audit findings, regulatory requirements, new equipment/processes, worker and supervisor input.
Output: target audience, performance gaps, learning objectives, priorities.
Prioritize high-risk tasks first (confined spaces, electrical, work at heights).
Keywords 'needs analysis' or 'gap identification' = Analyze phase.
FIRST step in developing training = needs assessment (not choosing a method or writing slides).
Defining baseline competency
Baseline competency is the minimum level of KSAs a worker must demonstrate to do a task safely. Comparing baseline (current) competency against required competency reveals the training gap.
Steps: identify job tasks and hazards -> determine required KSAs -> assess current workforce competency -> define competency standards -> use the gap to build the needs assessment.
Assessing current competency: pre-training tests, interviews, on-the-job observation, performance data (KPIs, incident reports).
Standards used as benchmarks: OSHA/ANSI requirements, ISO 45001, company SOPs.
Example: forklift operators - certification plus skill evaluation at least every 3 years (1910.178(l)).
'How do you decide whether workers need additional training?' = compare baseline (current) competency with required competency.
Tools for needs and competency assessment
Several practical tools link tasks to the skills needed and show where workers fall short.
Job Hazard Analysis: breaks a job into steps and links each to hazards and required skills.
Competency matrix: visual grid of required skills vs. employees, showing who is trained/qualified and when refreshers are due.
Pre-assessment tests: measure baseline knowledge.
Observation checklists: track safe behaviors vs. shortcuts.
Task analysis + interviews and surveys of workers and supervisors.
Human risk factors affecting performance
Training fails if human factors are ignored. Behavior, decision making, situational awareness, workload, risk perception and stress all determine whether workers apply what they learned.
Behavior: observable actions shaped by habits and culture - control with BBS and positive reinforcement.
Decision making: choices under pressure - scenario training, clear procedures, stop-work authority.
Situational awareness: perceive, understand, anticipate - hazard recognition training, checklists, pre-task briefings, fatigue management.
Workload: too much = fatigue/errors, too little = complacency - job rotation, breaks, staffing.
Risk perception: underestimating hazards leads to shortcuts - case studies, risk matrices.
Stress: reduces focus and memory - EAP, reasonable scheduling, stress management training.
Match the scenario: overwhelmed by demands = workload; anticipating hazards in dynamic settings = situational awareness; 'this low scaffold is not dangerous' = risk perception.
Who needs training: audience analysis
Different audiences need different content and depth: new hires, experienced workers, supervisors, managers, contractors and temporary workers.
Supervisors and managers need training on their responsibilities, leading by example and enforcing rules, not just hazard content.
Host and staffing agency share responsibility for temporary worker training; host provides site-specific training.
Consider language, literacy and culture - OSHA requires training in a manner and language workers understand.
Experienced workers still need training when tasks, equipment or rules change.
mcq: What is the primary purpose of conducting a Training Needs Assessment (TNA)?
To evaluate the effectiveness of past training programs
To identify specific training needs based on current competencies and desired performance levels
To assess the financial resources available for training
To finalize the training schedule for the year
A TNA identifies the gap between current and required performance so training targets real needs. Evaluating past training is effectiveness evaluation, not needs assessment.
What is the primary purpose of a gap analysis in a training needs assessment?
To count the number of employees requiring training
To determine the profitability of training programs
To identify discrepancies between current and desired performance levels
To evaluate the effectiveness of past training programs
Gap analysis compares actual performance (or KSAs) with the required standard; the difference defines what training must close.
A needs assessment reveals more training needs than can be addressed in the available time. What is the BEST approach?
Focus on the tasks that are performed most frequently
Train employees on tasks they already excel at to gain quick wins
Delay training until all needs can be addressed at once
Prioritize tasks with the highest risk or consequence of failure
Training priorities follow risk: tasks whose failure could cause serious injury or loss come first. Frequency alone is a trap; a rare but critical task may matter more.
Baseline competency is BEST defined as:
The minimum knowledge, skills, and abilities required to perform a job safely
The maximum level of performance expected from a worker
A supervisor's subjective rating of worker effort
The average score on a post-training quiz
Baseline competency is the minimum KSA level required for safe performance; it is the standard against which current ability is compared.
Which tool maps each employee's current skills against the competencies required for their role?
Hazard control matrix
Risk matrix
Competency (skills) matrix
Inspection checklist
A competency or skills matrix lists required competencies by role and shows who meets them, making training gaps visible. A risk matrix ranks hazards, not people's skills.
Which statement BEST distinguishes a competency from a qualification?
They are identical terms
Competency is only knowledge; a qualification is only skill
Qualifications are never required by OSHA
A qualification is a formal credential (certificate, license); competency is the demonstrated ability to perform the task to the required standard
A credential shows something was earned; competency is proven ability to perform. A worker can hold a certificate yet still lack demonstrated competence on the job.
Which OSHA regulation contains the general definitions of 'competent person' and 'qualified person' for construction?
29 CFR 1926.32 (definitions) defines competent person (f) and qualified person (m). 1926.21 covers safety training and education; 1910.120 is HAZWOPER; 1910.146 is permit-required confined spaces.
A construction supervisor identifies a cave-in hazard in a trench and immediately stops work until shoring is corrected. Under OSHA, the supervisor is acting as a:
Competent person
Qualified person
Professional engineer
Trainer
An OSHA competent person can identify existing and predictable hazards and has authorization to take prompt corrective measures. The key words are 'identify' plus 'authority to correct'.
Under 29 CFR 1926.32(m), a qualified person is one who:
Has jobsite experience but is not required to solve technical problems
Has authority to stop work and take prompt corrective action
By a recognized degree, certificate, or professional standing, or by extensive knowledge, training, and experience, has demonstrated the ability to solve problems relating to the subject matter
Has completed basic PPE training under supervision
The qualified person is defined by demonstrated problem-solving ability (e.g., designing scaffolds or anchorages). Authority to stop work is the competent-person trap.
An incident trend shows operators skipping a startup checklist step. The plant manager asks the CSP to schedule retraining for all operators. What should the CSP do FIRST?
Analyze whether the problem is caused by a lack of knowledge or skill, or by other factors such as time pressure, equipment design, or supervision
Schedule retraining for all operators immediately
Discipline the operators involved in the incidents
Purchase an online refresher course on startup procedures

A needs assessment first determines whether a performance gap is actually a training problem. If operators know the step but skip it, the fix is a management or design issue, and retraining will not work.

topics.title: Training Program Development
topics.bp: Develop training programs with training materials to address various learning styles (e.g., presentation methods and tools)
topics.definition: Training program development turns needs into structured instruction: writing measurable learning objectives, selecting content, methods and media for different learners, creating lesson plans, instructor guides, trainee materials and job aids, and piloting the course. ADDIE (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation) is the common instructional design model.
topics.easy: Decide exactly what learners must be able to do at the end, then build lessons, activities and materials that get them there - using pictures, talk, reading and hands-on practice so everyone can learn.
points: ADDIE: Analyze (needs, audience) → Design (objectives, assessments, sequence, methods) → Develop (materials, lesson plans, media, pilot) → Implement (deliver) → Evaluate (formative during, summative after).
Learning objectives (ABCD): Audience, Behavior (observable action verb), Condition, Degree (criterion). Avoid 'understand', 'know', 'be aware'.
Bloom's taxonomy (cognitive, low to high): Remember → Understand → Apply → Analyze → Evaluate → Create. Psychomotor and affective domains also exist.
Lesson plan contents: objectives, materials, time, content outline, activities, assessment, instructor notes - standardizes delivery and avoids omitting critical material.
Materials: instructor guide, participant workbook/handouts, job aids (checklists, flowcharts used on the job), visual aids, simulations, case studies.
Presentation design: 6 × 6 rule (about six lines, six words), large readable fonts, one idea per slide, images over text; lighting, room layout (U-shape for discussion), background noise low.
Accommodate diversity: literacy levels, language, generations (Gen Z prefers technology-based, interactive, short content), disabilities (captions, large print, audio description, braille), culture.
Pilot course with a representative sample to test content, timing and methods before full rollout; ethics - copyright/trademark compliance, test security, fairness and confidentiality.
topics.example: A plant needs confined-space attendant training. The developer writes the objective: 'Given a gas meter and entry permit, the attendant will verify atmospheric readings and record them with 100% accuracy.' The course combines a short lecture, a video of a real incident, a hands-on gas meter station and a mock rescue drill, and is piloted with one crew before rollout.
tips: Good objectives are measurable and observable.
Lesson plans standardize the presentation.
Applying a formula in a new situation = Bloom's 'Apply'; designing a new program = 'Create'.
Pilot with a representative sample of the real audience.
topics.yates: Ch. 19 Training, p. 483
subs: Training materials

Training materials are the lesson plans, slides, handouts, manuals, videos, job aids and assessments produced in the Develop phase of ADDIE. They must be accurate, current, job-specific and written at the audience's literacy level.
Develop phase outputs: lesson plans, slides, study guides, quizzes, case studies, videos, handouts.
ANSI Z490.1: materials should be clear, relevant and tied to measurable learning objectives.
Job aids (checklists, pictograms, flowcharts) support performance on the job after training.
Review and update materials after incidents, regulation changes and MOC.
'Creating quizzes and handouts' = Develop phase, not Design.
Learning styles
Learners differ in how they prefer to take in information; the VARK model groups them as visual, auditory, reading/writing and kinesthetic. Training should use a blend so every learner is reached.
VARK: Visual, Auditory, Reading/writing, Kinesthetic (detailed under 7.6).

The guide also lists expanded learner types: stress (learn under pressure), ease (calm settings), scribble (writing notes), trust (authority figures), teach (teaching others), copy (imitating models).
Kolb styles: diverging, assimilating, converging, accommodating.
Research gives limited support to matching instruction to a single preferred style; multimodal delivery is the safe design choice.
Best answer for a mixed workforce: use multiple methods/modalities, not one style.
Presentation methods
Presentation methods are how content is delivered: lecture, demonstration, discussion, case study, role play, drill and simulation. The method should match the objective and learning domain.
Knowledge (cognitive) objectives: lecture, reading, discussion, quizzes.
Skill (psychomotor) objectives: demonstration then supervised practice, drills, simulation.
Attitude (affective) objectives: case studies, testimonials, discussion, leadership example.
Adults disengage in theory-heavy lectures - add real examples and hands-on exercises.
Hands-on skill (SCBA donning, extinguisher use) cannot be verified by lecture or written test - choose demonstration and practice.
Training tools
Training tools are the aids and technology used to deliver and reinforce learning, from simple job aids to simulators.
Examples: projectors/slides, videos, props and actual equipment, mock-ups, LMS, VR/AR, simulators, polling/quiz apps, job aids.
Use real equipment or close mock-ups for skill training.
An LMS tracks completion, scores and due dates for records.
Engagement features: polls or quizzes every 10-15 minutes, short case studies, video clips of 2 minutes or less.
ADDIE instructional design model
ADDIE (Analyze, Design, Develop, Implement, Evaluate) is a systematic model for building training. Evaluation feeds back into analysis so the program continuously improves.
Analyze: needs assessment, audience, gaps.
Design: write learning objectives, choose methods, outline structure and schedule.
Develop: create materials, lesson plans, quizzes, videos.
Implement: deliver sessions, pre-assessments, interaction, post-assessments.
Evaluate: feedback surveys, pre vs. post test results, revise the program.
Selecting objectives or methods = Design; creating materials = Develop; delivering = Implement; survey after class = Evaluate.
Learning objectives
Objectives state what the learner will be able to do after training, in observable and measurable terms. They drive content selection and assessment design.
ABCD format: Audience, Behavior (action verb), Condition, Degree (standard).
Example: 'Given a lockout kit, the maintenance technician will apply LOTO to Press 4 following all 6 steps without error.'
Use measurable verbs (demonstrate, calculate, identify) - avoid 'understand', 'know', 'appreciate'.
Assessments must align with objectives (a skill objective needs a performance test).
If an objective cannot be observed or measured, it is poorly written.
Bloom's Taxonomy
A hierarchy of cognitive learning used to write objectives and design assessments, moving from recall up to creating new solutions.
Revised order (low to high): Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create.
Remember: list, define, state (recall exposure limits).
Understand: explain, summarize, interpret (explain the hierarchy of controls).
Apply: use in new situations (solve a fall clearance problem).
Analyze: compare, differentiate, break down (root causes from incident reports).
Evaluate: judge, assess, recommend (critique a fall protection plan). Create: design, develop (design a new safety program).
Recommending improvements = Evaluate; solving exposure calculations = Apply; designing a program = Create.
Domains of learning (cognitive, affective, psychomotor)
Effective safety training addresses the head (knowledge), heart (attitudes and values) and hands (physical skills).
Cognitive: knowledge and mental skills - quizzes, reading, written tests (memorizing exposure limits).
Affective: attitudes, values, motivation - discussions, testimonials, case studies, leadership example (believing PPE is essential).
Psychomotor: physical skill - hands-on practice, drills, simulation (fire extinguisher drills, safe lifting).
Bloom's taxonomy describes levels within the cognitive domain.
Changing a worker's belief that safety rules matter = affective domain.
Learner retention (learning pyramid)
The guide teaches that retention rises as learning moves from passive to active: reading 10%, hearing 20%, seeing 30%, hearing + seeing 50%, saying/talking 70%, saying + doing 90%.
Passive: reading, hearing, seeing. Active: discussing, practicing, teaching others.
Highest retention = talking + doing (role-plays, hands-on drills, teaching peers).
Use for high-risk training (confined space, LOTO): practice and explain-back.
Note: these exact percentages (Dale's Cone / learning pyramid) are not research-validated, but the principle that active learning beats passive learning is well supported.
'Which method gives the highest retention?' = hands-on practice combined with explaining/teaching (talking + doing).
Disequilibrium in training
A deliberate state of cognitive challenge that disrupts what learners currently believe so they must restructure their thinking. Based on Piaget's constructivist theory.
Example: showing real incident case studies where skipping PPE caused severe injury disrupts the belief that shortcuts save time.
Example: VR confined-space emergency simulation forces learners to reconsider procedures.
Benefits: builds critical thinking, helps unlearn unsafe habits, deepens retention by engaging emotion and problem solving.
Presenting an incident that challenges workers' current practices = disequilibrium.
Presentation slide design
Slides should clarify, not decorate. The guide gives practical rules for count, visuals, fonts, color and density.
Count: about 25-30 slides for 60 minutes; 8-12 for a 15-20 minute session.
Visuals: a relevant image or diagram every 2-3 slides; use pictograms (e.g., GHS) rather than text descriptions.
Fonts: sans-serif; titles 28-32 pt or larger, body text 20-24 pt or larger, footnotes at least 16 pt.
Contrast: dark on light or light on dark; avoid red-green combinations (color blindness).
6 x 6 rule: max 6 lines, max 6 words per line; bullets not sentences; one key idea per slide.
Accessibility: readable on small screens, alt text for shared slides, consistent templates.
Presentation-effectiveness answers emphasize clarity, engagement and less text/more practice.
mcq: A training designer is choosing between videos, role-plays, and e-learning modules to meet the course objectives. Which ADDIE phase applies?
Analyze
Design
Implement
Evaluate
In Design, objectives are written and instructional strategies and delivery methods are selected. Producing the actual materials comes later, in Develop.
While developing a chemical-safety course, you complete the ADDIE Analysis phase by reviewing incidents caused by chemical mishandling. What is the NEXT step?
Design the program, writing objectives focused on safe handling and emergency procedures
Deliver the training to a small group to test its effectiveness
Evaluate feedback from past sessions on similar topics
Document the training process for reporting purposes
ADDIE runs Analyze, Design, Develop, Implement, Evaluate. After Analysis comes Design (objectives, strategy). A pilot delivery happens only after materials are developed.
A course team is creating handouts, slides, and quizzes from an approved course outline. Which ADDIE phase is this?
Analyze
Design
Develop
Evaluate
Develop is where the actual training materials (handouts, slides, job aids, tests) are produced to match the design.
What is the primary purpose of conducting a pilot class during course development?
To give the primary instructors a break
To test the course materials and delivery methods before full rollout
To finalize the annual training schedule
To increase the course length
A pilot is a trial run with a representative audience so content, timing, materials, and methods can be corrected before the course is delivered widely.
Which document is used to standardize a presentation so that different instructors deliver the same content and no critical material is omitted?
Enabling objectives
Evaluation forms
Slide deck
Lesson plan
A lesson plan lays out objectives, content sequence, methods, timing, and assessments so delivery is consistent across instructors and sessions.
The 6 x 6 rule for presentation slides means:
A maximum of about 6 lines per slide and 6 words per line
6 slides per topic and 6 colors per slide
6 points for each question
6 slides every 6 minutes
The 6 x 6 guideline limits text density to prevent cognitive overload; slides should support the speaker, not replace them.
A training objective states: 'Trainees will calculate the required ventilation rate for a solvent storage room.' Which level of Bloom's taxonomy does this objective target?
Remember
Understand
Apply
Create
Using a learned procedure or formula in a new situation is Apply. Remember would be 'list' or 'state'; Create would be 'design a new system'.
When designing training materials for a workforce with mixed literacy levels and learning preferences, the trainer should:
Use technical language to convey expertise
Assume all participants read at the same level
Incorporate varied instructional strategies (visuals, demonstrations, discussion, plain-language text)
Remove all text and rely only on pictures
Varied methods reach visual, auditory, reading/writing, and kinesthetic learners and different literacy levels. Removing all text is an overcorrection.
What is the role of job aids in a training program?
To test trainees' knowledge at the end of the course
To introduce new theories unrelated to the course
To provide feedback to the instructor
To help trainees apply the skills learned to their daily tasks
Job aids (checklists, flowcharts, pocket cards) support correct performance on the job and reduce reliance on memory, especially for infrequent or critical tasks.
Which of the following is NOT an essential component of a comprehensive lesson plan?
Detailed marketing strategy for the course
Trainee materials such as handouts and job aids
Clear, measurable learning objectives
Methods for assessment and evaluation
Lesson plans contain objectives, content, methods, materials, and assessment. Marketing is not part of instructional design. Watch for the NOT.

topics.title: Continuous Improvement of Training
topics.bp: Describe how to implement training programs utilizing the Continuous Improvement model
topics.definition: Continuous improvement applies the PDCA (Plan-Do-Check-Act) cycle to training: plan the program, deliver it, check results through evaluation data, and act on findings to revise content, methods and delivery - so training stays current, effective and aligned with organizational goals.
topics.easy: Training is never 'done'. Deliver it, measure whether it worked, fix what didn't, and run it again better. Keep updating it when equipment, rules or incidents change.
points: PDCA for training: Plan (needs, objectives, design) → Do (deliver, pilot) → Check (evaluate: reactions, test scores, observations, incident trends) → Act (revise content, retrain, update materials, standardize improvements).
Formative evaluation: during development and delivery (pilot feedback, module checks) to improve. Summative evaluation: after completion, judges overall effectiveness.
Triggers for revision: new regulations/standards, MOC (new equipment or processes), incident investigations showing knowledge gaps, audit findings, poor evaluation results, learner feedback.

Implementation success factors: management support, alignment with organizational goals and culture, clear objectives, scheduling to minimize production impact (opportunity cost), resources (rooms, equipment, trainers), records.
Feedback loops: post-training reports, interim reports, trainer debriefs, refresher schedules, lessons learned database.
Remediation: coaching or extra practice for trainees who do not meet objectives (support, not punishment).
topics.example: After a new HazCom course, post-tests average 92%, but on-the-job observations three months later show only 60% of workers can find SDS Section 8 for PPE. The trainer adds a hands-on SDS scavenger hunt and quarterly 10-minute refreshers. The next observation cycle shows 90% proficiency.
tips: Check = evaluate results; Act = make improvements based on them.
Updating course materials should be driven first by current regulations and standards, not cost or popularity.
Formative = during; summative = after.
topics.yates: Ch. 19 Training, p. 483; Ch. 31 Safety Management System (PDCA)
subs: Continuous improvement of training

Training programs are improved through a closed loop: evaluate results, find gaps, revise content and delivery, then re-evaluate. Inputs include incidents, audits, worker feedback, assessment results and regulatory changes.
PDCA applied to training: Plan (needs/objectives), Do (deliver), Check (evaluate), Act (revise).
ADDIE Evaluate phase feeds back into Analyze.
Update triggers: incident or near miss, audit finding, poor test scores, new equipment/MOC, regulation change, worker feedback.
ANSI Z490.1 and ISO 45001 (clause 10.3) both require ongoing evaluation and improvement.
Track trends: repeated errors on the same quiz items signal a content or delivery problem.
If post-training observations show workers still not following a procedure, revise the training and look for non-training causes - do not just repeat the same course.
Kaizen (continuous improvement)
Kaizen is the Japanese philosophy of small, incremental, ongoing improvements made by everyone, rather than large one-time projects.
Guide's Kaizen cycle: make problems visible -> develop countermeasures -> determine root cause (5 Whys, fishbone) -> hypothesize solution -> test (pilot) -> implement -> standardize work.
Safety uses: employee improvement suggestions, near-miss learning, incremental ergonomic adjustments, continuous refinement of training.
Links to Domain 2 (culture, SMS), Domain 3 (risk controls) and Domain 7 (training effectiveness).
Employees proposing small weekly safety improvements = Kaizen.
Poka-yoke (error-proofing)
Poka-yoke, from Shigeo Shingo and the Toyota Production System, designs processes so errors cannot happen or are immediately obvious - reducing reliance on human memory and training alone.
Examples: plug that fits only one way, red/green scaffold tags, interlocked machine guards, keyed LOTO systems where keys cannot be removed until isolation is complete.
Benefits listed: preventing errors, waste reduction, cost reduction, satisfied customers, competitive advantage.
Two types: control (prevents the error) and warning (signals the error).
Aligns with prevention through design and the hierarchy of controls.
'Prevent errors through design rather than relying on training' = poka-yoke.
Learning curves
A learning curve plots practice or time against performance. CSPs use it to judge training effectiveness, plan refresher training and predict performance.
Positive accelerating: slow start, then rapid improvement (SCBA use).
Negative accelerating (diminishing returns): rapid early gains, then levels off (basic PPE).
S-curve (sigmoid): slow -> fast -> slow (confined space entry skills).
Plateau: improvement stops (lack of challenge, motivation or poor methods).
Declining: performance drops from disuse or poor transfer = skill decay - fix with refreshers and drills.
'Fast initial learning then plateau' = negative accelerating; 'slow, fast, slow' = S-curve.
Refresher training and skill decay
Skills that are rarely used decay over time, so periodic refreshers, drills and practice are scheduled to keep competence current.
Emergency skills (evacuation, rescue, spill response) decay fastest because they are rarely used - drill them regularly.
Retraining triggers (forklift example, 1910.178): unsafe operation, incident or near miss, poor evaluation, new truck type, changed workplace conditions.
Spaced repetition and short refreshers outperform a single long session.
Positive safety culture and training
Training only changes behavior when the culture supports it: open communication, psychological safety and emotionally intelligent leadership.
Open feedback: toolbox talks, anonymous reporting, leaders walking the floor and listening.
Psychological safety: workers can report hazards, admit mistakes and suggest ideas without fear of retaliation.
Emotional intelligence components: self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy, social skills.
Building culture: lead by example, involve workers (committees), recognize safe behavior, share investigation results, give continuous feedback.
Workers feel safe to report without fear = psychological safety; recognizing and managing emotions = emotional intelligence.
Training records and program review
Documentation supports compliance, competency tracking and improvement decisions.
ANSI Z490.1 records: trainee name/ID, course title, date, duration, trainer, assessment results, content/outline.
Use LMS or competency matrix data to spot overdue training and recurring weak topics.
Periodic program audits verify that training still matches hazards, regulations and job tasks.
mcq: During the pilot of a new course, the trainer collects feedback at the end of each module and revises the materials before full rollout. This is an example of:
Summative evaluation
Formative evaluation
Kirkpatrick Level 4 evaluation
Needs assessment
Formative evaluation occurs during development or delivery to improve the program; summative evaluation judges the finished program afterwards.
A company updates its safety courses after every incident review so that lessons learned are built into the next delivery. Which concept is demonstrated?
Risk perception
Pedagogical review
Behavioral control
Continuous improvement of training
Feeding incident findings and evaluation data back into course content is the continuous improvement loop (Plan-Do-Check-Act) applied to training.
Which principle focuses on small, continuous, incremental improvements rather than major overhauls?
Kaizen
Poka-yoke
Kirkpatrick model
Andragogy
Kaizen means continuous incremental improvement. Poka-yoke is mistake-proofing; Kirkpatrick is an evaluation model; andragogy is adult learning theory.
What is the primary goal of remediation in a training program?
To discipline trainees who did not meet the standard
To provide additional instruction and support so trainees can meet the learning objectives
To evaluate a trainee's future potential in the organization
To reduce the training time allocated to each trainee
Remediation closes individual learning gaps with targeted re-instruction and practice, then reassesses. It is corrective, not punitive.
What is the primary purpose of a post-training report?
To replace safety incident reports
To document only the employees who failed
To summarize key outcomes, attendance, and effectiveness of the training
To provide legal protection against employee complaints
A post-training report records what was delivered, who attended, and how effective it was; this data drives the next improvement cycle.
Which of the following is NOT typically included in an interim training report?
Participant feedback on training progress
Completion status of employees in training
Details of an unrelated accident investigation
Adjustments made to content based on participant understanding
Interim reports track progress, feedback, and mid-course adjustments. Unrelated incident details do not belong. Note the NOT.
A training coordinator applies the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle to a fall protection course. Comparing post-training field observation data against the course objectives occurs in which phase?
Plan
Do
Check
Act
Check is measuring results against objectives. Act is the next step: standardizing what worked or revising the course based on what Check found.
Post-training audits show workers pass the lockout/tagout quiz but often skip the zero-energy verification step in the field. What is the BEST continuous improvement action?
Determine why the step is being skipped, revise the training to include hands-on verification practice and supervisor follow-up, then re-measure field performance
Make the written quiz harder
Repeat the same course for all employees
Remove the verification step from the procedure

Passing a knowledge test without transfer to the job signals a gap in practice or reinforcement. Improve the program based on root cause and verify with Level 3 observation. Repeating unchanged training is the trap.
Which event should MOST directly trigger a review and update of an existing training program?
The trainer's annual vacation schedule
A request for new classroom furniture
A change in the color scheme of the company logo
Introduction of new equipment or a process change under Management of Change
New equipment, processes, hazards, regulations, or incident findings change required competencies, so MOC should include training review. Z490.1 also calls for periodic program review.
In a continuous improvement model of training, results from the ADDIE Evaluate phase should be used primarily to:
Archive the course permanently once evaluation is complete
Rank trainers for compensation purposes only
Justify removing all refresher training
Feed back into analysis and revise the design, materials, and delivery of the program
ADDIE is cyclic when used for continuous improvement: evaluation findings feed back into analysis and every other phase. Treating evaluation as the end point is the trap.

topics.title: Training Effectiveness Evaluation
topics.bp: Determine the effectiveness of training programs (e.g., surveys, on-the-job compliance, feedback, assessments, demonstrations, quizzes)
topics.definition: Training effectiveness evaluation determines whether training achieved its objectives and produced the intended changes in knowledge, behavior and organizational results. The Kirkpatrick four-level model (with Phillips' fifth level, ROI) is the standard framework.
topics.easy: Did they like it, did they learn it, do they use it on the job, and did it make the workplace safer? Measure each level, not just the end-of-class survey.
points: Kirkpatrick Level 1 Reaction (smile sheets, surveys); Level 2 Learning (pre-/post-tests, quizzes, demonstrations); Level 3 Behavior (on-the-job observation, compliance audits, supervisor feedback - usually weeks/months later); Level 4 Results (fewer incidents, lower costs, quality); Phillips Level 5 ROI (monetary benefit vs cost).
Pre-test establishes baseline knowledge; post-test measures learning gained. Delayed post-tests measure retention.
Demonstrations and return demonstrations are the best way to assess psychomotor skills; written tests assess knowledge.
Assessment quality: validity (measures what it is supposed to), reliability (consistent results), standardized administration, scoring rubrics, test security.
Questionnaires: mix of closed-ended (quantifiable) and open-ended (insight) questions; Likert scales measure attitudes.
Quantitative indicators: employees trained vs scheduled, pass rates, incident rate trends; qualitative: feedback, observations.
Self-assessment encourages reflection; 360-degree feedback gathers input from multiple perspectives.
topics.example: After forklift refresher training, Level 1 surveys show high satisfaction and Level 2 tests average 94%. Three months later, supervisors observe that 97% of operators perform complete pre-use inspections (Level 3), and forklift damage incidents fall by 40% in the next year (Level 4), saving $60,000 against a $15,000 program cost (Level 5 ROI = 300%).
tips: Observing behavior on the job after training = Kirkpatrick Level 3.
Pre- and post-tests measure learning (Level 2).
For practical skills, the BEST evaluation is observation/demonstration, not a written test.
The most persuasive argument to management is a cost-benefit comparison of training cost with injury cost.
topics.yates: Ch. 19 Training, p. 483
subs: Surveys
Post-training surveys and reaction forms measure participant satisfaction, engagement and perceived relevance - Kirkpatrick Level 1.
Tools: feedback forms (smile sheets), focus groups, interviews.
Useful for improving delivery, pacing and materials.
Does NOT prove learning or behavior change.
Follow-up surveys of supervisors weeks later can provide Level 3 (behavior) evidence.
A high satisfaction score does not show the training worked - it is the weakest level of evidence.
Compliance
Compliance measures whether required training was completed on time and whether workers follow the trained procedures on the job.
Training compliance: percent of required training completed, overdue refreshers, certifications current.
Behavioral compliance: observed adherence to procedures (LOTO audits, PPE use) - Kirkpatrick Level 3.
OSHA citations or audit findings tied to training gaps are lagging evidence.
100% course completion is an activity measure, not proof of effectiveness.
Feedback
Feedback flows in both directions: trainees and supervisors give feedback on the training, and trainers give learners feedback on their performance.
Sources: participant comments, supervisor observations, incident and near-miss data, audit results.
Timely, specific feedback during practice improves skill acquisition.
Feedback is an input to continuous improvement of the program (7.3).
Assessments
Assessments measure whether learning objectives were achieved, usually through pre- and post-tests or performance evaluations - Kirkpatrick Level 2.
Pre-test establishes baseline; post-test shows gain (learning gain = post - pre).
Must be valid (measures the objective) and reliable (consistent results).
Knowledge objectives: written tests; skill objectives: performance-based assessment.
Example: pre-test average 55%, post-test 85% = 30-point gain in knowledge.
Demonstrations
Learners physically perform the task while a qualified evaluator observes against a checklist; the best way to verify psychomotor skills.
Required by many standards: forklift operator practical evaluation (1910.178(l)), respirator donning and seal check, fall protection equipment inspection.
Teach-back or show-me demonstrations prove competency better than written tests.
Use an observation checklist with pass/fail criteria.
Verifying a hands-on skill = demonstration/performance evaluation, not a written quiz.
Quizzes
Short knowledge checks during or after training that measure recall and understanding and reinforce learning.
Cognitive domain, Kirkpatrick Level 2.
Spacing quizzes through a session (every 10-15 minutes) maintains engagement.
Item analysis: questions many learners miss reveal unclear content or poor items.
Quizzes alone cannot verify skills or on-the-job behavior.
Kirkpatrick's four levels of training evaluation
A four-level model for evaluating training beyond the classroom: Reaction, Learning, Behavior, Results.
Level 1 Reaction: satisfaction and engagement - surveys, feedback forms.
Level 2 Learning: knowledge/skill gained - pre/post tests, quizzes, demonstrations.
Level 3 Behavior: application on the job - observations, supervisor feedback, performance reviews.
Level 4 Results: organizational outcomes - incident rate reduction, cost savings, compliance, productivity.
Phillips adds Level 5 ROI: (monetary benefits - training costs) / costs x 100.
Higher levels are harder and costlier to measure but give stronger evidence.
On-the-job application = Behavior (Level 3); accident reduction = Results (Level 4); satisfaction = Reaction (Level 1).
Training ROI and outcome measures
Training effectiveness can be expressed in business terms by comparing the monetary benefits of improved safety outcomes with program costs.
ROI (%) = (net benefits / costs) x 100.
Example: training costs $20,000; avoided injury costs $50,000; ROI = (50,000 - 20,000) / 20,000 x 100 = 150%.
Outcome measures: incident/TRIR trend, near-miss reporting rate, observed safe-behavior percentage, audit scores.
Isolate training effects from other changes (new equipment, staffing) when attributing results.
mcq: Which of the following lists Kirkpatrick's four levels of training evaluation in the correct order?
Reaction, Learning, Behavior, Results
Learning, Reaction, Results, Behavior
Reaction, Behavior, Learning, Results
Behavior, Reaction, Results, Learning
Level 1 Reaction (satisfaction), Level 2 Learning (knowledge/skill gained), Level 3 Behavior (on-the-job transfer), Level 4 Results (organizational outcomes).
You will measure the impact of a hazardous materials handling course with tests. What is the MOST effective use of pre-tests and post-tests?
Give both tests after training and compare scores with industry standards
Give a pre-test to establish prior knowledge and a post-test to measure knowledge gained
Use only a post-test to save time
Skip the pre-test so low scorers are not demotivated
Comparing pre-test and post-test scores isolates what was learned during training (Kirkpatrick Level 2). A post-test alone cannot show improvement.
Workers complete post-training surveys rating their satisfaction with the course and trainer. Which Kirkpatrick level is this?
Reaction
Learning
Behavior
Results
Satisfaction surveys (smile sheets) measure Level 1 Reaction. They are easy to collect but do not prove learning or behavior change.
Supervisors check whether workers apply PPE procedures correctly on the job several weeks after training. Which Kirkpatrick level is this?
Level 1 - Reaction
Level 2 - Learning
Level 3 - Behavior
Level 4 - Results
Observing on-the-job application measures Level 3 Behavior (transfer of training). Level 4 would be outcomes such as fewer injuries.
After a training program, the organization records a 40% reduction in recordable incidents. This outcome corresponds to which Kirkpatrick level?
Reaction
Learning
Behavior
Results
Organizational outcomes such as reduced incidents, costs, or downtime are Level 4 Results.
Six months after a program, the company calculates that reduced injury costs returned $3 for every $1 spent on training. Which evaluation level is this?
Kirkpatrick Level 1 - Reaction
Kirkpatrick Level 2 - Learning
Kirkpatrick Level 3 - Behavior
Phillips Level 5 - Return on Investment
Converting results into monetary benefit versus cost is Phillips Level 5 (ROI), which extends Kirkpatrick's four levels. ROI = (3 - 1)/1 = 200%.
A written test for forklift operators consists mostly of questions about company history. Operators who score well still drive unsafely. What is the main problem with the test?
It has low reliability
It has low validity: it does not measure what it is intended to measure
It is too short
It was not timed
Validity means the test measures the intended competency. Reliability is consistency of results; a test can be reliable yet invalid.
What is the MOST effective way to evaluate job performance change following a safety training course?
Rely on participant self-assessment
Compare incident rates before and after training
Observe workers performing their tasks and provide feedback
Administer a written test immediately after training
Direct observation measures actual behavior change. Incident rates are lagging and influenced by many factors; a written test measures learning, not performance.
When designing a questionnaire to evaluate training, which type of questions gathers the most comprehensive feedback?
Open-ended questions only
Questions that focus solely on the trainer's performance
A mix of open-ended and closed-ended questions
Yes/no questions only
Closed-ended items (e.g., rating scales) give quantifiable, comparable data; open-ended items explain why. Together they give a complete picture.
A CSP must verify that newly trained powered industrial truck operators are competent before they operate independently. Which evaluation method BEST meets this need?
A practical performance evaluation of each operator in the workplace by a qualified evaluator
A post-course satisfaction survey
A written quiz on forklift terminology
A signed attendance roster

For skill-based tasks, competence is verified by demonstration; OSHA 1910.178(l) requires formal instruction, practical training, and evaluation of operator performance in the workplace. Attendance and quizzes do not prove skill.

topics.title: Education and Training Methods
topics.bp: Demonstrate working knowledge of education and training methods and techniques (e.g., classroom, online, simulation, computer-based, Artificial Intelligence, coaching, on-the-job training)
topics.definition: Training methods are the delivery approaches used to transfer knowledge and skills. The best method depends on objectives (knowledge vs skill), audience, risk, frequency of the task, resources and logistics. Blended learning combines several methods.
topics.easy: Pick the method that matches what people must be able to do. Facts can be taught online; hands-on skills need practice; rare, high-risk tasks need realistic simulation and drills.
points: Classroom/instructor-led: interaction, questions, discussion; costly to schedule; lecture alone is passive - add activities.
Online/e-learning: synchronous (live webinar, real-time) vs asynchronous (self-paced, any time - good for dispersed workers and schedules); consistent content, tracking in an LMS.

Computer-based training (CBT) and adaptive/AI-driven learning: personalizes pace and content to learner performance; virtual and augmented reality for immersive hazard recognition; AI tutors and chatbots - require content validation and human oversight.
Simulation and drills: realistic practice without real consequences - best for high-risk, low-frequency tasks (rescue, emergency response, crane operation simulators).
On-the-job training (OJT): job instruction training four-step method - prepare the worker, present the operation, try-out performance, follow up; mentoring and apprenticeships.
Coaching: one-on-one guidance and feedback to improve performance; also used for remediation.

Other techniques: case studies (real consequences, analysis), role play, brainstorming (generate many ideas without critique), fishbowl, tabletop exercises, toolbox talks (short, specific topic), games, micro-learning.

Facilitation skills: establish objectives, encourage participation from all, handle disruptive participants privately/politely, correct misinformation tactfully, manage conflict by finding common ground, read body language (kinesics) for disengagement.
topics.example: A company must train 600 dispersed field technicians on electrical hazard awareness and 20 rescue-team members on confined-space rescue. It uses an asynchronous e-learning module with knowledge checks for the technicians, and quarterly hands-on simulated rescues in a training vault with debriefs for the rescue team.
tips: High-risk, rarely performed tasks → simulation/drills.
Self-paced LMS module = asynchronous.
Four-step OJT: prepare, present, perform (try out), follow up.
Blended learning = online + classroom + hands-on.
topics.yates: Ch. 19 Training, p. 483
subs: Classroom (instructor-led) training
A facilitator delivers training in person, allowing high interaction and real-time feedback.
Best for: small groups, discussions, live demonstrations, drills, complex or high-hazard topics.
Strengths: immediate questions and feedback, trainer can adjust to audience.
Limits: limited scalability, travel/time costs, depends on trainer quality.
Toolbox talks/tailgate meetings are short informal instructor-led sessions focused on one topic.
In-person, hands-on facilitation for small groups = instructor-based learning.
Online (e-learning and virtual) training
Web-based training is often self-paced (asynchronous); virtual/blended learning mixes live instructor sessions with online content.
E-learning: flexible, scalable, cost-effective, consistent; lower engagement if not interactive.
Virtual/blended: live virtual classroom with Q&A plus online modules - needs reliable technology.
ANSI/ASSP Z490.2 = accepted practices for e-learning in SH&E training.
Online alone is insufficient where hands-on evaluation is required (forklift, respirator fit, fire extinguisher).
'Self-paced, online, recorded' = e-learning; 'live + online together' = virtual/blended.
Simulation
Simulation recreates a hazardous or rare situation so learners can practice safely - from tabletop exercises and drills to VR and full-scale simulators.
Examples: VR confined-space entry, crane or vehicle simulators, mock spill drills, emergency tabletop exercises.
Allows practice of high-consequence, low-frequency events without real exposure.
Engages psychomotor and decision-making skills; supports disequilibrium learning.
Computer-based training (CBT)
Training delivered through software on a computer or device, often with interactive modules, branching scenarios and built-in quizzes.
Consistent message, learner-paced, automatic record keeping through an LMS.
Good for awareness and knowledge topics (HazCom, policies) and refreshers.
Must include a way to ask a knowledgeable person questions when required (e.g., OSHA expects access to a qualified trainer for questions).
Weakness: little skill practice, easy to click through without learning.
AI-enabled training
Artificial intelligence personalizes training paths and adapts difficulty using learner data.
AI-personalized learning: adaptive quizzes that adjust difficulty to performance.
Adaptive learning systems: dynamically change pace and content.
Other emerging modalities: VR immersive training, social learning platforms (peer forums, group projects).
Issues: data privacy, accuracy of AI-generated content (must be reviewed by a qualified person), access to technology.
Coaching and mentoring
One-on-one guidance from an experienced worker, supervisor or safety professional to develop skills and safe behavior over time.
Coaching: short-term, task/performance focused, gives specific feedback (e.g., after BBS observations).
Mentoring: longer-term development relationship.
Uses adult learning principle of experience; experienced workers sharing lessons learned.
Effective for transferring tacit knowledge and reinforcing training on the job.
On-the-job training (OJT)
Training performed at the actual work location using real equipment, under supervision of a skilled trainer.
Job Instruction Training four steps: prepare the worker -> present (tell and show) -> try-out performance -> follow up.
Highly job-relevant with high transfer to work.
Risks: inconsistent content, bad habits passed on, exposure during learning - use a structured checklist and qualified trainer.
Often combined with classroom theory (e.g., forklift = formal instruction + practical training + evaluation).
Selecting the training method
Method choice depends on the objective, learning domain, audience, hazard level, number of trainees, cost and available technology.
Knowledge for large dispersed groups: e-learning/CBT.
High-risk skills: instructor-led demonstration + hands-on practice + simulation.
Attitudes/culture: discussions, case studies, leadership involvement.
Blended approaches usually give the best results.
Match method to objective: you cannot certify a hands-on skill with an online module alone.
mcq: A company introduces an AI-driven adaptive e-learning platform for HazCom refresher training. What is the PRIMARY advantage of adaptive learning?
It adjusts content and pace to each learner's demonstrated knowledge, focusing time on weak areas
It removes the need for any instructor oversight
It guarantees regulatory compliance automatically
It eliminates the need for hands-on training
Adaptive (AI-based) systems personalize the path based on learner performance. They still require human oversight, content validation, and practical skills verification.
You are developing a blended learning program for confined space entry. Which combination BEST exemplifies a blended approach?
Printed handouts and a classroom lecture only
A live webinar only
On-the-job mentoring only
An online self-paced module, an in-person session, and a hands-on field exercise
Blended learning combines online and face-to-face methods, and for a high-hazard task it should include hands-on practice. Single-method options are not blended.
A safety manager wants to roll out an electrical hazard awareness course without requiring all employees to attend at the same time. Which delivery method is asynchronous?
A live, instructor-led webinar
A scheduled group discussion in the break room
An in-person demonstration at the jobsite
A self-paced e-learning module available on the LMS at any time
